She gave a sober view: costs, risks, and how long profit might take. The boys went quiet, then started again, more carefully. A sober person is not drunk, and a sober judgement is not drunk on excitement either. So, what word describes a calm, realistic assessment?... Sober.
sober.example: A sober look at the club's finances showed that it could not afford a foreign coach for at least two more seasons.

gre.s: After years of wildly optimistic forecasts, the committee's latest report offered a more ____ assessment, acknowledging that the economy might not recover for a decade.
gre.clue: acknowledging that the economy might not recover for a decade

stern.hook: STERN: like the STERN (back) of a ship, firm and unmoving.
stern.story: Stern. Serious, strict and unyielding. Every student at Rosa's school feared the headmaster. He never smiled in the corridor, and one stern look could silence a whole classroom. But when Rosa's father lost his job, it was this stern man who quietly paid her school fees for two years and told nobody. Rosa learned it only on her last day. Picture a stern captain standing at the stern of his ship, unmoving while the waves crash. So, what word describes someone serious and strict, who rarely smiles?... Stern.
stern.example: The referee gave the captain a stern warning, and for the rest of the match nobody dared to argue with a single decision.

gre.s: Behind the judge's ____ exterior, which intimidated many lawyers, lay a deeply compassionate person.
gre.clue: which intimidated many lawyers

subjective.hook: SUBJECTIVE: depends on the SUBJECT, the person judging.
subjective.story: Subjective. Shaped by personal feelings and tastes, not by facts. Joe from the old city and Rita from the port town have argued for years about the best beef dish. Joe swears by the slow-cooked biryani from his neighbourhood. Rita says nothing beats the spicy beef feast of her home town. At their own wedding, they served both, and the guests still argued. The question will never be settled, because taste is subjective. Subjective depends on the subject, the person judging; objective depends on the object itself. So, what word describes a judgement that depends on personal taste?... Subjective.
subjective.example: Pain is partly subjective, so two patients with the same injury may describe it in very different ways.

gre.s: Because judges' scores in the competition are inevitably ____, organizers introduced a panel of five to reduce the influence of any one person's taste.
gre.clue: reduce the influence of any one person's taste

temper.hook: GRE trick: to TEMPER is to TONE DOWN, like tempering spicy food with yogurt.
temper.story: Temper. To make something milder or less extreme. When Ryan found a fresh dent in his new motorbike, he was furious with his younger brother and began shouting. Their mother stepped between them. She reminded Ryan, gently, of the time he had crashed their father's bicycle into a pond. Ryan went quiet, then almost smiled. Her words had tempered his anger. Temper shares its root with temperate and temperature: to temper something is to bring it to a moderate heat. So, what verb means to soften or tone something down?... Temper.
temper.example: Grandfather tempered his strict rules with generous helpings of sweets, so the children never stayed angry with him for long.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the committee's harsh conclusions, the chair added a paragraph acknowledging the team's genuine achievements under difficult conditions.
gre.clue: acknowledging the team's genuine achievements

thorough.story: Thorough. Complete, with attention to every detail. The week before the holiday, Anna's mother cleans the whole house. She wipes every fan blade, scrubs behind every cupboard, washes the curtains, and even dusts the tops of the door frames. Anna once tried to hide a little dust under a rug. Her mother lifted the rug at once. Nothing escapes such a thorough cleaning. Thorough was once simply a spelling of through: a thorough person goes through everything. So, what word describes work complete in every detail?... Thorough.
thorough.example: Before buying the secondhand car, Imtiaz asked a mechanic to do a thorough check of the brakes, engine, and wiring.

gre.s: Unlike the hasty earlier investigation, the new inquiry was ____, interviewing every witness and examining every document.
gre.clue: interviewing every witness and examining every document

token.hook: TOKEN: just a symbolic gesture, like a TOKEN coin.
token.story: Token. Done only for appearance; also, a symbol or sign. Every year, as the river ate away more of their village, families begged for a proper embankment. One morning, an official arrived with photographers, planted a single sapling on the riverbank, smiled for the cameras, and drove away. No embankment came. Even the sapling was soon washed away. It had been a token gesture. A token coin stands in for real money, and a token gesture stands in for real action. So, what word describes an action done only for show?... Token.
token.example: The landlord made a token repair, painting over the damp patch on the wall without fixing the leaking pipe behind it.

gre.s: The government's ____ efforts at reform, which changed a few official titles but left the corrupt system entirely untouched, fooled no one.
gre.clue: changed a few official titles but left the corrupt system entirely untouched

unprecedented.hook: UN-PRECEDENT-ED: no PRECEDENT, never happened before.
unprecedented.story: Unprecedented. Never done or known before. For generations, Vanessa's family crossed the mighty river by ferry, often waiting for hours at the landing in heat or fog. In June twenty twenty-two, the great bridge opened, and her father drove to the capital without a ferry for the first time in his life. He kept saying it was unprecedented. A precedent is an earlier example to follow; something unprecedented has no earlier example at all. So, what word describes an event that has never happened before?... Unprecedented.
unprecedented.example: The team's run of fourteen straight victories was unprecedented in the league's sixty-year history.

gre.s: The flood was truly ____: in two hundred years of written records, the river had never risen even half as high.
gre.clue: had never risen even half as high

viable.story: Viable. Practical and able to succeed; workable. In the low southern wetlands, fields stay under water for months each year. So farmers there weave water hyacinth into thick floating beds, cover them with mud, and plant vegetables on top. When the water rises, the garden simply rises with it. Visitors are often surprised that a floating garden is a viable way to farm. Viable comes from the French vie, meaning life: a viable plan can live and survive. So, what word describes a plan that can actually work?... Viable.
viable.example: Floating schools built on boats have proved a viable option for children in villages that monsoon floods cut off for months.

gre.s: Although solar power was once dismissed as too expensive, falling costs have made it a ____ alternative to coal in many countries.
gre.clue: falling costs have made it

affinity.hook: AFFINITY: a magnet with INFINITE attraction.
affinity.story: Affinity. A natural liking for someone or something; also, a close similarity. From the age of five, Paige felt a strange affinity for the pigeons on the rooftops of the old city. While other children played below, she sat among the birds, and they landed on her shoulders without fear. Her father, who once kept pigeons too, watched her with quiet pride. The same affinity ran through both of them. Affinity comes from the Latin for a neighbour sharing your border: things with an affinity sit naturally close together. So, what word means a natural pull toward something?... Affinity.
affinity.example: Growing up beside the Padma gave the painter a deep affinity for rivers, which appear in almost every canvas she has made.

gre.s: Despite growing up in different countries, the two composers shared a striking ____, and critics often mistook one's music for the other's.
gre.clue: critics often mistook one's music for the other's

apt.hook: APT: APpropriaTe. Also, APTitude for learning.
apt.story: Apt. Suitable for the situation; also, likely to do something, or quick to learn. The new puppy at Logan's house chewed everything: shoes, cushions, and above all, slippers. Within a week the family had named him Slipper. Everyone agreed it was an apt name. He was also an apt pupil: in two days he learned to sit for a biscuit. Apt shares its Latin root with aptitude, meaning fitted: an apt word fits the situation perfectly. So, what word describes a name that suits its owner exactly?... Apt.
apt.example: Calling the old library the brain of the university was an apt metaphor, since every important idea on campus seemed to start there.

gre.s: The critic's description of the novel as a maze was ____, for readers frequently lost track of which narrator was speaking.
gre.clue: for readers frequently lost track

brook.hook: GRE trick: BROOK isn't just a stream. 'She brooks no nonsense' means she TOLERATES none.
brook.story: Brook. To tolerate or allow, usually used with no or not. At Lauren's family table, her grandmother brooks no waste. Not a single grain of rice may be left on a plate. She grew up in hard years, when rice was precious, and she still remembers the hunger. When Lauren's cousin once pushed his plate away half full, one look from her was enough. She would not brook it. This brook is not a stream: it almost always comes with no, as in she brooks no excuses. So, what verb means to tolerate, usually in the negative?... Brook.
brook.example: The new captain would brook no complaints about early morning training, and he was always first on the field at six.

gre.s: The editor was famous for her exacting standards and would ____ no errors, however minor, in the articles she approved.
gre.clue: famous for her exacting standards

coherent.story: Coherent. Logical and consistent; clear and easy to follow. At three in the morning, Tommy's mother shook him awake to ask where he had put the house keys. Tommy mumbled something about cricket and mangoes, then fell straight back to sleep. Nothing he said was coherent. At breakfast, fully awake, he gave a perfectly coherent answer: the keys were in his jeans pocket. His mother just shook her head. Coherent shares its Latin root with adhere, to stick: in a coherent answer, all the parts stick together. So, what word describes speech that is logical and clear?... Coherent.
coherent.example: After the accident, the shaken bus driver could not give a coherent account of what had happened, so the police waited until morning.

gre.s: The committee's report, written hastily by six authors with conflicting views, failed to present a ____ argument; its chapters frequently contradicted one another.
gre.clue: its chapters frequently contradicted one another

contempt.hook: CONTEMPT: CON + TEMPT; you're not even tempted to respect it.
contempt.story: Contempt. The feeling that someone is worthless or beneath you. At a smart restaurant downtown, a man snapped his fingers at the young waiter, Jamie, and called him stupid for bringing the wrong drink. His voice dripped with contempt. Jamie said nothing. He simply brought the right drink, served the next table with a warm smile, and kept his dignity. Watching, the other diners felt only contempt for the man, not the waiter. In law, contempt of court means treating a judge with open disrespect. So, what word means looking down on someone as worthless?... Contempt.
contempt.example: The old chess master treated quick online games with open contempt, calling them a noisy kind of gambling.

gre.s: Far from offering measured criticism, the reviewer made no attempt to hide her ____ for the film, dismissing it as unworthy of even a single serious paragraph.
gre.clue: dismissing it as unworthy of even a single serious paragraph

derivative.hook: DERIVATIVE: DERIVED from someone else's work.
derivative.story: Derivative. Copied or imitated from others; not original. Cody's band played their first song at a university concert. Friends cheered, but afterwards, an old music teacher said gently, "It sounds like three famous songs stitched together." Cody's face burned. He knew it was true. The song was derivative. So he went home, picked up his guitar, and wrote about his own village and his own mother. That song was nothing but his. Derivative comes from derive: a derivative work is derived from someone else's. So, what word describes art that copies others?... Derivative.
derivative.example: Most of the new cafés in Banani feel derivative, each one copying the same exposed brick, hanging bulbs and avocado toast.

gre.s: Although the young composer's early works were largely ____, borrowing heavily from his teachers, his later symphonies are startlingly original.
gre.clue: borrowing heavily from his teachers

empirical.hook: EMPIRICAL: built on EXPERIENCE and EXPERIMENT, like an EMPIRE built brick by brick.
empirical.story: Empirical. Based on what is actually observed or tested, not on theory alone. Megan's father believed his old fertiliser was the best, because his own father had used it. Megan, an agriculture student, did not argue. She divided one field into two halves, used the old fertiliser on one side and a new one on the other, and weighed every sack of rice at harvest. Her empirical test settled it. Empirical comes from the Greek for experience: empirical knowledge is gained by seeing and testing. So, what word describes evidence gathered by observation and experiment?... Empirical.
empirical.example: The economist's claim was finally tested empirically when researchers tracked the spending of two thousand families over five years.

gre.s: Although the theory was elegant, it lacked ____ support; no one had ever observed the predicted particle in an actual experiment.
gre.clue: no one had ever observed the predicted particle in an actual experiment

feasible.hook: FEASIBLE: is it EASY-ble? If it can be done, it's feasible.
feasible.story: Feasible. Possible and practical to do. Holly wanted to cycle to her office downtown instead of sitting in traffic for two hours. Her friends said city roads were impossible for cycling. So, one Friday, she tested a route through quieter lanes and along the edge of a park, timing herself. Forty minutes, door to door. It was not only possible; it was feasible, and faster than the bus. Feasible comes from the French for doable: a feasible plan is one you can actually do. So, what word describes a plan that is practical and possible?... Feasible.
feasible.example: Digging a metro tunnel beneath the narrow lanes of Old Dhaka may not be feasible, so planners are also studying an elevated route.

gre.s: Engineers concluded that the bridge, though elegant on paper, was not ____ given the region's budget and the instability of its soil.
gre.clue: given the region's budget and the instability of its soil

imminent.hook: IMMINENT: IN a MINute it will happen.
imminent.story: Imminent. About to happen very soon. One April afternoon, the sky over Jenny's village turned the colour of a bruise. The air went still, the birds fell silent, and the smell of dust rose from the fields. A summer storm was imminent. Jenny's mother ran to pull the clothes off the line, shouting for the children to bring in the goats. Minutes later, the wind came roaring. Imminent means hanging over you, ready to fall; do not confuse it with eminent, which means famous. So, what word describes a storm about to break any moment?... Imminent.
imminent.example: With the monsoon imminent, farmers in Bogura worked late into the night to bring in the last of the boro rice.

gre.s: Although officials insisted there was no cause for alarm, residents could see that the dam's collapse was ____, as water was already spilling over its cracked walls.
gre.clue: water was already spilling over its cracked walls

imperative.hook: IMPERATIVE: an IMPERIAL command, must be done.
imperative.story: Imperative. Of vital importance; absolutely essential. When Lucas's high fever turned out to be dengue, the doctor was very clear with his parents. It was imperative that he drink fluids every hour, rest completely, and come back at once if his gums bled. His mother set an alarm and sat by his bed with oral saline through the night. Imperative comes from the same root as emperor and imperial: an imperative is like an emperor's command, which must be obeyed. So, what word describes something absolutely necessary that cannot be ignored?... Imperative.
imperative.example: For astronauts on long missions, daily exercise is imperative, since muscles and bones weaken quickly without gravity.

gre.s: With the river rising by the hour, the engineers considered it ____ that the embankment be reinforced before nightfall; any delay could flood the entire district.
gre.clue: any delay could flood the entire district

indictment.story: Indictment. A formal charge of a serious crime; also, a strong criticism. After just twenty minutes of rain, a main road in the city turned into a brown river. Victor took a photo: a rickshaw puller wading through water up to his waist, pulling a schoolgirl holding her bag above her head. The photo spread everywhere. People called it an indictment of the city's drainage. Indictment hides a silent c, and it shares a root with dictate: an indictment speaks the charge aloud. So, what word means a strong condemnation, or a formal criminal charge?... Indictment.
indictment.example: The empty classrooms in the new school were a silent indictment of the officials who had spent the teachers' salaries on decorations.

gre.s: The report was a damning ____ of the agency's leadership, detailing years of ignored warnings, falsified data, and entirely preventable deaths.
gre.clue: detailing years of ignored warnings

invasive.story: Invasive. Spreading harmfully into new areas; also, intrusive. Abby's grandfather remembers when the village pond was clear enough to see the fish. Then a few plants of water hyacinth floated in. Within two summers, the thick green carpet covered every inch, blocking sunlight and choking the fish below. Water hyacinth first came from South America, and in the delta it is one of the most invasive plants of all. Invasive comes from invade: an invasive plant invades and takes over. So, what word describes something that spreads harmfully into new places?... Invasive.
invasive.example: Lionfish, an invasive species in the Caribbean, eat so many young reef fish that divers are now encouraged to spear them.

gre.s: Ecologists warn that the ____ beetle, introduced accidentally through shipping crates, threatens to wipe out the region's native oaks.
gre.clue: introduced accidentally through shipping crates

manifest.hook: MANIFEST: so obvious it's in your hand (manus).
manifest.story: Manifest. Clearly visible and obvious; as a verb, to show or display. Little Max's love of numbers manifested early. At four, he counted every stair in his building. At six, he added up the grocery bill faster than the shopkeeper, who gave him a free toffee for it. By his tenth birthday, his gift was manifest to everyone who met him. Think of a ship's manifest, the list that makes every piece of cargo plain to see. So, what word describes something clear and obvious to everyone?... Manifest.
manifest.example: Her talent for languages was manifest by the age of six, when she was chatting with tourists in English, Hindi and Arabic.

gre.s: Although the director insisted the project was on schedule, its failure was ____ to everyone else: half the buildings stood unfinished and the funds were gone.
gre.clue: half the buildings stood unfinished and the funds were gone

obsolete.hook: OBSOLETE: 'OBviously SOLD long ago', not sold anymore.
obsolete.story: Obsolete. No longer in use; out of date. Clearing out his grandfather's cupboard, Sean found a shoebox of cassette tapes, a tangle of brown ribbon, and an old Walkman with no batteries. He held one up and asked what it was. His grandfather laughed and told him how he once rewound tapes with a pencil to save the batteries. To Sean, it all looked obsolete, like objects from a museum. Obsolete comes from a Latin verb meaning to wear out with age. So, what word describes technology that nobody uses anymore?... Obsolete.
obsolete.example: Mobile banking has made the old postal money order nearly obsolete, even in the most remote villages of Bangladesh.

gre.s: Within a decade of its introduction, the once-revolutionary device had become ____, displaced by smaller and cheaper alternatives.
gre.clue: displaced by smaller and cheaper alternatives

peculiar.hook: PECULIAR: PECULIAR things are PECULIARLY yours.
peculiar.story: Peculiar. Strange or unusual; also, belonging only to one place or person. When Kelsey first tasted beef cooked with a wild hill lemon at her friend's home in the hills, she paused. The flavour was peculiar: sour, slightly bitter, and wonderfully fragrant all at once. Her friend explained that the fruit, a large bitter citrus, grows mainly in that one region. The dish is peculiar to those hills. Peculiar first meant one's own private property in Latin, so something peculiar belongs to one place alone. So, what word describes something strange, or special to one place only?... Peculiar.
peculiar.example: The sharp smell of drying fish is peculiar to the shutki yards of Cox's Bazar, and visitors notice it long before they see the racks.

gre.s: The custom of exchanging salt as a gift is ____ to the region and is unknown even in neighboring provinces.
gre.clue: unknown even in neighboring provinces

pedestrian.hook: GRE trick: PEDESTRIAN = as dull as plodding along on foot.
pedestrian.story: Pedestrian. Ordinary and dull, with no imagination. Rachel's first essay on her favourite season began, "The year has four seasons. Winter is cold. Winter is nice." Her teacher wrote one word in the margin: pedestrian. So Rachel tried again. She wrote about fog on the pond, steam rising from her mother's rice cakes, and her grandfather's shawl smelling of mustard oil. This time the teacher wrote: beautiful. Ped means foot, as in pedal; a pedestrian walks, and pedestrian writing plods along instead of flying. So, what word describes writing that is dull and unimaginative?... Pedestrian.
pedestrian.example: Her translation was accurate but pedestrian, turning the poet's playful lines into the flat language of a government notice.

gre.s: Although the film's special effects were dazzling, its plot was disappointingly ____, recycling clichés that audiences had seen countless times before.
gre.clue: recycling clichés that audiences had seen countless times before

peripheral.hook: PERIPHERAL: on the PERIMETER, at the edge.
peripheral.story: Peripheral. Of minor importance; also, on the outer edge. Dylan spent his first GRE week making the perfect study space. He bought coloured pens, designed a timetable, decorated his notebook, and arranged his desk lamp just right. On Friday he realised he had not solved a single question. All of it had been peripheral, while the real work sat waiting at the centre. Peripheral comes from the Greek for around, the same peri as in perimeter, the outer edge. So, what word describes things at the edge, not at the heart of the matter?... Peripheral.
peripheral.example: In the court case, the question of who owned the car was peripheral, since the only real issue was who had been driving it.

gre.s: The committee dismissed the objection as ____, since it concerned the project's color scheme rather than its safety or cost.
gre.clue: rather than its safety or cost

plausible.hook: PLAUSIBLE: deserves APPLAUSE for sounding right.
plausible.story: Plausible. Reasonable enough that it might be true. Nick had not finished his assignment. He told his professor that a power cut had lasted all evening and his laptop battery had died. In the city, during a hot summer, that was perfectly plausible, and the professor gave him one more day. But when his classmate claimed a goat had eaten his pen drive, the professor laughed out loud. That excuse was far less plausible. Plausible comes from the Latin for deserving applause: a plausible story sounds good enough to applaud. So, what word describes an explanation that seems believable?... Plausible.
plausible.example: Many scientists find it plausible that comets carried water to the young Earth, though the evidence is still debated.

gre.s: Although the detective's theory was ____ enough to persuade the jury, later DNA evidence showed that the actual sequence of events had been quite different.
gre.clue: enough to persuade the jury

potent.story: Potent. Very powerful; having a strong effect. At a family picnic in the hills, Jay's cousins dared him to bite into a naga chilli straight from the garden. He took a big bite. Seconds later his face turned red, tears streamed from his eyes, and he gulped down a whole jug of water. The naga chilli is among the most potent chillies in the world. Potent shares its root with potential: both are about power. So, what word describes something with a very strong effect?... Potent.
potent.example: A single photograph of a cracked riverbed became a potent symbol of the drought, printed on posters across the country.

gre.s: Though the drug is administered in tiny doses, it is remarkably ____: a single milligram is enough to sedate a full-grown horse.
gre.clue: a single milligram is enough to sedate a full-grown horse

proxy.hook: PROXY: like a PROXY attendance a friend gives for you in class.
proxy.story: Proxy. A person authorised to act for someone else; a substitute. In a big lecture hall, the teacher called the roll. When she said "Steve," a voice from the back called out "Present," though Steve was home asleep. His friend was his proxy. The teacher looked up, smiled, and called Steve's number again, staring straight at the friend. Students call this giving proxy: answering in someone else's place. So, what word means a person who stands in for someone else?... Proxy.
proxy.example: Economists often use satellite images of city lights at night as a proxy for economic activity in countries with poor statistics.

gre.s: Since thermometers did not exist in the Middle Ages, climatologists use the width of tree rings as a ____ for direct temperature records from that period.
gre.clue: Since thermometers did not exist in the Middle Ages

quarantine.hook: QUARANTINE: from Italian 'quaranta', forty days of isolation for ships.
quarantine.story: Quarantine. Forced separation to stop a disease from spreading; as a verb, to separate in this way. When Mark flew home from abroad during a dangerous outbreak, he spent two weeks in quarantine in a single room of his house. His daughter could not hug him, so every evening she pressed a drawing against the window glass, and he pressed his hand against it from inside. The word comes from the Italian for forty: in old Venice, ships from plague ports had to wait forty days before landing. So, what word means isolation to stop a disease spreading?... Quarantine.
quarantine.example: New fish should be quarantined in a separate tank for two weeks before they join the others in the main aquarium.

gre.s: Health officials decided to ____ the entire village after the outbreak, barring anyone from leaving until tests confirmed that the virus was no longer spreading.
gre.clue: barring anyone from leaving

suppress.story: Suppress. To forcibly stop something; to hold back a feeling. During the school's morning assembly, the headmaster was giving a very serious speech. Then a pigeon landed on his head and calmly sat there. Five hundred students bit their lips, stared at their shoes and tried to suppress their laughter. Ellie pressed both hands over her mouth, but a tiny sound escaped. She could not suppress it. Suppress means to press down, from the Latin for pressing under: you press a feeling down until it stays hidden. So, what verb means to hold something back by force?... Suppress.
suppress.example: The company tried to suppress the safety report, but one of its engineers leaked it to a journalist in Khulna.

gre.s: Though the regime tried to ____ news of the protests, reports spread quickly through encrypted messaging apps beyond the reach of state censors.
gre.clue: beyond the reach of state censors

tangible.hook: TANGIBLE: you can TOUCH it (tangere = to touch).
tangible.story: Tangible. Able to be touched; real and definite. For a year, Erin's online fundraiser for a flooded village school was only numbers on a screen. Some days, she wondered if any of it mattered. Then she visited. A new tin roof shone in the sun, children sat at new desks, and books lay dry on the shelves. She ran her hand along a desk. The result was tangible at last. Tangible comes from the Latin for touch, as in tangent, a line that touches a circle. So, what word describes results you can see and touch?... Tangible.
tangible.example: After six months of tutoring, the children's reading scores showed tangible progress, and two of them won places at the district school.

gre.s: Despite years of lofty promises about reform, the government had produced few ____ improvements that ordinary citizens could actually see in their daily lives.
gre.clue: that ordinary citizens could actually see in their daily lives

temporal.hook: TEMPORAL: TEMPORARY earthly things versus eternal spiritual ones.
temporal.story: Temporal. Relating to worldly life rather than spiritual matters; also, relating to time. At a riverside fair, an old folk singer sat with his one-string lute under a banyan tree. Houses, money and fame, he sang, are temporal; they fade like footprints on the riverbank. Only the soul remains. Jordan, who had come to sell phones, stopped and listened until the song ended. Temporal comes from the Latin tempus, time, as in temporary: temporal things belong to this passing time. So, what word describes worldly matters rather than spiritual ones?... Temporal.
temporal.example: Many Sufi teachers urged their followers to look beyond temporal rewards such as wealth and fame toward a life of the spirit.

gre.s: The medieval church claimed authority not only over spiritual life but also over ____ affairs, collecting taxes and settling property disputes like any secular ruler.
gre.clue: collecting taxes and settling property disputes like any secular ruler

trivial.hook: TRIVIAL: like TRIVIA, small unimportant facts.
trivial.story: Trivial. Too small or unimportant to matter. Katie and her sister Lisa stopped speaking for three whole weeks. The reason? Who had eaten the last piece of fish at dinner. Their mother pleaded, their father sighed, and the house felt cold. Finally, Katie bought two plates of street snacks and knocked on Lisa's door. They both wondered how such a trivial fight had lasted so long. Trivial shares its root with trivia: small, unimportant facts. So, what word describes a problem too small to matter?... Trivial.
trivial.example: The two ministers quarrelled over trivial details of the seating plan while the flood relief budget went undiscussed.

gre.s: Although the error seemed ____ at the time, a mere decimal point out of place, it eventually cost the company millions.
gre.clue: it eventually cost the company millions

undermine.hook: UNDER-MINE: digging a MINE UNDER a wall until it collapses.
undermine.story: Undermine. To weaken something gradually or secretly. Every monsoon, the great river eats quietly away at the soil beneath its banks. From above, the land in Hank's village looks solid, green with jute. But below, the river is hollowing it out. One morning, a whole strip of field cracks and slides into the water. The river had undermined it for months. The word began in war: soldiers dug mines under castle walls until the walls fell. So, what verb means to weaken something from beneath, slowly or secretly?... Undermine.
undermine.example: Constant rumors that the coach would be sacked undermined the players' confidence throughout the second half of the season.

gre.s: Critics warned that the new law would ____ judicial independence by allowing politicians to dismiss judges at will.
gre.clue: by allowing politicians to dismiss judges at will

versatile.hook: VERSATILE: works in every VERSE, every situation.
versatile.story: Versatile. Able to do many different things well. Amber's aunt Diane teaches maths at a village school. On weekends, she repairs neighbours' sewing machines, cooks for every family wedding, and coaches the girls' football team. When the school's harmonium player fell ill before a concert, Diane sat down and played it herself. Everyone agreed she was the most versatile person they knew. Versatile comes from the Latin for turning, as in reverse: a versatile person turns easily from one task to another. So, what word describes someone skilled at many different things?... Versatile.
versatile.example: Jute is a versatile fiber, woven into sacks and carpets, pressed into car panels, and even blended into fashionable shirts.

gre.s: The ____ actor, equally convincing as a villain, a comic sidekick, or a tragic hero, has worked in nearly every genre.
gre.clue: equally convincing as a villain, a comic sidekick, or a tragic hero

volatile.hook: VOLATILE: like a VOLCANO, could explode any moment.
volatile.story: Volatile. Likely to change suddenly and without warning, often for the worse. Gary sells onions at a town market. One week, a kilo is cheap. The next, after news of a bad harvest or a border closure, the price jumps two or three times overnight. Customers shout, and Gary shrugs helplessly. Onion prices there are famously volatile. Volatile comes from the Latin for flying: a volatile liquid like petrol flies off into the air, and volatile prices fly up without warning. So, what word describes something that can change suddenly and wildly?... Volatile.
volatile.example: The mood in the dressing room was volatile after the defeat, so the captain waited until morning to discuss what had gone wrong.

gre.s: Investors fled the ____ market, where prices could swing by double digits in a single afternoon.
gre.clue: where prices could swing by double digits in a single afternoon

weary.hook: WEARY: worn out from WEARING the same burden too long.
weary.story: Weary. Very tired; also, tired of something and out of patience. Two days before the holiday, Tina spent eight hours in the crowds of the big market, bargaining for a dress, shoes and bangles. By evening her feet ached, her voice was hoarse, and she was weary of bargaining. On the bus home, she leaned her head on the window, utterly weary, but holding her shopping bags tight. Do not confuse weary with wary: weary means worn out, wary means cautious. So, what word describes someone tired out after a long, hard day?... Weary.
weary.example: Readers had grown weary of the columnist's weekly complaints about traffic, and many of them simply skipped her page.

gre.s: After a decade of conflict, the population had grown ____ of war and overwhelmingly supported the peace agreement.
gre.clue: overwhelmingly supported the peace agreement

withstand.story: Withstand. To hold up against something without being harmed. When Roy built his new house near the coast, he raised it on strong concrete pillars and tied the roof down with steel. Neighbours thought he was overdoing it. Then a cyclone struck. Trees fell, and tin roofs flew across the fields, but Roy's house withstood the storm, and his neighbours sheltered inside. In old English, with meant against, so to withstand is to stand against. So, what verb means to resist a force without breaking?... Withstand.
withstand.example: Though it lost its nine spires in an earthquake, the Kantajew temple continues to withstand the monsoon rains, as it has for nearly three centuries.

gre.s: Unlike the flimsy bridges that collapsed during the flood, the new suspension bridge was engineered to ____ even the most violent currents.
gre.clue: Unlike the flimsy bridges that collapsed during the flood

abide.hook: ABIDE: can't ABIDE it = can't stand it. ABIDE BY = obey.
abide.story: Abide. To tolerate something; also, to accept or obey a rule, as in abide by. Brandon's university dorm had one strict rule: lights out at eleven. Brandon abided by it without complaint. What he could not abide was his roommate's snoring, loud as a passing truck. After a week of sleepless nights, he bought earplugs at the market and finally slept. The trick: if you abide by a rule, you obey it; if you cannot abide something, you cannot stand it. So, what verb means to obey, or, with not, to be unable to bear something?... Abide.
abide.example: Grandmother cannot abide wasted food, so leftover rice in her kitchen always reappears the next morning as panta bhat.

gre.s: A meticulous editor, she could not ____ even minor errors of punctuation, and she returned any manuscript that contained them without reading further.
gre.clue: returned any manuscript that contained them

adhere.story: Adhere. To stick firmly to something; also, to stay faithful to a rule or belief. Stephanie's father worked as a clerk in a government office for thirty years. People often offered him gifts to move their files faster: sweets, saris, once even a goat. He refused every one. He adhered to his principles, even when money at home was tight. Stephanie grew up proud of a father who adhered to the truth. Adhere shares its root with adhesive, like tape that stays stuck. So, what verb means to stick firmly to a rule or belief?... Adhere.
adhere.example: The bakery adheres strictly to its founder's recipe, using no preservatives and baking every loaf by hand before dawn.

gre.s: Although the committee claimed to ____ to the principle of transparency, it conducted most of its deliberations behind closed doors and published no minutes.
gre.clue: it conducted most of its deliberations behind closed doors

amend.hook: AMEND: MEND something to make it better.
amend.story: Amend. To change something in order to improve or correct it. In Riley's neighbourhood, the playground committee had an old rule: only boys could use the field. When a group of girls kept turning up with a borrowed cricket bat, Riley's mother asked the committee to think again. After a long meeting, they amended the rule. Now girls play on Friday mornings, and they are winning. Mend is actually a shortened form of amend: to amend something is to mend it. So, what verb means to change a rule or text to improve it?... Amend.
amend.example: After readers pointed out several errors, the newspaper amended the article and printed a correction on its front page.

gre.s: Faced with mounting evidence of its flaws, the legislature voted to ____ the law rather than repeal it entirely.
gre.clue: rather than repeal it entirely

articulate.hook: ARTICULATE: every ARTICLE of speech placed perfectly.
articulate.story: Articulate. Able to express ideas clearly; as a verb, to express clearly. Nicole came from a small northern town to a job interview in the city, her hands shaking. Then they asked why she wanted to work in public health. She spoke about her mother's village clinic, the queue of women at dawn, and her plan to train local health workers. Her words were calm and clear. Afterwards, the panel praised how articulate she was. Articulate comes from the Latin for a small joint: articulate speech is clearly jointed, each part distinct. So, what word describes someone who expresses ideas clearly?... Articulate.
articulate.example: Shy at home, Tahmina became remarkably articulate in front of a microphone, and her radio show soon had listeners across Rajshahi.

gre.s: Although the witness was only fourteen, her testimony was remarkably ____, laying out the events in clear, precise sentences that impressed even the hostile lawyers.
gre.clue: laying out the events in clear, precise sentences

benchmark.hook: BENCHMARK: a mark on the workbench to measure against.
benchmark.story: Benchmark. A standard against which other things are measured. Every sweet yogurt Aidan has ever tasted, he compares with his grandmother's homemade yogurt, set in a clay pot until it is thick enough to hold a spoon upright. City restaurants try, but none comes close. For the whole family, her yogurt is the benchmark. Benchmark began as a surveyor's mark carved into stone, a fixed point for measuring heights. A benchmark is the fixed point you measure everything else against. So, what word means the standard others are compared with?... Benchmark.
benchmark.example: Ten seconds for the hundred metres remains the benchmark that separates good sprinters from truly great ones.

gre.s: For decades, the textbook's rigorous treatment of the subject served as the ____ against which all later introductions were judged, and few of them measured up.
gre.clue: against which all later introductions were judged

catastrophic.story: Catastrophic. Causing sudden, terrible harm or ruin. In November two thousand seven, a great cyclone struck the southwest coast of the delta. Winds tore down homes, a storm surge swept across villages, and thousands of lives were lost. For coastal families, the damage was catastrophic. Since then, more shelters and early warnings have saved countless lives in later storms. Catastrophic comes from catastrophe, the Greek word for an overturning: a catastrophic event turns life upside down. So, what word describes a disaster that brings sudden and terrible ruin?... Catastrophic.
catastrophic.example: A single typo in the guidance software had catastrophic results, sending the rocket off course seconds after takeoff.

gre.s: Engineers warned that even a small crack in the aging dam could prove ____, releasing a flood that would drown every village in the valley below.
gre.clue: releasing a flood that would drown every village in the valley below

cerebral.hook: CEREBRAL = cerebrum, the thinking part of the brain.
cerebral.story: Cerebral. Intellectual rather than emotional; also, relating to the brain. On Friday nights, Kelly wants old family films where everyone cries at the end. Her brother Todd wants cerebral films about time loops, memory and puzzles that he explains for an hour afterwards. Their mother settles it by making them alternate weeks. Kelly says Todd's films have no heart; Todd says they make you think. The cerebrum is the thinking part of the brain, so cerebral things appeal to the mind. So, what word describes something intellectual rather than emotional?... Cerebral.
cerebral.example: Chess may be a cerebral game, but grandmasters train their bodies too, since a six-hour match is physically exhausting.

gre.s: Critics who expected a stirring, emotional drama found the film disappointingly ____, more interested in testing the audience's logic than in moving its heart.
gre.clue: more interested in testing the audience's logic than in moving its heart

cloak.hook: CLOAK: like an invisibility cloak, hiding the truth.
cloak.story: Cloak. A loose outer coat; also, something that hides; as a verb, to hide or disguise. On winter mornings at the ferry landing, a thick fog cloaks the river. You cannot see the river, the boats, or even the far end of the jetty. Only the low horn of a ferry tells Zach that it is out there somewhere. By ten, the sun burns through, and the cloak lifts. Picture an invisibility cloak: whatever it covers simply disappears. So, what verb means to cover something so it cannot be seen?... Cloak.
cloak.example: Morning fog cloaked the Jamuna so thickly that the ferry crew had to sound the horn every few minutes.

gre.s: The regime tried to ____ its crackdown in the language of public safety, describing mass arrests as routine precautions.
gre.clue: describing mass arrests as routine precautions

commence.hook: COMMENCE: COMMENCEMENT is when graduates BEGIN their new life.
commence.story: Commence. To begin. The hall at Priscilla's final exam centre fell silent. Two hundred students sat with pens ready, hearts pounding. The invigilator looked at the clock and announced, "The examination will now commence." Papers rustled, and Priscilla took a deep breath and wrote her name. Months of night study had led to this moment, and now it had commenced. Think of a commencement ceremony at a university: graduates are not ending, but commencing a new life. So, what formal verb means to begin?... Commence.
commence.example: Construction of the new bridge will commence as soon as the rainy season ends and the river falls.

gre.s: Although the ceremony was scheduled to ____ at nine, the chief guest's late arrival meant that nothing actually happened until nearly noon.
gre.clue: nothing actually happened until nearly noon

complementary.hook: COMPLEMENTARY with an E COMPLETES. Complimentary with an I means free or praising.
complementary.story: Complementary. Combining to complete or improve each other. Frank and Annie run a tiny bakery in a hill town. Frank wakes at four to bake bread and cakes, but he hates talking to customers. Annie cannot bake at all, but she remembers every customer's name and keeps the accounts perfectly. Alone, each would struggle. Together, their complementary skills make the bakery the busiest on the street. Complementary with an e completes; complimentary with an i means free or full of praise. So, what word describes two things that complete each other?... Complementary.
complementary.example: Rice and lentils are nutritionally complementary, since each supplies amino acids that the other lacks.

gre.s: The two researchers' skills proved ____: her expertise in statistics filled exactly the gaps in his knowledge of biology.
gre.clue: filled exactly the gaps in his knowledge

contend.hook: CONTEND: CONTENDERs fight in a competition; scholars contend in arguments.
contend.story: Contend. To struggle against a difficulty; also, to argue that something is true. In the dry red uplands, farmers contend with hard red soil, fierce heat and a falling water table. Ray has farmed there all his life, watching the wells go deeper every year. His daughter, now a researcher, contends that farmers should switch to crops that need less water. Slowly, some are listening. A contender is someone who contends, struggling to win a contest. So, what verb means to struggle with difficulties, or to argue a point?... Contend.
contend.example: The defense contends that the security video was recorded on a different night, and it has asked an expert to examine the timestamps.

gre.s: Some economists ____ that the recession was caused by excessive regulation, while others argue that deregulation was to blame.
gre.clue: while others argue

covert.story: Covert. Secret; not openly shown. For eleven years, Jeremy's mother kept a covert savings plan. Every week, she slipped a few coins and folded notes into a clay money bank hidden behind the rice sacks. Nobody knew. When Jeremy got into university, she broke the clay bank in front of him, and coins rolled across the floor. Her covert savings bought his first laptop. Covert comes from the same root as cover: something covert is kept under cover. Its opposite is overt, meaning open. So, what word describes something done in secret?... Covert.
covert.example: The journalist used a covert camera hidden in a pen to film inspectors accepting bribes at the port.

gre.s: Unlike his opponent's openly hostile campaign, the senator's attacks were ____, conducted through anonymous leaks and rumors spread by intermediaries.
gre.clue: conducted through anonymous leaks and rumors

detrimental.story: Detrimental. Causing harm or damage. During her exam month, Ashley studied until midnight, then lay in bed scrolling her phone until three. Every morning she woke with a heavy head and read the same page four times. Her doctor aunt finally told her that late-night scrolling was detrimental to her sleep, and poor sleep was detrimental to her memory. Ashley left the phone in the kitchen that night. Detriment means harm; it comes from the Latin for rubbing away, as harm slowly rubs you down. So, what word describes a habit that causes damage?... Detrimental.
detrimental.example: Heavy pumping of groundwater has proved detrimental to Dhaka's soil, which is slowly sinking in several neighborhoods.

gre.s: Although the pesticide boosted crop yields in the short term, it proved ____ to the region's bees, whose populations collapsed within a few years.
gre.clue: whose populations collapsed within a few years

dictate.story: Dictate. To give orders with authority; also, to control or determine something. In the great northeastern wetlands, water dictates everything. For half the year, villages become islands, and people travel only by boat. In the dry months, the same water turns into rice fields as far as the eye can see. When to plant, when to harvest, even when to hold weddings: the water dictates it all. A dictator dictates orders; here, nature is the one in charge. So, what verb means to control or determine what happens?... Dictate.
dictate.example: In the end, the weather will dictate whether the farmers of Dinajpur plant wheat or maize this winter.

gre.s: The tiny budget seemed to ____ every decision the filmmakers made, from the choice of actors to the length of each scene.
gre.clue: from the choice of actors to the length of each scene

dissent.story: Dissent. To disagree with an official or widely held view; as a noun, that disagreement. At a family meeting, eleven relatives agreed to sell the ancestral pond to a developer for a good price. Only one voice dissented: Seth's grandmother. She said the pond had fed three generations and would feed three more. Her dissent made everyone pause. In the end, they kept the pond. Dissent comes from the Latin for feeling differently, the same root as in sentiment. So, what word means disagreeing with what most people have decided?... Dissent.
dissent.example: When the board approved the merger, only one director dissented, warning that thousands of workers would lose their jobs.

gre.s: Although most of the committee endorsed the proposal enthusiastically, two members chose to ____, arguing that its costs had been badly underestimated.
gre.clue: arguing that its costs had been badly underestimated

distressed.story: Distressed. Suffering from anxiety, sorrow or pain; also, in serious difficulty. At a crowded spring fair, four-year-old Mia let go of her father's hand to look at the balloons. When she turned back, he was gone. She stood frozen, crying, deeply distressed. A tea seller lifted her onto his counter and asked the loudspeaker man to call her father. Ten minutes later, her father pushed through the crowd and held her tight. Stress is actually a shortened form of distress: a distressed person is under heavy stress. So, what word describes someone filled with fear or sorrow?... Distressed.
distressed.example: The lifeguard spotted a distressed swimmer waving near the rocks and reached him moments before he went under.

gre.s: Hotline volunteers are trained to calm ____ callers, many of whom are panicking or in tears when they first phone in.
gre.clue: many of whom are panicking or in tears

eccentric.hook: EC-CENTRIC: off-center, not in the middle like everyone else.
eccentric.story: Eccentric. Unconventional and slightly strange. In a lane in the old city lives an old man who wears a yellow raincoat every single day, even in the dry heat of April. He talks to the potted plants on his balcony and greets each one by name. Children once laughed at him, but he gives free English lessons every evening, and now half the lane calls him teacher. He is eccentric, and deeply loved. Eccentric means off centre, from Greek: an eccentric person lives a little away from the middle. So, what word describes someone pleasantly odd and unconventional?... Eccentric.
eccentric.example: The eccentric poet kept a pet goose on his rooftop in Old Dhaka and read his new verses to it every evening.

gre.s: The billionaire was known for his ____ habits, such as wearing a raincoat indoors and dining only on food that was blue.
gre.clue: wearing a raincoat indoors and dining only on food that was blue

induce.story: Induce. To persuade someone to do something; also, to cause something. Michelle could not induce her little brother to eat bitter gourd. He clamped his mouth shut every time. Then their grandmother told him that bitter gourd was the secret food of famous fast bowlers. That evening he ate a whole plate, and asked for more. Grandmother had induced him with a story. Induce comes from the Latin ducere, to lead, as in conductor: to induce is to lead someone into doing something. So, what verb means to persuade or bring about?... Induce.
induce.example: The company offered free mobile data to induce farmers to try its new weather app before the planting season.

gre.s: No amount of flattery could ____ the reclusive author to grant an interview; she had refused every request from journalists for over thirty years.
gre.clue: she had refused every request from journalists for over thirty years

intuitive.hook: INTUITIVE: you just KNOW, by INTUITION.
intuitive.story: Intuitive. Based on instinct rather than conscious reasoning; also, easy to use without instructions. Travis called his mother from his dorm in the city and said, "Everything is fine, Mom." She was quiet for a moment, then asked, "Who has upset you?" He had said nothing, but she knew. A mother's understanding is intuitive. Within five minutes he was telling her everything. Intuitive comes from intuition, knowing something without being told. So, what word describes understanding that comes from instinct, not reasoning?... Intuitive.
intuitive.example: Experienced nurses often have an intuitive feel for which patient is about to get worse, long before the monitors show it.

gre.s: Rather than calculating the odds, the veteran player relied on an ____ sense of when to attack, a feel for the game that she could never fully explain.
gre.clue: a feel for the game that she could never fully explain

latitude.hook: LATITUDE: lots of room, wide like LATITUDE lines across the globe.
latitude.story: Latitude. Freedom to act or decide as one chooses. Most art teachers at Naomi's school gave strict instructions: draw a village scene, a boat, or the national flag. But the new teacher gave her students latitude. "Paint anything that matters to you." Naomi painted her grandmother's wrinkled hands holding a cup of tea. With that latitude, she found her own style. Latitude comes from the Latin for wide: the lines of latitude run across the width of the globe, and latitude gives you wide room. So, what word means freedom to choose your own way?... Latitude.
latitude.example: Judges have some latitude in sentencing, so two people convicted of the same crime may receive very different punishments.

gre.s: The new editor gave her reporters considerable ____, allowing them to pursue whatever stories interested them rather than assigning topics herself.
gre.clue: rather than assigning topics herself

lax.story: Lax. Not strict or careful enough. The guard at Billy's apartment building was a kind man, but very lax. He dozed through the afternoon heat, let delivery men in without asking, and left the gate open at night. Then one morning, three bicycles were missing from the garage. After that, the residents set up a sign-in book, and nobody called the building lax again. Lax and relaxed come from the same Latin word for loose: lax rules are far too loose. So, what word describes security that is careless and not strict enough?... Lax.
lax.example: Parents complained that the school was lax about homework, since some teachers had not set any for an entire term.

gre.s: The audit blamed the fraud on ____ oversight, noting that no one had reviewed the accounts in over three years.
gre.clue: no one had reviewed the accounts in over three years

lucrative.hook: LUCRATIVE: brings in lots of LUCRE (money).
lucrative.story: Lucrative. Producing a lot of profit. Dana learned graphic design from free videos on a second-hand laptop. At first, she earned a few dollars making logos for small shops abroad. Within three years, clients from five countries were sending her work, and she was earning more than her father ever had. Freelancing had turned out to be lucrative. Lucrative comes from lucre, an old word for money, from the Latin for profit. So, what word describes work that brings in a lot of money?... Lucrative.
lucrative.example: Exporting frozen shrimp has become a lucrative trade for farmers in Satkhira, though it has also made their land saltier.

gre.s: Many talented scientists abandon research for more ____ careers in finance, where salaries can be ten times higher.
gre.clue: where salaries can be ten times higher

mitigate.hook: MITIGATE: put MITTENS on the GATE — softens the blow.
mitigate.story: Mitigate. To make something less severe or painful. When a great cyclone struck in two thousand seven, the coastal mangrove forest took the first blow. Its thick roots and dense trees broke the force of the wind and the waves before they reached many villages. Allen, a forest guard, says the forest is like a wall of green. The mangroves did not stop the storm, but they mitigated its damage. Mitigate comes from the Latin mitis, meaning soft or mild: to mitigate is to soften. So, what verb means to make harm less severe?... Mitigate.
mitigate.example: Wide, tree-lined avenues help mitigate the heat of a city summer by shading the pavements and cooling the air.

gre.s: Planting mangroves along the coast can ____ the impact of storm surges, though it cannot prevent them entirely.
gre.clue: though it cannot prevent them entirely

nominal.story: Nominal. Very small, far below the real value; also, existing in name only. The little library in Melissa's village charges a nominal fee: a few cents a month. For that, children can borrow any book on the shelves. The librarian, a retired teacher, says the fee is only nominal, just enough to make children feel the books are truly theirs. Nominal comes from the Latin nomen, name: a nominal fee is a fee in name only. So, what word describes a cost so small that it is almost symbolic?... Nominal.
nominal.example: The king remained the nominal ruler of the country, but parliament had long since taken over every real decision.

gre.s: Although she was the ____ chair of the committee, real authority rested with her deputy, who set the agenda and made every major decision.
gre.clue: real authority rested with her deputy

prevail.story: Prevail. To prove stronger and win; also, to be widespread. On sports day at a village school, the girls' tug of war team faced a much bigger team. Everyone expected them to lose. But they had practised together all month, pulling in rhythm to a chant. Slowly, step by step, the rope moved their way, and the bigger team tumbled over. Teamwork had prevailed. Prevail and prevalent share a Latin root meaning to be stronger. So, what verb means to win in the end, against the odds?... Prevail.
prevail.example: After a fierce debate, common sense prevailed, and the council agreed to keep the old banyan tree instead of widening the road.

gre.s: Though the reformers were outnumbered and underfunded, their persistence allowed them to ____ in the end, and the law they had championed passed by a wide margin.
gre.clue: the law they had championed passed by a wide margin

quirky.hook: QUIRKY: full of QUIRKS, odd little habits.
quirky.story: Quirky. Having unusual habits or features that are odd in a charming way. Randy's uncle names every cow after a famous poet. There is a Byron who kicks, a Keats who stares at the sky, and a gentle little calf named Shelley. He also plays old film songs to them every evening, saying it improves the milk. Neighbours think he is quirky. Randy thinks he is the best uncle in the world. Quirky simply means full of quirks, odd little habits. So, what word describes someone with charmingly unusual habits?... Quirky.
quirky.example: The quirky little bookshop in Nilkhet arranges its novels by the colour of their covers rather than by author.

gre.s: Fans love the director's ____ films, which feature talking furniture, symmetrical sets, and characters who speak only in rhyme.
gre.clue: talking furniture, symmetrical sets, and characters who speak only in rhyme

rampant.story: Rampant. Spreading without control; widespread. One evening, a rumour spread across the city on social media: salt was about to run out. By night, panic buying was rampant. Shannon saw people at the corner shop carrying away five, ten, even twenty packets. Prices shot up. The next day, officials announced there was plenty of salt, and the panic faded as quickly as it had begun. In old coats of arms, a lion rampant rears up on its hind legs, wild and unstoppable. So, what word describes something spreading wildly out of control?... Rampant.
rampant.example: Weeds grew rampant in the abandoned garden, and within two summers they had swallowed the path to the front door.

gre.s: In the absence of any regulatory oversight, fraud became ____ in the industry, spreading so widely that honest firms struggled to compete.
gre.clue: spreading so widely that honest firms struggled to compete

redundant.story: Redundant. Unnecessary because it repeats something; also, no longer needed. Megan proudly gave her essay to her editor. It began, "In my own personal opinion, I personally think." Her editor crossed out five words and left only "I think." "Own, personal and opinion are all redundant here," he said. "I think already says it." Megan laughed and started cutting every redundant word in her essay. Redundant comes from the Latin for overflowing, like a wave spilling over: more than is needed. So, what word describes words that repeat without adding anything?... Redundant.
redundant.example: Once every train was fitted with automatic doors, the guard who used to stand at each carriage became redundant.

gre.s: Because the new software performs all of its checks automatically, the old manual inspections have become ____, and the company plans to eliminate them next year.
gre.clue: the company plans to eliminate them next year

superficial.hook: SUPER-FICIAL: only on the SURFACE (super = above).
superficial.story: Superficial. Existing only on the surface; lacking depth. A glamorous new restaurant opened downtown, with chandeliers, gold-painted walls and waiters in bow ties. Isaac and his friends waited an hour for a table. Then the food came: cold rice, bland curry and dry chicken. They left hungry. All its charm was superficial. Superficial comes from Latin super, above, and facies, face: it stays on the face of things, never going deeper. So, what word describes something impressive only on the surface?... Superficial.
superficial.example: A superficial reading of the poem suggests a simple love story, but a closer look reveals a protest against the war.

gre.s: Reviewers faulted the biography as ____, noting that it catalogued its subject's achievements without ever probing his motives or inner life.
gre.clue: without ever probing his motives or inner life

wary.hook: WARY sounds like WORRY: you worry, so you're careful.
wary.story: Wary. Cautious and alert to possible danger. Every spring, honey collectors enter the mangrove forest in small groups. They move slowly through the mangroves, watching the mud for paw prints and listening for the slightest sound. A Bengal tiger could be hiding anywhere. Old Abe tells the young men that only the wary come home. Wary shares its root with beware and aware. Do not confuse it with weary, which means tired. So, what word describes someone cautious and watchful of danger?... Wary.
wary.example: Having been badly stung once, the village beekeeper is wary of opening the hives without his net and gloves.

gre.s: Having been misled by flattering forecasts before, the investors were ____ of the startup's promise to triple its revenue within a year.
gre.clue: Having been misled by flattering forecasts before

alleviate.hook: ALLEVIATE: to LEVITATE the weight; making the burden lighter.
alleviate.story: Alleviate. To make pain, suffering or a problem less severe. During a brutal April heatwave in the city, Sean watched rickshaw pullers pedalling in the blazing sun with no water. So he set up a table outside his shop with clay jugs of cold water, lemon and a little salt. By noon, a long line had formed. It was a small act, but it alleviated real suffering. Alleviate shares its Latin root with lever and levitate, all about making things light: to alleviate is to lighten a burden. So, what verb means to ease pain or hardship?... Alleviate.
alleviate.example: Volunteers handed out cold water and rehydration salts to alleviate the suffering of rickshaw pullers during the April heatwave.

gre.s: The new subway line was expected to ____ congestion downtown, but traffic has, if anything, grown worse.
gre.clue: but traffic has, if anything, grown worse

arresting.hook: ARRESTING: it ARRESTS your attention — you can't move on.
arresting.story: Arresting. Striking; catching your attention so strongly that you stop. One clear November morning at the far northern tip of the country, Audrey stepped out of her guesthouse with a cup of tea. Above the green tea gardens, the snowy peaks of the great mountains glowed pink in the sunrise. She forgot her tea completely. The sight was arresting. The trick: police arrest a person and stop him in his tracks; an arresting sight arrests your attention, and you cannot move on. So, what word describes a view so striking that it stops you still?... Arresting.
arresting.example: The novel opens with an arresting line about a man who wakes to find his house floating down the river.

gre.s: Although the exhibition as a whole was forgettable, one ____ portrait of a fisherman's weathered face held visitors in front of it for minutes at a time.
gre.clue: held visitors in front of it for minutes at a time

avid.hook: AVID: an AVID reader DEVOURS books.
avid.story: Avid. Showing great eagerness and enthusiasm. Every Thursday afternoon, a mobile library bus stops near Susie's school. Susie is always first in line. She returns three books, borrows three more, and has usually finished one before she reaches home, reading as she walks. Her mother calls her a bookworm. The librarian calls her the most avid reader on his whole route. Avid comes from the Latin for eager or hungry: an avid reader is hungry for the next book. So, what word describes someone with eager enthusiasm for something?... Avid.
avid.example: An avid birdwatcher, Professor Alam spends his winter weekends at Tanguar Haor counting migrating ducks.

gre.s: A lifelong and ____ collector of rare maps, he spent nearly every weekend combing antique shops and could rarely resist bidding at auctions, however steep the prices.
gre.clue: could rarely resist bidding at auctions, however steep the prices

benign.story: Benign. Kind and gentle; also, harmless. When a long snake slid across the pond behind Shane's village home, his city cousins screamed and ran. Shane's grandmother laughed gently and kept washing the pots. "It is only a water snake. It has no venom. It eats frogs, not people." Her benign smile calmed everyone, and the snake, just as benign, disappeared into the reeds. Benign comes from the Latin bene, good, as in benefit: something benign means no harm. Its opposite is malignant. So, what word describes something gentle and harmless?... Benign.
benign.example: Most of the bacteria living in the human gut are benign, and many of them actually help us digest our food.

gre.s: Although the pesticide was marketed as ____, later studies showed it accumulated in rivers and harmed fish populations.
gre.clue: later studies showed it accumulated in rivers and harmed

boon.story: Boon. Something that brings great help or benefit. When Rosie first came from her northern village to work in a garment factory near the city, sending money home meant a long trip and a trusted messenger. Then mobile banking arrived. Now, on payday, she taps a few buttons, and minutes later her mother receives it in the village. For millions of workers like Rosie, it has been a boon. In old stories, a boon was a favour granted by a king or a god, a gift that changes your life. So, what word means something that is a great blessing?... Boon.
boon.example: Cheap solar panels have been a boon to fishing families on remote islands, who can now charge phones and light their homes at night.

gre.s: Far from being the burden that critics had predicted, the new metro line has proved a ____ to commuters, cutting their daily travel time in half.
gre.clue: cutting their daily travel time in half

candid.hook: CANDID camera: it catches you as you really are, no filter.
candid.story: Candid. Honest and open; saying plainly what you think. When Aunt Rita arrived for the holiday with a dramatic new hairstyle, the whole family praised it politely. Then five-year-old Nora looked up and said, "You look like a broom." The room burst into laughter, and Aunt Rita laughed loudest. Children are always candid. In Latin, candidus meant white and pure; Roman candidates wore white togas to look honest. A candid answer has nothing to hide. So, what word describes someone who says exactly what they think?... Candid.
candid.example: In a candid letter to her students, the retiring teacher admitted that she had failed her own university entrance exam twice.

gre.s: Unlike his predecessors, who issued carefully vague statements, the new spokesman was refreshingly ____ about the company's mistakes.
gre.clue: who issued carefully vague statements

cherish.hook: CHERISH: like a CHERRY on top, the most treasured part.
cherish.story: Cherish. To value something deeply and care for it with love. Faith's mother keeps a bundle of letters tied with a red ribbon in her steel trunk. Her husband wrote them every month from Dubai during the eight years he worked there, before phones were cheap. The paper is yellow now, and the ink is fading. Some nights, she still reads one by lamplight. She cherishes every word. Cherish comes from the French cher, meaning dear: what you cherish is dear to you. So, what verb means to hold something dear and care for it lovingly?... Cherish.
cherish.example: Bangladeshis cherish the memory of the 1952 Language Movement, and every February thousands lay flowers at the Shaheed Minar.

gre.s: Though the village has little wealth, its people ____ their traditions, preserving songs and festivals that have vanished elsewhere.
gre.clue: preserving songs and festivals that have vanished elsewhere

collaborate.story: Collaborate. To work together with others; also, to cooperate with an enemy. Every monsoon, the narrow canal between two river villages cut children off from school. One dry season, families from both villages collaborated to build a bamboo bridge. One village brought bamboo, the other brought rope, and everyone brought tea and puffed rice. In three days the bridge was done, and children walked across, cheering. Collaborate holds labour inside it: co means together, so to collaborate is to labour together. So, what verb means to work jointly on a shared goal?... Collaborate.
collaborate.example: A Bangladeshi singer and a Norwegian violinist collaborated on the album, recording their parts in studios thousands of kilometres apart.

gre.s: Scientists from rival nations agreed to ____ on the project, pooling their data in the hope of an earlier breakthrough.
gre.clue: pooling their data

cunning.hook: CUNNING: as clever as a fox.
cunning.story: Cunning. Clever at getting what you want, often by trickery. Every child in the village knows the tale of the jackal who promised to teach a crocodile's seven babies to read. Each day the crocodile asked to see her children, and each day the jackal held up the same baby seven times. By the time she understood, the jackal had escaped. Such a cunning trick! Cunning first meant knowing; it is related to the old word can, as in being able. So, what word describes someone clever at getting what they want by trickery?... Cunning.
cunning.example: With great cunning, the smugglers hid the gold inside hollowed-out mangoes packed among hundreds of real ones.

gre.s: The diplomat was admired less for her eloquence than for her ____: she repeatedly outmaneuvered rivals by letting them believe they had already won.
gre.clue: outmaneuvered rivals by letting them believe they had already won

deter.hook: DETER: like a TERROR that keeps you away.
deter.story: Deter. To discourage someone from doing something, often by making them afraid. Every winter, crows and parrots raided the ripening rice in Doug's field. So his grandfather built a scarecrow from bamboo, dressed it in his own old shirt and a clay-pot head with a painted moustache. Tin cans hung from its arms and rattled in the wind. The birds stayed away. The scarecrow deterred them all season. Deter shares its Latin root with terror: to deter is to frighten someone away. So, what verb means to discourage by making afraid?... Deter.
deter.example: Thorny bushes planted along the fence deter goats from wandering into the vegetable garden.

gre.s: Lawmakers hoped that steeper fines would ____ drivers from using their phones at the wheel, but accident rates remained unchanged a year later.
gre.clue: hoped that steeper fines would

dubious.story: Dubious. Doubtful; of questionable value or honesty. A banner outside a coaching centre in town promised one hundred percent success in every university admission test. Howard's father read it, frowned, and asked the receptionist for a list of last year's successful students. She said the list was private. He asked for just one name. She could not give one. He walked out, sure the claim was dubious. Dubious and doubt share a Latin root: a dubious claim is full of doubt. So, what word describes a claim you have good reason to doubt?... Dubious.
dubious.example: The record for the longest kite flight rests on dubious evidence, a single blurry photograph and the word of the flier's cousin.

gre.s: The study's conclusions are ____ at best: its sample was tiny, its funding came from the very company whose product it praised, and no one has replicated it.
gre.clue: its funding came from the very company whose product it praised

elusive.story: Elusive. Hard to find, catch or achieve; always slipping away. For three weeks, the wildlife photographer Aaron waited in the mangrove forest for a single photo of a Bengal tiger. He found fresh paw prints in the mud, heard a deep roar one night, and once saw a flash of orange between the mangroves. But the tiger never stood still for his camera. It remained elusive. Elusive comes from elude, to escape or slip away. So, what word describes something that keeps slipping away whenever you try to catch it?... Elusive.
elusive.example: Sleep remained elusive on the night before the results, so Farhan sat on the balcony watching trucks rumble along the highway.

gre.s: Although researchers have studied the disease for decades, a cure has remained ____, slipping out of reach every time a promising treatment fails in clinical trials.
gre.clue: every time a promising treatment fails in clinical trials

heed.hook: HEED: use your HEAD and listen.
heed.story: Heed. To pay careful attention to advice or a warning. One afternoon off the southern coast, Sam's fishing boat radio announced a storm signal. The sea still looked calm, and his young crew wanted to stay for one more catch. Sam heeded the warning and turned the boat for home. That night, the storm struck with fierce winds. Every boat that had heeded the signal was safe in harbour. A heedless person pays no attention; to heed is to listen and act. So, what verb means to take careful notice of a warning?... Heed.
heed.example: Had the builders heeded the engineer's warnings about the cracks, the factory might still be standing today.

gre.s: The near-collision could easily have been avoided if the pilots had bothered to ____ the repeated warnings from air traffic control.
gre.clue: could easily have been avoided

hysterical.hook: HYSTERICAL: emotions out of control, crying or laughing.
hysterical.story: Hysterical. Wildly emotional and out of control; also, extremely funny. At his cousin's pre-wedding turmeric ceremony, Shawn decided to show off his dance moves. He spun once, spun twice, slipped, and landed in the big brass plate of turmeric paste. He sat up bright yellow from head to toe. The aunts laughed until they were almost hysterical, wiping tears with their saris. Even the bride could not stop. The scene was hysterical. Hysterical can mean emotion out of control, or something so funny that laughter goes out of control. So, what word describes something wildly funny?... Hysterical.
hysterical.example: When the stage lights exploded, the concert crowd grew hysterical, and stewards struggled to stop people from trampling one another.

gre.s: News of the crash reached the families before any official statement, and the airport lounge became a scene of ____ grief, with relatives sobbing and screaming uncontrollably.
gre.clue: sobbing and screaming uncontrollably

implicit.story: Implicit. Suggested without being said directly; also, complete and unquestioning. When Rachel's father went to his village for a week, he handed her the keys to his pharmacy. He gave no speech about responsibility, no list of rules. He simply placed the keys in her palm and smiled. His trust in her was implicit, and his message was implicit too: I know you can do this. Implicit means implied; its opposite is explicit, meaning stated openly. So, what word describes trust or meaning that is understood without being spoken?... Implicit.
implicit.example: In many offices there is an implicit rule that no one leaves before the boss, even when the day's work is done.

gre.s: Although the contract never states it outright, both parties share the ____ understanding that the tenant will maintain the garden in exchange for lower rent.
gre.clue: never states it outright

intrinsic.story: Intrinsic. Belonging naturally to something; essential. Fiona's grandfather taught himself to play the bamboo flute as a boy. He never performed on stage, never won a prize, never earned a single penny from it. Yet every evening for sixty years, he sat on the veranda and played as the sun went down. The joy was intrinsic, found in the music itself. Intrinsic means from within; its opposite, extrinsic, means from outside, like prizes and praise. So, what word describes value that lies within a thing itself?... Intrinsic.
intrinsic.example: A coin made of cheap metal has almost no intrinsic value, since its worth comes entirely from the government that stands behind it.

gre.s: Her friends insisted that honesty was ____ to the founder's character, not a strategy adopted for appearances: even as a child she had refused to lie.
gre.clue: not a strategy adopted for appearances

mimic.hook: MIMIC: a MIME copies your every move.
mimic.story: Mimic. To imitate someone's voice or actions, often to amuse. Simon's grandmother keeps a hill myna in a cage on the veranda. One morning, Simon heard his grandmother call his name from the courtyard. He ran out, but she was at the market. The voice called again, and he saw the bird tilting its head at him. The myna could mimic her perfectly. Mimic comes from the Greek for an actor, the same root as mime, someone who copies every movement. So, what verb means to imitate someone closely?... Mimic.
