mimic.example: Engineers shaped the bullet train's nose to mimic a kingfisher's beak, which lets the bird dive into water with barely a splash.

gre.s: Certain harmless butterflies ____ the coloring of poisonous species, deterring predators that have learned to avoid the toxic originals.
gre.clue: deterring predators that have learned to avoid the toxic originals

perennial.story: Perennial. Lasting a long time, or returning again and again. Every June, the same lane in the port city floods after heavy rain. Shopkeepers lift their goods onto bricks, children float paper boats, and Kenny's mother ties up her sari to wade to the market. Officials promise new drains each year, but the water always returns. Waterlogging is a perennial problem there. Perennial comes from Latin per, through, and annus, year: lasting through the years, like a perennial plant that blooms again every season. So, what word describes a problem that keeps coming back year after year?... Perennial.
perennial.example: Water shortages are a perennial complaint in the hostel, and every summer students queue with buckets at the single working tap.

gre.s: Far from being a passing fad, the debate over free will is a ____ concern of philosophy, revived by every generation since antiquity.
gre.clue: revived by every generation since antiquity

picturesque.story: Picturesque. Visually charming, as pretty as a picture. Before dawn, Ross and his friends climbed to the top of a high hill in the southeast, shivering in their jackets. Then the sun rose. Below them, a sea of white clouds filled the valleys, with green hilltops rising through it like islands. Ross forgot to take a photo for a full minute. Nobody had told him his own country could look so picturesque. The word is simply picture with a French ending: a picturesque place looks like a painting. So, what word describes a scene charming enough to paint?... Picturesque.
picturesque.example: The picturesque hills of Bandarban draw photographers every winter, when mist settles between the peaks at dawn.

gre.s: Tourists drawn by brochures promising a ____ fishing village were dismayed to find that the old harbor had been replaced by a concrete port and rows of warehouses.
gre.clue: had been replaced by a concrete port and rows of warehouses

reconcile.hook: RE-CONCILE: bring back to COUNCIL, back together.
reconcile.story: Reconcile. To restore friendly relations; also, to make two things fit together. Two brothers in a farming village had not spoken for six years after a fight over a strip of family land. Then, on the morning of the holiday, the younger one walked across the field with a plate of sweet noodles and knocked on his brother's door. They stood in silence, then embraced. By noon, their children were playing together. They had reconciled. Concile means to bring together, as in a council; to reconcile is to bring people back together. So, what verb means to make peace after a quarrel?... Reconcile.
reconcile.example: Rumana struggled to reconcile her love of travel with her parents' wish that she stay close to home in Khulna.

gre.s: The theory struggles to ____ two sets of findings that appear to contradict each other.
gre.clue: that appear to contradict each other

residual.story: Residual. Remaining after most of something has gone. When the flood water finally left Linda's house, a line of brown mud ran around every wall, marking where the water had stood. A residual smell of river and damp hung in the rooms for weeks. Even after the walls were painted, the children had a residual fear, waking up at the sound of heavy rain. Residual comes from residue, what is left behind. So, what word describes what remains after most of something is gone?... Residual.
residual.example: Even after the factory closed, residual chemicals in the soil kept nearby wells unsafe for more than a decade.

gre.s: Although the fever subsided within a week, the patient suffered from ____ fatigue that persisted for months after the infection itself had cleared.
gre.clue: after the infection itself had cleared

resilient.hook: RESILIENT: RE-SPRINGS back like a spring.
resilient.story: Resilient. Able to recover quickly from trouble or hardship. The river took Morris's house on a river island three times in ten years. Each time, he moved his family to higher ground, built again with bamboo and tin, and started over. Now he grows pumpkins in the sandbars the river left behind, and sells them in town. His neighbours call him the most resilient man they know. Resilient comes from the Latin for leaping back: a resilient person springs back after every fall. So, what word describes someone who bounces back from hardship?... Resilient.
resilient.example: Mangrove forests are remarkably resilient, regrowing within a few years even after a cyclone has stripped them bare.

gre.s: The economy proved surprisingly ____: although the crisis wiped out a fifth of its output, it regained its former strength in less than two years.
gre.clue: it regained its former strength in less than two years

sensational.hook: SENSATIONAL: designed to excite the SENSES.
sensational.story: Sensational. Causing great excitement; also, presented in a shocking way to grab attention. One morning, a news website ran a sensational headline: a ghost had been seen dancing in an old house in town. The story spread across every phone in town. Crowds gathered at the gate at midnight with torches. Then the truth came out: it was a white curtain flapping in a broken window. Sensational stories excite the senses more than the mind. So, what word describes news designed to shock and excite?... Sensational.
sensational.example: Sensational headlines about a ghost in Lalbagh Fort brought crowds of curious visitors but no evidence of anything unusual.

gre.s: Serious journalists criticized the tabloid's ____ coverage of the trial, which emphasized lurid details while ignoring the legal issues.
gre.clue: emphasized lurid details while ignoring the legal issues

sentimental.story: Sentimental. Driven by tender feelings or nostalgia, sometimes too much. Allison's father keeps a rusty blue scooter in the garage of their house. It has not run in fifteen years. Mechanics offer to buy it, and Allison's brother wants the space for his motorbike. But her father refuses. It was on that scooter that he took Allison's mother to see her first film. He is sentimental about it. Sentimental comes from sentiment, meaning feeling. So, what word describes someone who keeps things for the sake of tender memories?... Sentimental.
sentimental.example: The retirement speech grew so sentimental that even the stern old accountant was wiping his eyes by the end.

gre.s: The critic faulted the film for being cloyingly ____, relying on tearful reunions and swelling violins rather than on genuine emotional insight.
gre.clue: tearful reunions and swelling violins

sham.story: Sham. Something that is not what it pretends to be; fake. At Tamara's dorm, the dining hall suddenly served chicken roast, fresh salad and sweet yogurt on the day the provost came to inspect. The provost tasted it, smiled, and wrote a glowing report. The next day, the students were back to watery dal and stones in the rice. The whole inspection had been a sham. Picture a sham as a stage set: a painted front with nothing real behind it. So, what word means something fake, dressed up to look real?... Sham.
sham.example: Villagers later learned that the developer's town hall meeting had been a sham, because the land deal was signed weeks earlier.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the election as a ____, noting that opposition candidates had been banned and the results announced before the polls closed.
gre.clue: the results announced before the polls closed

speculate.story: Speculate. To form a theory without firm evidence; also, to invest with risk. When a new family moved into the flat upstairs, the whole building began to speculate. They never came out in the daytime. Was the father a spy? A film star in hiding? Then Sadie's mother knocked with a plate of rice cakes and learned the truth: both parents were night-shift nurses. Everyone had speculated wildly. Speculate comes from the Latin for a watchtower: you look out and guess. So, what verb means to guess without real evidence?... Speculate.
speculate.example: Astronomers can only speculate about what lies beneath the icy crust of Jupiter's moon Europa until a probe lands there.

gre.s: In the absence of reliable records, historians can only ____ about the poet's early years; even the city of her birth remains a matter of dispute.
gre.clue: In the absence of reliable records

subordinate.story: Subordinate. Lower in rank or importance; as a verb, to treat as less important. When Ivan became the manager of a small-town bank branch, he did something unusual. He learned every subordinate's name, ate lunch with the junior staff, and gave them credit in front of the head office. His subordinates worked harder for him than for any manager before. Sub means below, as in subway, and ordinate comes from order, rank: a subordinate is ranked below you. So, what word describes someone lower in rank?... Subordinate.
subordinate.example: In the young architect's designs, beauty is always subordinate to safety, so every balcony is built to hold twice the required load.

gre.s: In the director's view, every other goal was ____ to profit: any project that failed to raise revenue was promptly cancelled.
gre.clue: any project that failed to raise revenue was promptly cancelled

tedious.story: Tedious. So long, slow or dull that it becomes tiring. Neil arrived at the passport office at seven in the morning. He waited in one line for a token, another for photos and fingerprints, and a third for a signature. The fans barely turned, and the queue barely moved. By late afternoon, he finally walked out with a receipt. It had been the most tedious day of his life. Tedious comes from tedium, meaning weary boredom. So, what word describes a task so slow and dull that it wears you out?... Tedious.
tedious.example: Sorting ten thousand old photographs by date was tedious work, but it let the museum trace how the city's skyline had changed.

gre.s: Although the documentary covered a fascinating subject, its endless statistics and droning narration made it ____ for most viewers.
gre.clue: endless statistics and droning narration

tentative.hook: TENTATIVE: like a TENT, temporary, not permanent.
tentative.story: Tentative. Not certain or fixed; also, hesitant. One evening in the courtyard of their home, eleven-month-old Ivy let go of the bench and took her first tentative step. She wobbled, waved her arms, and took another. The whole family held its breath, then cheered so loudly that she sat down in surprise. The next day her steps were less tentative. Tentative shares its Latin root with attempt: a tentative step is only a try. So, what word describes something hesitant, not yet sure?... Tentative.
tentative.example: The toddler took a few tentative steps across the courtyard before sitting down hard and laughing at herself.

gre.s: The two governments reached only a ____ agreement, one that both sides stressed could be revised or even abandoned after further talks.
gre.clue: could be revised or even abandoned after further talks

turbulent.hook: TURBULENT: like airplane TURBULENCE, shaking and chaotic.
turbulent.story: Turbulent. Full of disorder, conflict or violent movement. Where two great rivers meet, and in the monsoon their waters churn together. When Nancy's ferry crossed that stretch one stormy July evening, the deck rolled, waves slapped over the rails, and passengers gripped each other's arms. The water was turbulent for almost an hour before it calmed. Think of turbulence on a plane, when the cabin shakes; turbulent shares its root with disturb. So, what word describes water, or times, full of wild and violent movement?... Turbulent.
turbulent.example: The 1790s were a turbulent decade in France, as revolution, terror and war followed one another in quick succession.

gre.s: The country's ____ history, marked by frequent coups and civil unrest, makes its recent decade of stability all the more remarkable.
gre.clue: marked by frequent coups and civil unrest

barrage.hook: BARRAGE: like a BARRAGE of artillery fire.
barrage.story: Barrage. An overwhelming outpouring of many things at once. The day Mitch's university results came out, he went to his grandmother's house for lunch. Before he could sit down, the relatives began. What was his grade? Which job would he get? Why was he so thin? When would he marry? Mitch smiled and kept eating through the barrage. Think of a barrage of artillery, shell after shell falling at once; a barrage of questions is just as relentless. So, what word means a flood of many things coming at you all at once?... Barrage.
barrage.example: The new referee faced a barrage of whistles and jeers from the home fans after he disallowed their team's late goal.

gre.s: Upon announcing the controversial policy, the minister faced a ____ of criticism so relentless that she withdrew the proposal within a week.
gre.clue: so relentless that she withdrew the proposal within a week

barren.hook: BARREN: as empty as a BARREL with nothing inside.
barren.story: Barren. Unable to produce crops or results; empty. After a storm surge swept salt water across the coastal fields, Albert's land lay barren for two years. Nothing grew but a white crust of salt, cracking under the sun. Every morning he walked the empty field, and every morning he came back with nothing. Then the rains slowly washed the soil clean, and the first green shoots appeared. Barren is the opposite of fertile: a barren field gives nothing back. So, what word describes land too empty to grow anything?... Barren.
barren.example: Salt water from repeated storm surges has left many coastal fields in Khulna barren, and farmers there have turned to raising crabs.

gre.s: Years of intensive farming without rest had left the once fertile valley ____, its exhausted soil yielding barely enough to feed the families who tilled it.
gre.clue: its exhausted soil yielding barely enough

betray.hook: GRE trick: BETRAY often means REVEAL — your trembling hands betray your nerves.
betray.story: Betray. To be disloyal; also, to reveal something without meaning to. At her thesis defence, Madeline answered every question in a calm, steady voice. She seemed perfectly confident. But under the table her hands were trembling, and when she reached for her glass of water, it shook so much it spilled. Her hands betrayed her nerves. The examiners smiled kindly, and she passed. On the GRE, betray often means reveal: a blush can betray embarrassment. So, what verb means to give away a hidden feeling without intending to?... Betray.
betray.example: The card player kept a straight face, but a slight tremor in his voice betrayed his excitement about the hand he held.

gre.s: Although the novelist insists her characters are invented, certain details ____ an intimate knowledge of her own family's history.
gre.clue: Although the novelist insists her characters are invented

bogus.hook: BOGUS sounds like a fake BOGEYMAN — not real.
bogus.story: Bogus. Fake or false, though made to look real. At a weekly country market, a man with a loudspeaker stood on a wooden box, waving a small bottle of oil. It cured headaches, baldness, joint pain and even a broken heart, he shouted, all for just one dollar. A small crowd gathered. Old Joe shook his head and walked on. The man's claims were completely bogus. Bogus sounds a little like bogeyman, and like a bogeyman, it is not real. So, what word describes a claim that is fake but dressed up to look real?... Bogus.
bogus.example: Tax officials uncovered dozens of bogus companies that existed only as names on paper and were used to move money abroad.

gre.s: Investigators discovered that the clinic's impressive medical certificates were ____, printed by a shop that specialized in forgeries.
gre.clue: printed by a shop that specialized in forgeries

contemplate.hook: CONTEMPLATE: sit in the TEMPLE and think.
contemplate.story: Contemplate. To think deeply about something; also, to consider it as a possibility. When Simon received a job offer in Canada, he did not answer right away. That evening, he sat alone on the river steps in his hometown, watching the river turn gold. He contemplated his parents growing older, the friends he would miss, and the life he might build far away. Contemplate has temple inside it, from the Latin for a sacred space where priests watched the sky. So, what verb means to think long and deeply?... Contemplate.
contemplate.example: Only after the third flood in five years did the family contemplate selling their land and moving to Gazipur.

gre.s: Although the board had once rejected the idea outright, the company's mounting losses forced its directors at least to ____ a merger with their longtime rival.
gre.clue: mounting losses forced its directors at least to

counterfeit.hook: COUNTER-FEIT: made COUNTER to the real one.
counterfeit.story: Counterfeit. Fake; made to look like the real thing in order to deceive. Before the holiday, Bob sold his best bull at a big cattle market. The buyer paid with a thick bundle of large notes. Something felt wrong, so Bob took the bundle to the bank booth set up at the market. The officer held a note under ultraviolet light. Half the bundle was counterfeit. Counter means against, and feit comes from the French for made: counterfeit money is made against the real thing. So, what word describes fake money made to deceive?... Counterfeit.
counterfeit.example: Pharmacists warn that counterfeit medicines, which look identical to the real ones, may contain nothing but chalk and sugar.

gre.s: The handbags looked convincingly authentic, but customs officials determined that they were ____, manufactured in an unlicensed workshop and stamped with a stolen logo.
gre.clue: manufactured in an unlicensed workshop and stamped with a stolen logo

daunting.hook: DAUNTING sounds like 'DON'T even try', which is what the task seems to say.
daunting.story: Daunting. So difficult that it seems discouraging. On her first night of GRE preparation, Rose opened a list of three thousand words. She scrolled and scrolled, and the list never seemed to end. It felt daunting, almost impossible. Then her tutor showed her how to learn just thirty words a day, with a story for each one. One small set at a time, the mountain became a staircase. The opposite is undaunted, meaning not discouraged at all. So, what word describes a task so big that it seems to say: do not even try?... Daunting.
daunting.example: Swimming across the Bosphorus seemed daunting to Rehana, but she trained for a year and finished the race in under two hours.

gre.s: Though the task of cataloguing ten thousand manuscripts seemed ____ at first, the archivists found it manageable once they divided the work.
gre.clue: found it manageable once they divided the work

discreet.hook: DISCREET keeps secrets; DISCRETE means separate. Two E's together are 'discreet' — they keep each other's secrets.
discreet.story: Discreet. Careful about what you say or do, to avoid offence or keep secrets. When Sheila's father lost his job, the family had no money for her school fees. Her neighbour, Aunt Ruth, heard about it. She did not tell anyone in the lane. Instead, she quietly paid the fees and slipped the receipt to Sheila's mother in a folded newspaper. Nobody else ever knew. She was always discreet. Discreet keeps secrets; discrete means separate. In discreet, the two e's sit together, keeping each other's secret. So, what word describes someone careful to keep things private?... Discreet.
discreet.example: The hotel staff are famously discreet, so film stars can stay there for weeks without their visit appearing in the papers.

gre.s: The ambassador was chosen for the delicate mission because she was famously ____, never revealing confidential information even to close friends.
gre.clue: never revealing confidential information even to close friends

dormant.story: Dormant. Inactive for now, as if asleep, but able to wake later. Tess's grandmother had been a fine singer as a young bride, but she stopped singing when life grew busy. For forty years her voice stayed silent. Then, at Tess's wedding, the women began a folk song and forgot the second verse. Grandmother quietly sang it, clear and strong. Her talent had only been dormant. Dormant comes from the Latin for sleep, as in dormitory, the room where students sleep. So, what word describes something sleeping now, but able to wake again?... Dormant.
dormant.example: The chickenpox virus can lie dormant in nerve cells for decades before returning as shingles later in life.

gre.s: Scientists warned that the volcano, though ____ for nearly two centuries, had begun showing signs of renewed activity and could erupt within months.
gre.clue: had begun showing signs of renewed activity

emulate.hook: EMULATE: your hero's EMblem; you copy them to become as good.
emulate.story: Emulate. To imitate someone you admire, hoping to equal or surpass them. When Jill's cousin became the first doctor from their village, the whole village came out to greet her. Jill was twelve. From that day she tried to emulate her cousin in every way: she woke early to study, and kept neat notes. Ten years later, Jill entered medical college too. Emulate means more than copy; it carries a sense of friendly rivalry, aiming to match your hero. So, what verb means to copy someone you admire, hoping to match them?... Emulate.
emulate.example: Hoping to emulate South Korea's rapid rise, the government poured money into technical schools and electronics factories.

gre.s: Many young composers sought to ____ the master's style, hoping that by imitating his methods they might one day equal his achievements.
gre.clue: hoping that by imitating his methods they might one day equal

evade.story: Evade. To escape or dodge something, often cleverly. Every Friday, Erin's family tries to give their cat Muffin a bath. Every Friday, she evades them. She slips under the bed, squeezes behind the fridge, and once climbed onto the top of the cupboard. This week, three people chased her for half an hour, and she still evaded every hand. Evade comes from the Latin for going out: e means out, so to evade is to slip out of reach. So, what verb means to cleverly dodge or escape something?... Evade.
evade.example: The fox evaded the hunting dogs by doubling back through a shallow stream, where they lost its scent.

gre.s: The fugitive managed to ____ capture for nearly a decade by moving constantly and using a series of false identities.
gre.clue: by moving constantly and using a series of false identities

extravagant.hook: EXTRA-VAGANT: goes EXTRA far beyond limits.
extravagant.story: Extravagant. Spending far too much; excessive and beyond what is sensible. With his very first salary, Robert bought the newest phone on the market, paying almost three months' wages in instalments. He showed it proudly to his mother. She held it, quiet for a moment, then thought of the leaking roof at home. "Very beautiful," she said softly. Robert suddenly felt how extravagant it was. Extra means beyond, and vagant comes from the Latin for wandering, as in vagabond: extravagant spending wanders far beyond the limits. So, what word describes spending that goes far too far?... Extravagant.
extravagant.example: The club's extravagant spending on foreign players left it unable to pay its groundskeepers by the end of the season.

gre.s: Critics condemned the mayor's ____ renovation of his office, which included marble floors and gold fixtures, at a time of severe budget cuts.
gre.clue: marble floors and gold fixtures

futile.story: Futile. Producing no useful result; pointless. Caught in a sudden city downpour, Rhonda sat in a rickshaw with a thin plastic sheet held over her knees. She pulled it up to her chin, and the rain soaked her back. She tucked it behind her, and the rain soaked her feet. Within minutes she was wet from head to toe. She gave up and let the rain fall. Every effort had been futile. Futile comes from the Latin for leaky: like pouring water into a leaking pot. So, what word describes an effort that achieves nothing?... Futile.
futile.example: Bailing water out of the leaking boat was futile, so the fishermen rowed hard for the nearest sandbank instead.

gre.s: Realizing that further resistance would be ____, the outnumbered garrison surrendered without firing another shot.
gre.clue: the outnumbered garrison surrendered

hinder.story: Hinder. To create difficulties that slow something down. On the morning of her final exam, Shelby stepped out of her house to find the road under knee-deep water. No rickshaw would come. The flood hindered her at every step, but she tied up her dress, held her bag over her head, and waded for twenty minutes. She reached the hall just in time. The water could hinder her, but not stop her. Hinder shares its root with hind and behind: what hinders you holds you back. So, what verb means to slow someone down with obstacles?... Hinder.
hinder.example: Thick smoke from the burning warehouse hindered the firefighters, who could barely see the hoses in their own hands.

gre.s: Bureaucratic delays continue to ____ the delivery of aid, leaving thousands of flood victims without food.
gre.clue: leaving thousands of flood victims without food

hypocrite.hook: HYPOCRITE: a Greek actor (hypokrites), playing a role.
hypocrite.story: Hypocrite. A person who claims beliefs or virtues they do not practise. At every family dinner, Uncle Morris gives the children a long speech about phones. No screens at the table, he says; talk to each other. One evening, little Robbie noticed his uncle's phone glowing under the tablecloth, and he was watching cricket. Everyone saw it. Uncle Morris blushed and admitted he was a hypocrite. Hypocrite comes from the Greek word for an actor on a stage, playing a role. So, what do you call someone who preaches what they do not practise?... Hypocrite.
hypocrite.example: Ruma called her brother a hypocrite for nagging her about screen time while he scrolled through his phone at every meal.

gre.s: The minister who lectured citizens about saving electricity was exposed as a ____ when reporters discovered that his own residence ran air conditioners day and night.
gre.clue: his own residence ran air conditioners day and night

indefinite.story: Indefinite. Lasting for an unknown length of time; not clearly defined. One morning, a notice went up at Russell's university: all classes were suspended for an indefinite period. No date for reopening, no reason given. Students packed their bags and went home, unsure whether to study, find a job or simply wait. For Russell, the indefinite break felt like a pause button nobody would press again. Indefinite means not definite: no fixed end, no clear limit. So, what word describes a period with no fixed end?... Indefinite.
indefinite.example: After the knee injury, the striker was ruled out for an indefinite period, and the club began searching for a replacement.

gre.s: The strike was declared to be ____: union leaders refused to set any end date and vowed to continue until every one of their demands had been met.
gre.clue: refused to set any end date

intermittent.hook: INTER-MITTENT: stopping and starting, with gaps IN BETWEEN.
intermittent.story: Intermittent. Starting and stopping at irregular times. Annie was in the middle of an online interview with a university abroad when her internet began to fail. The screen froze, then came back, then froze again. The professor's voice arrived in pieces. Annie kept smiling, repeating her answers patiently, while her brother ran to restart the router. The connection stayed intermittent all hour, but she got the offer. Inter means between, and the word means leaving gaps in between. So, what word describes something that keeps stopping and starting?... Intermittent.
intermittent.example: The lighthouse gives out an intermittent flash, so sailors can tell it apart from the steady lights of the town behind it.

gre.s: Electricity in the village was ____ at best, flickering on for an hour or so and then vanishing for the rest of the evening.
gre.clue: flickering on for an hour or so and then vanishing

lavish.hook: LAVISH: like a LAVA flow of luxury.
lavish.story: Lavish. Rich and generous; as a verb, to give generously. When her grandchildren visit her for the holidays, Grandma lavishes food on them from morning to night. There is beef curry, three kinds of fish, spiced rice, sweet yogurt, and fresh rice cakes every afternoon. The children beg her to stop. She only fills their plates again. It is a lavish welcome, every single year. Lavish comes from an old French word for a downpour of rain: lavish generosity pours down like rain. So, what word describes a welcome that is rich and generous?... Lavish.
lavish.example: For the school's hundredth anniversary, former students paid for a lavish dinner in the courtyard, with musicians brought from Kolkata.

gre.s: Critics accused the company of hypocrisy: even as it cut workers' wages, it held a ____ banquet for its executives, complete with imported wine and live music.
gre.clue: complete with imported wine and live music

mundane.story: Mundane. Ordinary and everyday, with nothing exciting about it. Every day, Harold wakes at six, takes the same bus to his office downtown, files the same papers, and comes home at seven. When his daughter asked what he did at work, he said it was all mundane. Then she showed him her school diary: every evening, she had written how happy she felt when he came home. His mundane life meant everything to her. Mundane comes from the Latin mundus, world: mundane things belong to the everyday world. So, what word describes life that is ordinary and routine?... Mundane.
mundane.example: The poet's notebooks are full of mundane lists, such as eggs, lamp oil and stamps, scribbled between drafts of famous poems.

gre.s: The novelist has a gift for transforming ____ events, such as a trip to the grocery store, into moments of startling beauty.
gre.clue: such as a trip to the grocery store

ominous.hook: OMINOUS: an OMEN of bad things.
ominous.story: Ominous. Suggesting that something bad is about to happen. Crossing the old bamboo bridge over the canal near his school, Jacob heard a long, low creak beneath his feet. Then another, louder. The whole bridge swayed slightly. The sound was ominous. He hurried back to the bank and warned the other children to go around by the road. Two days later, the middle of the bridge collapsed. Ominous comes from omen, a sign of what is to come. So, what word describes a sound or sign that warns of trouble ahead?... Ominous.
ominous.example: An ominous creak came from the old wooden bridge as the loaded truck rolled slowly onto it.

gre.s: The doctors' sudden silence and averted eyes were ____, and the family braced themselves for bad news before a single word was spoken.
gre.clue: braced themselves for bad news

provocative.story: Provocative. Causing a strong reaction, especially anger or deep interest. The topic at the university debate was, "Exams kill learning." Half the audience murmured angrily before anyone had spoken. Teachers frowned. Students leaned forward. By the end, the hall was arguing loudly, and the discussion went on for hours in the canteen. The topic was deliberately provocative. Provocative comes from provoke, to call forth a reaction. So, what word describes something designed to stir strong feelings?... Provocative.
provocative.example: The columnist's provocative claim that cricket was ruining Bangladeshi schools drew thousands of angry letters in a single week.

gre.s: The museum's ____ exhibit, featuring images designed to shock, drew both furious protests and record crowds.
gre.clue: featuring images designed to shock

prudent.hook: PRUDENT: a PRUDE about risk; careful, never wild.
prudent.story: Prudent. Careful, sensible and thinking about the future. For years, Carrie's mother set aside a small part of every salary in a savings account. Her husband teased her, saying she should enjoy the money now. Then the factory where he worked closed, and he was without a job for eight months. Those savings paid for rent, food and school fees until he found new work. Her husband never teased her again. She had been prudent. Prudent is a shortened form of provident: seeing ahead and providing for it. So, what word describes someone wise and careful about the future?... Prudent.
prudent.example: Before the long hike, the students thought it prudent to leave a copy of their route with the forest office at Lawachara.

gre.s: Given the volatile market, analysts considered it ____ to diversify investments rather than stake everything on a single stock.
gre.clue: rather than stake everything on a single stock

repertoire.hook: REPERTOIRE: the REPORT of everything you can perform.
repertoire.story: Repertoire. The full set of songs, skills or works that someone can perform. On the slow country train, a blind singer named Clarence walks from coach to coach with his old guitar. Passengers call out requests: old folk songs, hymns, old film songs, even new ones from the radio. He seems to know them all, hundreds of songs held in memory. His repertoire never runs dry. Repertoire comes from the Latin for an inventory, a full list of everything stored. So, what word means the complete range of songs or skills someone can perform?... Repertoire.
repertoire.example: By her third season, the young spin bowler had added a quicker ball and a googly to her repertoire.

gre.s: Although the pianist was celebrated mainly for her Chopin, her ____ was surprisingly broad, extending from medieval dances to experimental contemporary works.
gre.clue: extending from medieval dances to experimental contemporary works

sanction.hook: SANCTION has two opposite meanings: APPROVAL and PUNISHMENT. Watch the context!
sanction.story: Sanction. To give official approval; also, a penalty for breaking a rule. The school committee finally sanctioned the class ten picnic to the beach. The students cheered so loudly the headmaster had to cover his ears. Then he announced the rules: anyone caught littering on the beach would face sanctions, including a week of cleaning the school grounds. Sanction has two opposite meanings: approval, and punishment. Watch the context. So, what word can mean both official permission and a penalty?... Sanction.
sanction.example: The cricket board refused to sanction the tour, so the players travelled to the tournament as private individuals.

gre.s: Although the council refused to formally ____ the festival, it took no action to stop the residents from holding it.
gre.clue: it took no action to stop the residents

strife.story: Strife. Angry, bitter quarrelling between people or groups. After their father died, three brothers in a farming town fought over his land for years. They took each other to court, stopped attending each other's weddings, and their children grew up as strangers. The strife spread to wives, cousins, and even neighbours. At last their elderly mother gathered them in the courtyard and said she would not live to see it continue. The strife ended that day. Strife is related to strive: both involve struggle. So, what word means bitter conflict between people?... Strife.
strife.example: Years of family strife over the inheritance ended only when the eldest sister sold the house and divided the money equally.

gre.s: Years of ethnic ____ had left the region impoverished, its villages divided and its farms abandoned.
gre.clue: its villages divided and its farms abandoned

stringent.hook: STRINGENT: tied up with tight STRINGS.
stringent.story: Stringent. Strict, precise and demanding. At the export garment factory where Sandra works, every shirt passes through stringent checks. Inspectors measure each seam with a ruler, count stitches per inch, and pull on every button. One loose thread, and the shirt goes back. Sandra once found the rules too stringent, but now she is proud that her shirts sell in shops around the world. Stringent shares a Latin root with strict and constrict, meaning to draw tight. So, what word describes rules that are strict and exacting?... Stringent.
stringent.example: Garment factories in Gazipur must now meet stringent fire safety rules, including sprinklers and at least two exits on every floor.

gre.s: Because the drug's side effects were potentially severe, regulators imposed ____ testing requirements before approving it.
gre.clue: potentially severe

ubiquitous.story: Ubiquitous. Seeming to be everywhere at once. Wherever you go in the country, you find a tea stall. On city corners and village crossroads, beside ferry landings and hospital gates, at bus stops and university gates, someone is pouring milky tea into small glass cups. Andy's friend from Japan said he had never seen anything so ubiquitous. Ubiquitous comes from the Latin ubique, meaning everywhere. So, what word describes something you find everywhere you look?... Ubiquitous.
ubiquitous.example: Plastic is now so ubiquitous that scientists have found tiny fragments of it in Arctic snow and even in human blood.

gre.s: Once a luxury owned by a privileged few, the mobile phone has become so ____ that even remote villages now rely on it for banking.
gre.clue: Once a luxury owned by a privileged few

visionary.hook: VISIONARY: has a VISION of the future.
visionary.story: Visionary. Thinking about the future with imagination and wisdom. Thirty years ago, on a remote river island, Helen started a school for girls on a boat. Parents laughed, saying girls would only marry young anyway. She ignored them. The boat sailed from village to village, carrying books and a teacher. Today, many of her students are teachers and nurses. Everyone now calls her a visionary. Visionary comes from vision: a visionary sees a future others cannot yet imagine. So, what word describes someone who imagines a better future and builds it?... Visionary.
visionary.example: Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain was a visionary who imagined, in 1905, a land where women ran the country and men stayed at home.

gre.s: Dismissed in her own time as a dreamer, the urban planner is now hailed as a ____ whose ideas anticipated modern sustainable cities.
gre.clue: whose ideas anticipated modern sustainable cities

vitality.story: Vitality. Lively energy and strength of body or spirit. Every morning at six, a seventy-year-old woman named Flora leads a walking group around the city park. She walks faster than people half her age, cracks jokes, and scolds anyone who falls behind. Younger members try to keep up, panting. Her vitality inspires the whole group. Vitality comes from the Latin vita, life, as in vital and vitamin: vitality is life energy itself. So, what word means lively energy and spirit?... Vitality.
vitality.example: Street vendors, buskers and late-night tea stalls give the old quarter a vitality that the new shopping malls cannot match.

gre.s: Even at eighty, the sculptor retained a remarkable ____, working twelve hours a day and climbing scaffolding that exhausted assistants half her age.
gre.clue: working twelve hours a day

warranted.story: Warranted. Justified; having good reason. When Megan's mother made her carry a raincoat on a sunny day in the hills, Megan rolled her eyes all the way to the bus stop. By afternoon, black clouds rolled in and heavy rain hammered the city. Megan pulled out the raincoat, dry and grateful. Her mother's caution had been warranted. A warrant is an official document that gives authority; warranted means backed by good reason. Unwarranted means without reason. So, what word describes worry or action that is justified?... Warranted.
warranted.example: The coach's anger was warranted, since three players had skipped training to attend a party the night before the final.

gre.s: Given the company's long record of concealing defects, the regulators' skepticism about its latest safety claims seems entirely ____.
gre.clue: Given the company's long record of concealing defects

affluent.story: Affluent. Wealthy; having plenty of money. Every winter, Lucy's family took the bus across town to visit her mother's cousin in the wealthy part of the city. The gate opened onto a green lawn and a dining table so long that Lucy counted the chairs twice. Her cousin was kind, but Lucy suddenly felt shy in her old school shoes. It was her first close look at an affluent home. Affluent comes from the Latin for flowing toward, the same root as fluent: in an affluent family, money simply flows in. So, what word describes a family with plenty of money?... Affluent.
affluent.example: As the suburb grew more affluent, its small tailoring shops gave way to boutiques selling imported clothes.

gre.s: Although the town was once ____, sustained by a booming textile trade, it sank into poverty when the mills closed and its young people moved away.
gre.clue: sustained by a booming textile trade

all-encompassing.hook: ALL-ENCOMPASSING: a COMPASS that circles everything.
all-encompassing.story: All-encompassing. Covering every part, leaving nothing out. In the last month before Natalie's final school exams, her preparation took over the whole house. Formula charts were taped to the kitchen wall, her younger brother quizzed her at breakfast, and her father stopped watching the evening news so the flat stayed quiet. Nobody in the family escaped it. The exam had become all-encompassing. To encompass is to draw a circle around something, like the circle a compass makes, so an all-encompassing thing holds everything inside its circle. So, what word describes something that takes in every part, leaving nothing out?... All-encompassing.
all-encompassing.example: Her grief after the accident was all-encompassing, colouring every meal, every conversation and every song she heard on the radio.

gre.s: Far from the narrow survey its modest title suggested, the study was nearly ____, covering every aspect of the region's economy from river fishing to software.
gre.clue: covering every aspect of the region's economy

analogous.story: Analogous. Similar or comparable in some way. The class nine biology students were lost in diagrams of the heart. Then their teacher, Mister Kelly, pointed out of the window at the tube well in the school yard. "The heart pushes blood the way that pump pushes water, and its valves stop the flow from running back." One by one, the faces lit up. The heart is analogous to a pump. Analogous and analogy share a Greek root: analogous things are alike enough to make an analogy. So, what word describes two things similar enough to compare?... Analogous.
analogous.example: A bird's wing and a butterfly's wing are analogous structures, since both allow flight but they evolved entirely separately.

gre.s: The author argues that the decline of the empire is ____ to the collapse of a modern corporation, since both were undone by overexpansion and internal rivalry.
gre.clue: since both were undone by overexpansion and internal rivalry

archaic.hook: ARCHAIC: as old as ARCHAEOLOGY digs.
archaic.story: Archaic. Very old-fashioned; no longer in everyday use. In a tin trunk at her grandmother's house, Jade found a bundle of letters from the nineteen sixties, written in a grand, formal old style. She read one aloud, stumbling over the grand, stiff verbs, and her grandmother clapped her hands. "That is how we wrote then!" To Jade the language sounded archaic, yet she loved every line. Archaic shares a Greek root with archaeology, the study of ancient things: archaic words belong to an older world. So, what word describes language no longer in everyday use?... Archaic.
archaic.example: Several archaic words, such as thou and hath, survive in the old hymns the choir still sings each Christmas.

gre.s: Although the statute remains on the books, it is so ____ that no court has enforced it in over a century.
gre.clue: no court has enforced it in over a century

byzantine.hook: BYZANTINE: like the ancient Byzantine Empire's maze-like bureaucracy.
byzantine.story: Byzantine. Excessively complicated and confusing, especially rules and paperwork. To register his small tailoring shop, Carl needed a form from one office, a stamp from another, and a signature from an officer who was never at his desk. Each clerk sent him to a different floor. After three months in hot corridors, he was holding the same form he started with. The process was byzantine. The word recalls the Byzantine Empire, whose court became famous for its maze of officials and rules. So, what word describes paperwork so tangled that nobody can find a way through?... Byzantine.
byzantine.example: Getting a refund from the airline involved a byzantine process of forms, phone calls and emails that dragged on for nearly six months.

gre.s: The tax code has become so ____ that even professional accountants struggle to navigate its thousands of overlapping rules and exceptions.
gre.clue: thousands of overlapping rules and exceptions

censor.hook: CENSOR: CUTS out what's forbidden. Not censure (criticize).
censor.story: Censor. To examine books, films or news and remove the parts considered unacceptable. Hannah's grandfather edited a newspaper during a time of strict government control. Every night, officials read his pages and cut out any line they disliked. Some mornings the paper appeared with blank white columns, and readers understood exactly what had been censored. The officials were called censors, a title borrowed from ancient Roman officers who judged public behaviour. Do not confuse it with censure, which means to criticise harshly. So, what verb means to cut parts from the news before anyone reads them?... Censor.
censor.example: Wartime officials censored soldiers' letters home, blacking out any mention of where the troops were stationed.

gre.s: Rather than ____ the novel's explicit passages, as the publisher had demanded, the author withdrew the manuscript entirely, insisting that every word remain intact.
gre.clue: insisting that every word remain intact

conspicuous.hook: CON-SPIC-uous: SPIC sounds like 'spec', as in spectacle. Everyone can see it.
conspicuous.story: Conspicuous. Standing out clearly; easy to notice. At his cousin's wedding, everyone wore soft pastel colours. Then Austin walked in wearing the bright orange suit his mother had chosen. Heads turned and aunties whispered. Austin felt his ears grow hot, but his little niece ran over, and said he looked like a marigold. He was the most conspicuous man in the hall. The spic inside conspicuous comes from the Latin for look, as in spectacle: a conspicuous thing makes everyone look. So, what word describes something impossible to miss?... Conspicuous.
conspicuous.example: As the only tall tree among the paddy fields, the old palm is conspicuous from miles away and guides travelers to the village.

gre.s: The detective was puzzled that the thief had chosen such a ____ getaway car, a bright yellow convertible that half the town would remember.
gre.clue: half the town would remember

cosmopolitan.hook: COSMOS = world, POLIS = city. A citizen of the world.
cosmopolitan.story: Cosmopolitan. At ease in many countries and cultures. Megan's aunt has worked as a nurse in London, Nairobi and Toronto. At a family dinner, she chatted with a visiting Japanese engineer, switched to Spanish to tease her nephews, then explained a Kenyan bean stew to Megan's grandmother. She seemed at home with everyone. Megan decided she wanted to be that cosmopolitan one day. The word joins the Greek kosmos, world, and polites, citizen, so a cosmopolitan person is a citizen of the world. So, what word describes someone comfortable in many cultures?... Cosmopolitan.
cosmopolitan.example: Chattogram has long been a cosmopolitan port, where Arab, Portuguese and Burmese traders once mingled along the banks of the Karnaphuli.

gre.s: The port's ____ character, shaped by centuries of traders from dozens of nations, contrasted sharply with the insular villages of the interior.
gre.clue: contrasted sharply with the insular villages

delusion.hook: DELUSION: an ILLUSION you won't let go of.
delusion.story: Delusion. A false belief someone clings to despite clear proof. Trevor skipped every mock test, yet he told his friends he would score near the top of the GRE because he was naturally sharp. When his practice scores came back low, he blamed the website. Finally his friend Sally said gently, "Trevor, the scores are real. Let's study together." Slowly, the delusion cracked. An illusion fools your eyes; a delusion fools your mind, and you refuse to let it go. So, what word means a false belief held on to against all evidence?... Delusion.
delusion.example: Many smokers cling to the delusion that they can quit whenever they like, long after the habit has taken hold.

gre.s: Despite mounting evidence that his company was bankrupt, the founder clung to the ____ that a single blockbuster product would restore its fortunes.
gre.clue: Despite mounting evidence that his company was bankrupt

disciple.hook: DISCIPLE: follows the DISCIPLINE of a master.
disciple.story: Disciple. A follower of a teacher, leader or way of thinking. Every evening, in an old house by the river, a group of young singers sat on the floor learning folk songs from an elderly master. They copied his breath, his gestures, even the way he closed his eyes. Years later, one of them became famous, and in every interview he called himself a humble disciple of that master. Disciple and discipline come from the same Latin root for learning: a disciple accepts a teacher's discipline. So, what word means a devoted follower of a teacher?... Disciple.
disciple.example: As a young disciple of the sitar master, Nazmul spent years practising scales before he was allowed to perform in public.

gre.s: Far from rejecting his mentor's theories, the young economist proved to be her most faithful ____, defending her ideas long after the rest of the profession had abandoned them.
gre.clue: defending her ideas long after the rest of the profession had abandoned them

divergent.hook: DI-VERGE: two paths going different ways.
divergent.story: Divergent. Moving apart in different directions; different from each other. Twin sisters Penny and Polly shared one room, one bicycle and one cricket bat until they were eighteen. Then their paths split. Penny went to study medicine in the capital, while Polly stayed in their hill town, took over their father's tea stall and later opened her own small restaurant. Their lives became divergent, yet every night they still talked on the phone. To diverge is to split away, like a road forking in two; its opposite, converge, means to come together. So, what word describes paths that move apart?... Divergent.
divergent.example: Raised in the same house, the two cousins held sharply divergent views on almost every political question of the day.

gre.s: The two economists' forecasts are sharply ____, one predicting rapid growth and the other a deep recession.
gre.clue: one predicting rapid growth and the other a deep recession

eclectic.hook: ECLECTIC: ELECTS a bit from everywhere.
eclectic.story: Eclectic. Choosing freely from many different sources or styles. Jodie's dorm room surprises every visitor. A classical record sits beside a Korean pop poster, an old banjo hangs above a shelf of Japanese comics, and her bedspread is a patchwork quilt her grandmother stitched. Her friends call it a museum. Jodie simply says she keeps whatever she loves. Her taste is eclectic. The word comes from a Greek verb meaning to pick out, so think of select: an eclectic person selects the best from everywhere. So, what word describes taste drawn from many different styles?... Eclectic.
eclectic.example: Nilufar's bookshelf is wonderfully eclectic, holding Bengali folk tales, Russian novels, cookbooks and a manual for repairing motorbikes.

gre.s: The architect's style resists easy categorization: drawing freely on Mughal domes, Bauhaus minimalism, and rural bamboo construction, it is thoroughly ____.
gre.clue: drawing freely on Mughal domes, Bauhaus minimalism, and rural bamboo construction

endemic.hook: EN-DEMIC: IN the people (demos), always present there.
endemic.story: Endemic. Regularly found in a particular place or among a particular group. Every monsoon, as rainwater gathers in flowerpots and old tyres, dengue returns to the city. Doctors are no longer surprised; hospitals prepare beds before the rains even begin. Dengue is endemic in that region, always present, rising and falling with the seasons. The word can also describe plants or animals native to one place. Endemic joins en, meaning in, and demos, meaning people: it lives in the people. Its cousin epidemic is a sudden outbreak. So, what word describes a disease that is always present in one region?... Endemic.
endemic.example: Cheating was endemic at the exam centre, so the board sent outside invigilators and installed cameras in every hall.

gre.s: Corruption was so ____ in the old regime that bribery was considered a routine cost of doing business rather than a scandal.
gre.clue: considered a routine cost of doing business rather than a scandal

equitable.story: Equitable. Fair and impartial. When their father decided to retire and divide his mango orchard, three brothers feared a quarrel. Their father walked the whole orchard, counted every tree, and drew the lines so that each son got the same number of fruiting trees and an equal path to the pond. The youngest brother smiled with relief. Everyone agreed the division was equitable. Equitable shares its root with equal and equity: an equitable split is equal for all. So, what word describes a division that is fair to everyone?... Equitable.
equitable.example: The roommates worked out an equitable rota for washing dishes, based on how often each of them actually cooked.

gre.s: Critics argued that the new tax was hardly ____, since it fell most heavily on the poorest families while leaving the wealthy almost untouched.
gre.clue: fell most heavily on the poorest families while leaving the wealthy almost untouched

escalate.hook: ESCALATE: like an ESCALATOR, going up and up.
escalate.story: Escalate. To grow quickly bigger, worse or more serious. It began when a rickshaw brushed a motorbike's mirror in a narrow lane of the old city. The rider shouted, the rickshaw puller shouted back, and soon shopkeepers were taking sides. Within ten minutes a crowd blocked the lane. Then an old tea seller stepped in with two cups of tea and calmed everyone before it could escalate further. The word escalate was formed from escalator: picture a moving staircase carrying a quarrel up and up. So, what verb means to grow quickly more serious?... Escalate.
escalate.example: Prices at the cattle markets escalated sharply in the final days before Eid, as buyers rushed to find animals.

gre.s: What began as a minor quarrel over a parking space threatened to ____ into a brawl as neighbours poured out of their houses to take sides.
gre.clue: as neighbours poured out of their houses to take sides

immaculate.story: Immaculate. Perfectly clean and tidy; flawless. The night before the dorm inspection, Isabel scrubbed her floor twice, folded every dress, lined up her books by height, and wiped the window bars with a damp cloth. In the morning, the strict warden ran one finger along the shelf, looked at it, and found nothing. "Immaculate," she said, and for the first time she smiled. Isabel sank onto her bed. In Latin, macula means a spot or stain, so immaculate means without a single spot. So, what word describes a room so clean you cannot find a speck of dust?... Immaculate.
immaculate.example: Even after a twelve-hour flight, the captain's white uniform looked immaculate as he walked through the terminal.

gre.s: Though the pianist had been ill all week, her performance was ____: critics who listened for even a single wrong note found none.
gre.clue: critics who listened for even a single wrong note found none

ingenious.hook: INGENIOUS: a GENIUS idea. Not to be confused with ingenuous (innocent).
ingenious.story: Ingenious. Cleverly inventive, especially at solving problems. In the southern wetlands, fields stay underwater for months each year. Long ago, farmers there found an answer. They piled water hyacinth into thick floating rafts, topped them with mud, and grew vegetables that rose and fell with the water. On a field trip, Martin watched an old farmer pull fresh okra from a raft and felt a quiet pride. The floating gardens were ingenious. Ingenious shares a Latin root with engine, meaning natural talent; do not confuse it with ingenuous, innocent. So, what word describes a clever, inventive solution?... Ingenious.
ingenious.example: The ingenious puzzle box has no visible lock and opens only when its wooden panels are slid in a precise order.

gre.s: The engineer's ____ design, which used ordinary bicycle parts to power a water pump, succeeded where expensive imported machines had repeatedly failed.
gre.clue: used ordinary bicycle parts to power a water pump

intrigue.hook: INTRIGUE: the palace's secret plots that INTRIGUE you.
intrigue.story: Intrigue. A secret plot or scheme; as a verb, to make someone curious. Lena found a historical novel about the last prince of an old kingdom on her uncle's shelf. In its pages, courtiers whispered in dark corridors and plotted with foreign traders to bring their ruler down. The palace intrigue intrigued her so deeply that she read until two in the morning, catching her breath at every betrayal. Intrigue shares its root with intricate: both come from the Latin for tangled, and a plot is a tangle of secrets. So, what word names a secret plot, and also the curiosity it stirs?... Intrigue.
intrigue.example: The novel follows a young clerk caught up in the intrigue of a family firm, where cousins secretly plot to seize control.

gre.s: The royal court was rife with ____: ministers formed secret alliances, spread rumors about their rivals, and plotted against one another behind the king's back.
gre.clue: plotted against one another behind the king's back

opaque.hook: OPAQUE: light can't pass through; meaning can't pass through either.
opaque.story: Opaque. Letting no light through; also, hard to understand. The bathroom window in Steven's flat is frosted glass: light comes in, but no one can see through it. That same afternoon, his economics professor spent an hour on monetary policy, filling the board with symbols and never stopping for questions. Steven looked down at his notes and saw nothing but fog. The lecture was as opaque as his window. Opaque is the opposite of transparent: when meaning cannot pass through, an explanation is opaque. So, what word describes writing or speech you simply cannot see into?... Opaque.
opaque.example: The ministry's scholarship selection process remained opaque, and no applicant was ever told why they had been rejected.

gre.s: Critics complained that the company's accounting was deliberately ____, making it nearly impossible for investors to understand where the money went.
gre.clue: nearly impossible for investors to understand

pertinent.story: Pertinent. Closely connected to the subject being discussed. In his first job interview at a shipping company, Ricky was asked how he handled pressure. Instead, he described one night during his internship when a shipment was delayed and he called the port every hour until it moved. The panel leaned forward and nodded. His answer was short and pertinent. Pertinent sounds like pertain, and they share a root: a pertinent point pertains to the topic. So, what word describes a remark directly relevant to the matter at hand?... Pertinent.
pertinent.example: Before the vote, the councillor raised a pertinent question about who would pay to maintain the new park once it was built.

gre.s: The judge excluded the testimony as not ____ to the case, since it concerned events that occurred years after the alleged crime.
gre.clue: concerned events that occurred years after the alleged crime

pervasive.hook: PERVASIVE: PERVADES everything, like a smell filling a house.
pervasive.story: Pervasive. Spreading through every part of a place or group. On the first morning of the holidays, Frankie's mother fried onions for the biryani. Within minutes the rich smell had spread into every room, every curtain and every pillow. Two days later, Frankie opened his cupboard, and even his shirts smelled of onions. The smell was pervasive. Pervasive comes from pervade, from the Latin per, through, and vadere, to go: a pervasive thing goes through everything. So, what word describes something that has spread into every corner?... Pervasive.
pervasive.example: Fear of failure was so pervasive at the coaching centre that students hid their practice scores even from close friends.

gre.s: Researchers found the influence of social media so ____ that it shaped nearly every aspect of teenagers' daily lives.
gre.clue: shaped nearly every aspect of teenagers' daily lives

prescribe.story: Prescribe. To recommend a medicine; also, to state with authority what must be done. Tara went to a clinic with a fever. The doctor listened to her chest, then wrote on a slip of paper: one tablet three times a day and complete rest for five days. He had prescribed both medicine and rules, and Tara, who hated sitting still, reluctantly obeyed. Prescribe comes from the Latin for write before: the doctor writes down what must happen. Do not confuse it with proscribe, which means to forbid. So, what verb means to order a remedy?... Prescribe.
prescribe.example: School rules prescribe a white shirt and navy trousers, but many pupils add bright socks as a small act of rebellion.

gre.s: Unlike earlier grammarians, who sought to ____ rigid rules for correct usage, modern linguists aim merely to describe how people actually speak.
gre.clue: modern linguists aim merely to describe how people actually speak

resent.hook: RE-SENT: the insult is SENT back again and again in your mind.
resent.story: Resent. To feel bitter about unfair treatment. For years, Isaac's younger brother got the new clothes, the bigger room and all the praise, while Isaac carried the shopping and fixed the ceiling fan. He never complained aloud, but he resented every small unfairness. Then one holiday, his brother quietly handed him the first new shirt and said, "Your turn, big brother." Isaac felt the old resentment loosen. Resent comes from the French re, again, and sentir, to feel: to resent is to feel a hurt again and again. So, what verb means to feel bitter at being treated unfairly?... Resent.
resent.example: Local fishermen resent the new trawlers from the city, which sweep up in one night what a small boat catches in a month.

gre.s: Veteran staff members tended to ____ the newcomers' rapid promotions, which they attributed to favoritism rather than to merit.
gre.clue: which they attributed to favoritism rather than to merit

satirical.hook: SATIRICAL: SATIRE makes fun of the powerful.
satirical.story: Satirical. Using humour, irony or exaggeration to criticise foolishness. Every week, Curtis waits for the cartoon page of his newspaper. This week it showed a minister cutting the ribbon on a new bridge while the bridge itself floated away in the flood behind him. Curtis showed it to his father, and both laughed, then fell quiet. The joke had a sharp point about wasted money. The cartoon was satirical. Satire smiles, but it bites: its laughter always carries a criticism. So, what word describes humour used to expose foolishness or wrongdoing?... Satirical.
satirical.example: Swift's satirical essay proposed that the poor of Ireland sell their babies as food, a shocking idea meant to expose official cruelty.

gre.s: The magazine's ____ cartoons, which exaggerated the president's vanity to absurd lengths, made him a laughingstock across the country.
gre.clue: exaggerated the president's vanity to absurd lengths

sparse.story: Sparse. Thinly scattered; small in number or amount. One winter, Amanda's family drove far north. Near the city the roads were packed with shops and people, but by evening the villages grew sparse: a few tin roofs, a lone tea stall, wide fields of yellow mustard under fog. Amanda rolled down her window and breathed the cold, quiet air. Even the street lights were sparse. Sparse comes from the Latin for scattered, like seeds tossed loosely across a field. Its opposite is dense. So, what word describes things thinly scattered across a wide space?... Sparse.
sparse.example: Data on the rare river dolphins of the Sangu is sparse, so researchers rely partly on reports from local fishermen.

gre.s: Attendance at the lecture was ____: barely a dozen listeners sat dotted across an auditorium built to hold five hundred.
gre.clue: barely a dozen listeners

spartan.hook: SPARTAN: like the warriors of SPARTA, tough and simple.
spartan.story: Spartan. Simple and plain, with no comfort or luxury. When Zack joined a cadet college, his room held a narrow iron bed, a thin mattress, one table and a steel trunk. Wake-up was at five, the water was cold, and lights went out at ten. At first, he wrote home every night. By the end of the year, he was proud of how little he needed. Life there was spartan. The ancient Spartans of Greece were famous for their tough, simple way of life. So, what word describes a plain lifestyle with no luxuries at all?... Spartan.
spartan.example: Mountaineers on the expedition lived a spartan life, melting snow for water and sleeping in thin tents at minus thirty.

gre.s: The monks' ____ quarters contained nothing but a narrow cot, a wooden stool, and a single candle.
gre.clue: contained nothing but a narrow cot, a wooden stool, and a single candle

subdued.story: Subdued. Quiet and restrained, often a little sad; also soft and toned down. Bobby was usually the loudest boy in the hostel, telling stories at every meal. But in the week after his grandmother passed away, he ate slowly, answered in single words, and spent his evenings by the window. They understood why he was so subdued. The word also describes soft, gentle light, like the subdued lamps of a library. To subdue is to bring under control, so a subdued person holds their feelings down. So, what word describes someone unusually quiet and a little sad?... Subdued.
subdued.example: After the heavy defeat, the usually noisy bus ride back to Sylhet was subdued, and most players slept or stared out of the windows.

gre.s: In contrast to his usual exuberance, the comedian seemed oddly ____ throughout the interview, speaking softly and rarely smiling.
gre.clue: speaking softly and rarely smiling

surrogate.hook: SURROGATE: a SUBSTITUTE who stands in.
surrogate.story: Surrogate. Someone or something that takes the place of another. When Tiffany's parents went to work in Dubai, her aunt raised her. She packed her lunch every morning, went to every parents' meeting, and sat beside her through every fever. On the day Tiffany passed her board exams, it was her aunt she hugged first. For ten years, her aunt had been a surrogate mother. Surrogate comes from the Latin for putting someone in another's place, so think of a substitute. So, what word means someone who stands in for another?... Surrogate.
surrogate.example: Keepers at some panda reserves wear panda costumes and act as surrogate mothers for cubs that are being prepared for the wild.

gre.s: Unable to attend the ceremony himself, the ailing laureate sent his daughter as a ____ to accept the award and read the speech he had written.
gre.clue: Unable to attend the ceremony himself

transient.hook: TRANSIENT: in TRANSIT, just passing through.
transient.story: Transient. Passing quickly; not lasting long. When Spencer failed his first university exam, the pain felt enormous. He skipped dinner and stared at the hostel ceiling all night. A month later he passed the retake, and by the next term he could hardly remember why he had been so upset. The pain had been transient. Like a spring thunderstorm in April, it came hard and passed quickly. Transient shares its root with transit: something transient is only passing through. So, what word describes a feeling that does not last long?... Transient.
transient.example: The town's population is largely transient, since most residents are construction workers who move on once each project ends.

gre.s: The economist argued that the price spike was ____, the result of a temporary shortage rather than a lasting change in demand.
gre.clue: a temporary shortage rather than a lasting change

treatise.hook: TREATISE: a book that TREATS a subject thoroughly.
treatise.story: Treatise. A formal written work that deals with a subject systematically. Nancy's grandfather was a soil scientist who spent twenty years writing one book on the rice varieties of Bengal. Chapter by chapter, it covered soil, seasons, history and cooking, every claim carefully argued. When young researchers came to his house to thank him, Nancy felt a glow of pride. His book was a true treatise. A treatise treats its subject fully; do not confuse it with a treaty, an agreement between nations. So, what word names a formal, systematic book on one subject?... Treatise.
treatise.example: In the eleventh century, Ibn Sina wrote a medical treatise so thorough that European universities taught from it for centuries.

gre.s: Far from being a casual collection of anecdotes, the book is a rigorous ____, methodically working through every aspect of the philosopher's theory of justice.
gre.clue: methodically working through every aspect

acclaim.hook: AC-CLAIM: everyone CLAIMS it's great — loudly.
acclaim.story: Acclaim. Enthusiastic public praise; as a verb, to praise publicly. Rebecca, a young director from a small town, shot her first film in her grandmother's village with local actors and almost no money. She sent it to an international festival without much hope. At the premiere, the audience rose and clapped for ten long minutes, and Rebecca covered her face with both hands. Critics around the world acclaimed it. Acclaim comes from the Latin for shouting toward, the same root as clamour: acclaim is praise you can hear. So, what word means loud, public praise?... Acclaim.
acclaim.example: The young cricketer from Sylhet was acclaimed across the country after scoring a century in his very first test match.

gre.s: Although her early novels were ignored, her final book won universal ____, earning every major literary prize that year.
gre.clue: earning every major literary prize that year

adept.hook: ADEPT: an ADEPT is an ADEPT-ed expert.
adept.story: Adept. Very skilled at something. Nobody in Ralph's family could fix anything electrical, except his twelve-year-old niece, Maya. With a tiny screwdriver and a few online videos, she repaired the ceiling fan, rewired a frayed charger, and brought her grandfather's old radio back to life. When the radio crackled into a song, her grandfather clapped like a boy. Maya was adept at repairs. Do not mix up adept with inept, which sounds similar but means clumsy: adept is its opposite. So, what word describes someone very skilled at a task?... Adept.
adept.example: My grandmother is so adept at bargaining that vendors at Kawran Bazar lower their prices the moment they see her coming.

gre.s: Although new to the job, she proved remarkably ____ at calming angry customers, defusing complaints that had defeated her far more experienced colleagues.
gre.clue: defusing complaints that had defeated her far more experienced colleagues

ascertain.story: Ascertain. To find out for sure, usually by checking carefully. A rumour spread through Nolan's dorm that the hill-country bus would leave at five in the morning instead of seven. Half the floor rushed to the counter at dawn, yawning in the cold. Nolan did not trust rumours. He called the bus company twice and checked his ticket online to ascertain the real time. It was seven, and he slept two extra hours. Ascertain hides the word certain inside it: to ascertain is to make certain. So, what verb means to find out for certain by checking?... Ascertain.
ascertain.example: Before signing the lease, Rumana phoned the previous tenants to ascertain whether the flat really stayed dry during the monsoon.

gre.s: Before publishing the story, the editor insisted that reporters ____ the facts from at least two independent sources.
gre.clue: from at least two independent sources

baroque.hook: BAROQUE: so ornate it might BREAK under all the decoration.
baroque.story: Baroque. Highly ornate and extravagant; also, far too complicated. The wedding stage in the convention hall was astonishing: golden pillars carved with peacocks, crystal chandeliers, thousands of roses, and mirrors on every surface. Not one inch was left plain. Irene's grandmother stopped at the entrance, then whispered that she did not know where to look first. It was truly baroque. The name comes from the richly decorated style of European churches and music in the seventeenth century, full of golden curls. So, what word describes decoration so ornate that nothing is left plain?... Baroque.
baroque.example: The tax form was so baroque, with its endless sub-clauses and cross-references, that even the accountant needed a whole afternoon to finish it.

gre.s: Readers accustomed to the author's spare early style were startled by the ____ prose of her later novels, with their elaborate, ornamented sentences.
gre.clue: with their elaborate, ornamented sentences

benevolent.story: Benevolent. Kind and well-meaning; charitable. Every winter, when cold winds sweep across the northern plains, Thomas's grandfather, a retired schoolteacher, spends part of his pension on blankets. Before dawn, he walks through the poorest lanes of town, handing them out quietly, with no photographs and no speeches. An old rickshaw puller once wrapped himself in one and simply held his hand. The neighbours call him a benevolent man. Bene means good and vol means wish, so a benevolent person wishes others well; its opposite is malevolent. So, what word describes someone kind and generous to others?... Benevolent.
benevolent.example: The mill owner was remembered as a benevolent employer who quietly paid school fees for every worker's children.

gre.s: Far from being the ____ patron he appeared to be in public, the landlord privately evicted any tenant who fell even a single week behind on rent.
gre.clue: privately evicted any tenant who fell even a single week behind on rent

bolster.hook: BOLSTER: a BOLSTER is a long pillow that props you up.
bolster.story: Bolster. To support or strengthen. Andrea's thesis claimed that coastal mangroves protect coastal villages from cyclones. Her supervisor frowned. "A big claim needs strong support." So Andrea spent two months gathering storm records, satellite maps, and interviews with fishermen on the coast. At her final presentation, nobody could find a weak point. She had bolstered her argument. A bolster is a long, firm pillow that props you up; to bolster a claim is to prop it up with evidence. So, what verb means to support and strengthen?... Bolster.
bolster.example: A run of easy wins early in the tournament bolstered the young team's confidence before they faced the defending champions.

gre.s: The prosecutor hoped the new forensic evidence would ____ a case that had, until then, rested almost entirely on a single witness.
gre.clue: rested almost entirely on a single witness

conclusive.hook: CONCLUSIVE: brings the argument to a CONCLUSION.
conclusive.story: Conclusive. Settling a question completely, with no room for doubt. For weeks, Samantha's hostel floor argued about who was stealing milk from the shared fridge. Everyone had a theory, and friendships began to crack. Then the warden checked the corridor camera, and leaned closer. The footage showed a large grey cat nudging the fridge door open every night. The whole floor cheered. The video was conclusive. Conclusive comes from conclude: conclusive proof brings an argument to its conclusion. Do not confuse it with conducive, which means helpful. So, what word describes evidence that leaves no doubt?... Conclusive.
conclusive.example: DNA testing finally gave conclusive proof that the bones belonged to the explorer who vanished in the Arctic in 1845.

gre.s: Although the early studies were suggestive, they were far from ____, and regulators insisted on a much larger trial before declaring the drug effective.
gre.clue: insisted on a much larger trial before declaring the drug effective

contentious.story: Contentious. Likely to cause argument; also, fond of arguing. At a holiday lunch, someone mentioned the coming election. Within a minute, uncles were raising their voices, aunties were taking sides, and a cousin had walked out to the balcony. Grandmother tapped her spoon on her glass until the table went quiet. "Not today." Everyone knew politics was the most contentious topic in the family. Contentious comes from contend, to fight or compete: a contentious subject makes people contend. So, what word describes a topic sure to start an argument?... Contentious.
contentious.example: A plan to cut down the old banyan tree in the village square and pave a parking lot turned contentious within days.

gre.s: The proposal to build the dam proved highly ____, provoking furious debates in parliament and protests across the region.
gre.clue: provoking furious debates in parliament and protests

disdain.hook: DIS-DAIN: you won't DEIGN to look at it.
disdain.story: Disdain. The feeling that someone or something is not worthy of respect; scorn. At a restaurant downtown, a man in a gold watch glanced at the plate a young waiter set down, then pushed it away with two fingers, as if it were dirty. The waiter's cheeks burned. At the next table, Natasha felt sick watching. The man's disdain filled the room. Disdain is related to dignity and deign: to disdain something is to treat it as beneath your dignity. So, what word names the cold feeling that someone is beneath your respect?... Disdain.
disdain.example: The veteran chef spoke of instant noodles with open disdain, though his students often caught him eating them late at night.

gre.s: The aristocrat made no effort to hide his ____ for the newly rich merchants, refusing their invitations and mocking their manners at every opportunity.
gre.clue: mocking their manners at every opportunity

disperse.hook: DIS-PERSE: like a SPRAY spreading out.
disperse.story: Disperse. To break up and move off in many directions. Thousands of people had gathered in the city square for an evening concert when a sudden storm broke. In seconds, the crowd dispersed: under shop awnings, into rickshaws, down every side street. Tanya squeezed into a tiny tea stall with six soaked strangers. Within ten minutes the square was empty, with only a few paper flags left in the rain. Disperse shares a Latin root with sparse, meaning scattered: when a crowd disperses, it scatters. So, what verb means to break up and scatter in all directions?... Disperse.
disperse.example: Wind and ocean currents dispersed the oil slick along hundreds of kilometres of coastline within a single week.

gre.s: Once the morning fog began to ____, the hikers could see the trail clearly again, though only an hour earlier the valley had been completely hidden.
gre.clue: the hikers could see the trail clearly again
