cavalier.hook: CAVALIER: a horse-riding knight who looks DOWN on everyone.
cavalier.story: Cavalier. Showing careless, arrogant disregard for something important. When the flood warning came over the radio, most families in the river island village packed their goats and rice onto boats. But one landowner waved it away. "The river has never reached my house," he said, and refused to move his workers' families. That night the water rose waist-high. His cavalier attitude had put everyone at risk. A cavalier was a horse-riding gentleman; picture him high on his horse, looking down on danger and on the people below. So, what word describes careless disregard for something serious?... Cavalier.
cavalier.example: The landlord's cavalier response to the cracked staircase, a shrug and a vague promise to look next month, alarmed every tenant.

gre.s: Regulators criticized the company's ____ approach to safety, noting that it had ignored dozens of warnings from its own engineers.
gre.clue: had ignored dozens of warnings from its own engineers

circumstantial.hook: CIRCUMSTANTIAL: around (circum) the facts, not the facts themselves.
circumstantial.story: Circumstantial. Based on indirect evidence that suggests but does not prove. When Betty's lunch box vanished from the office fridge, everyone looked at Jay. He had been seen near the kitchen, and he smelled of biryani all afternoon. But nobody had seen him take it. The evidence was circumstantial. The next day the cleaner admitted he had thrown the box away by mistake, and Jay demanded an apology biryani. Circum means around: circumstantial evidence circles around the truth without touching it. So, what word describes evidence that hints but does not prove?... Circumstantial.
circumstantial.example: Historians have only circumstantial clues, a ship's log and a few unsigned letters, that the poet ever visited Chattogram.

gre.s: Because no witness saw the defendant at the scene, the prosecution's case rested entirely on ____ evidence, such as phone records placing him nearby.
gre.clue: no witness saw the defendant at the scene

condone.hook: CONDONE: CON + DONE, letting a con be done without objection.
condone.story: Condone. To accept or overlook wrong behaviour. In Sasha's class, a few students always copied each other's assignments, and the teacher pretended not to notice. One day Sasha asked him why. He was quiet for a moment, then admitted that by staying silent, he had been condoning cheating. The next week, he set everyone a fresh test in class. Condone comes from the Latin for forgive, the same root as donate: to condone a wrong is to give it away for free. So, what verb means to quietly accept bad behaviour?... Condone.
condone.example: The coach insisted he did not condone the brawl, yet he refused to drop the two players involved from the next match.

gre.s: By remaining silent while his colleagues falsified the data, the director effectively chose to ____ the fraud, even though he never took part in it himself.
gre.clue: By remaining silent

cumbersome.story: Cumbersome. Large, heavy and hard to carry or use; also, slow and complicated. Mike's grandmother insisted on sending him back to his city dorm with a huge steel trunk full of pickles, rice, a pillow and two jars of ghee. He dragged it off the ferry, through the crowd at the river port, and onto a bus, sweating all the way. The trunk was cumbersome, but every jar arrived safely. Cumbersome is related to encumber, to weigh someone down: cumbersome things burden you. So, what word describes something bulky and awkward to carry?... Cumbersome.
cumbersome.example: Early mobile phones were so cumbersome that businessmen carried them in a shoulder bag along with a heavy battery.

gre.s: Engineers replaced the ____ old filing system, which required three separate forms for every request, with a simple online portal.
gre.clue: which required three separate forms for every request

decipher.story: Decipher. To figure out the meaning of something hard to read or understand. In a cupboard, Eva found her great-grandmother's handwritten recipe book. The ink had faded, the letters curled in an old style, and some pages were stained with turmeric. Eva and her grandmother spent an evening deciphering a recipe for coconut rice cakes, word by word. When they cooked it, her grandmother clapped: it tasted just as she remembered. A cipher is a secret code; to decipher is to undo the code. So, what verb means to make sense of something hard to read?... Decipher.
decipher.example: Using a stone carved with the same text in three scripts, scholars finally deciphered Egyptian hieroglyphs in the 1820s.

gre.s: The doctor's handwriting was so illegible that even the experienced pharmacist could not ____ the prescription without calling the clinic for help.
gre.clue: handwriting was so illegible

deflect.hook: DEFLECT: like a shield DEFLECTING an arrow.
deflect.story: Deflect. To make something turn aside; also, to dodge or avoid. At the press conference after a heavy defeat, a reporter asked the captain why the team kept losing early wickets. He smiled and talked about the weather, the pitch and the crowd. Every hard question was deflected. Susan, watching at home, shook her head. Deflect comes from the Latin for bend away, the same root as flexible: like a shield bending an arrow off course, you deflect a question away from yourself. So, what verb means to turn something aside or dodge it?... Deflect.
deflect.example: The new sea wall is designed to deflect storm waves away from the fishing harbour at Cox's Bazar.

gre.s: Rather than address the allegations directly, the spokesperson tried to ____ them, steering every question back toward the company's charitable work.
gre.clue: steering every question back toward the company's charitable work

esoteric.hook: ESOTERIC: 'ESO' sounds like 'inside'. Only insiders understand it.
esoteric.story: Esoteric. Understood by only a small group of specialists. At a family dinner, Anthony's cousin, a physicist, began explaining his research on string theory. Within two minutes he was using words nobody at the table had heard. His aunt kept passing the rice, and his little nephew fell asleep. The topic was simply too esoteric. Even Anthony, an engineer, gave up. Esoteric comes from a Greek word meaning inner: esoteric knowledge belongs to an inner circle. Its opposite is exoteric, open to everyone. So, what word describes knowledge only a few specialists understand?... Esoteric.
esoteric.example: Kabir's hobby is esoteric even among stamp collectors, since he collects only postmarks from village post offices that have closed.

gre.s: The journal publishes highly ____ research that only a few hundred specialists worldwide are equipped to understand.
gre.clue: only a few hundred specialists worldwide are equipped to understand

fortitude.hook: FORTITUDE: a FORT inside your mind.
fortitude.story: Fortitude. Courage and strength of mind in facing pain or hardship. When a great cyclone destroyed Rachel's family home on the coast, she was fourteen. Her family lived under a plastic sheet for months. Yet every morning she walked three kilometres to a relief school, studied by lamplight, and helped her mother rebuild. Years later she became a nurse in that same district. Everyone admired her fortitude. Fortitude comes from the Latin fortis, strong, as in a fort: fortitude is a fort inside the mind. So, what word names courage in facing hardship?... Fortitude.
fortitude.example: The rescued miners credited their survival to the fortitude of their foreman, who kept them calm through nine days underground.

gre.s: The patient endured months of painful treatment with remarkable ____, never complaining even when the doctors warned that recovery might take years.
gre.clue: never complaining even when the doctors warned

grievance.hook: GRIEVANCE: something that makes you GRIEVE and complain.
grievance.story: Grievance. A real or imagined cause for complaint. For months, the workers at a shoe factory outside the city had worked overtime without extra pay. Their grievance grew with every unpaid evening. Finally, Zack, a quiet machine operator, wrote it all down: dates, hours and missing wages. He handed the letter to the manager, and a week later the back pay was settled. A grievance is something that makes you grieve; grief and grievance share a Latin root meaning heavy. So, what word names a cause for complaint?... Grievance.
grievance.example: The tenants gathered every grievance, from leaking pipes to a broken lift, into a single letter for the landlord.

gre.s: Rather than being addressed, the workers' ____ about unpaid overtime was ignored for months, until it finally erupted into a strike that shut down the port.
gre.clue: until it finally erupted into a strike

impede.hook: IM-PEDE: 'ped' is foot. Something catching your feet.
impede.story: Impede. To slow down or block progress. Every monsoon, the road to Poppy's school turns to deep mud. Bicycles sink, rickshaws tip over, and a walk that takes fifteen minutes in winter takes an hour. The mud badly impedes the children's journey. One summer, Poppy's father and the neighbours laid bricks along the worst stretch, and she raced her friends to school the next morning. Impede comes from the Latin for foot, as in pedal: to impede is to catch someone's feet. So, what verb means to slow or block progress?... Impede.
impede.example: A lack of reliable data has impeded efforts to measure how fast the Sundarbans coastline is eroding.

gre.s: Heavy snowfall continued to ____ the rescue effort, preventing helicopters from reaching the stranded climbers for three days.
gre.clue: preventing helicopters from reaching the stranded climbers

inept.story: Inept. Having no skill; clumsy. On his first day as a waiter at a busy restaurant by the port, Shane spilled soup on a customer, brought tea instead of coffee, and dropped a stack of plates in front of the whole room. He felt hopelessly inept. The owner patted his shoulder. "Everyone starts clumsy." Six months later, he was the fastest waiter there. Inept means not apt, not suited; it is the opposite of adept, which means skilled. So, what word describes someone clumsy and without skill?... Inept.
inept.example: The inept burglar locked himself inside the shop's storeroom and had to phone the police to let him out.

gre.s: Critics charged that the agency's response to the flood was ____: supplies arrived at the wrong villages, and rescue boats sat idle for days for lack of fuel.
gre.clue: rescue boats sat idle for days for lack of fuel

intermediary.story: Intermediary. A person who acts as a link between two parties. When Daisy's family began arranging her marriage, they did not approach the groom's family directly. Instead, Daisy's aunt, who knew both sides, carried messages, questions and photographs back and forth for weeks. She smoothed over misunderstandings and made sure both families felt respected. She was the perfect intermediary. Inter means between and medius means middle: an intermediary stands in the middle between two sides. So, what word names a person who links two parties?... Intermediary.
intermediary.example: Many farmers in Rangpur sell their potatoes through an intermediary, who takes a large cut before the crop reaches city markets.

gre.s: Because the two governments had no formal diplomatic relations, they were forced to negotiate through a neutral ____, who relayed each side's proposals to the other.
gre.clue: who relayed each side's proposals to the other

makeshift.hook: MAKESHIFT: MAKE do in a SHIFT.
makeshift.story: Makeshift. Serving as a temporary substitute. When the floods reached Ryan's village, the school went underwater. So the teachers built a makeshift classroom on the embankment: bamboo poles, a blue plastic sheet for a roof, and benches made from planks. The children sat close together, books on their knees. For three weeks, lessons continued under that sheet. When the school reopened, Ryan almost missed the makeshift room. Makeshift comes from the old phrase make a shift, meaning to manage with what you have. So, what word describes something put together to serve for now?... Makeshift.
makeshift.example: During the power cut, the students kept studying by a makeshift lamp made from a phone torch and a bottle of water.

gre.s: Because the hospital had been destroyed by the earthquake, doctors treated patients in a ____ clinic set up in a school gymnasium until a permanent facility could be built.
gre.clue: until a permanent facility could be built

perilous.story: Perilous. Very dangerous; likely to bring harm. Ava's father ferries passengers across a wide river in a small wooden boat. One April afternoon, black clouds rolled in, the wind turned the river white, and waves slapped over the sides. He steered slowly toward the shore while everyone held on and prayed. They made it, soaked and shaking. Ava ran down to the bank to meet him. The crossing had been perilous. Perilous simply means full of peril, and peril means danger. So, what word describes a journey full of danger?... Perilous.
perilous.example: Early explorers made the perilous voyage around Cape Horn in wooden ships, and many never returned.

gre.s: Despite warnings that the mountain pass was ____ in winter, the travelers set out without guides and were soon trapped by an avalanche.
gre.clue: were soon trapped by an avalanche

pretentious.story: Pretentious. Trying to seem more important or cultured than you are. After one month in London, Miles came home with a strange new accent. He pretended he had forgotten simple everyday words and complained loudly that the tea was too sweet. His old friends at the tea stall exchanged looks. "Miles, you left last month." He was being pretentious. Pretentious comes from pretend: a pretentious person pretends to be grander than they are. So, what word describes someone showing off to seem more important?... Pretentious.
pretentious.example: The restaurant's pretentious menu called plain rice and dal a deconstructed lentil experience and charged triple the usual price.

gre.s: Critics found the novel ____, stuffed with Latin quotations and obscure philosophical references that seemed designed to impress rather than to illuminate.
gre.clue: designed to impress rather than to illuminate

propensity.story: Propensity. A natural tendency to behave in a certain way. Nina's little brother has a propensity for taking things apart. At three, he unscrewed the television remote; at six, the ceiling fan switch; at ten, his father's old radio. His mother has hidden every screwdriver in the house. Yet the same propensity now earns him top marks in science. Propensity comes from the Latin for leaning forward, the same root as pendulum: a propensity is the way you naturally lean. So, what word names a natural tendency to behave a certain way?... Propensity.
propensity.example: Some breeds of dog have a propensity to overeat, so vets advise owners to measure every meal.

gre.s: Given his well-known ____ to exaggerate, his colleagues learned to divide every figure he quoted by at least two.
gre.clue: his colleagues learned to divide every figure he quoted by at least two

refute.hook: REFUTE: REFUSE to accept, and PROVE it false.
refute.story: Refute. To prove a statement or theory wrong. At a village tea stall, an old man insisted that the moon landing had been filmed in a studio. Kendra, a physics student home for the holidays, listened politely. Then she showed him pictures of the mirrors astronauts left on the moon, which scientists still bounce lasers off today. The old man scratched his head and ordered another tea. She had refuted the claim with evidence. To deny is just to say no; to refute is to prove false. So, what verb means to prove a claim wrong?... Refute.
refute.example: The young historian refuted the old claim about the fort's age by carbon-dating charcoal found beneath its walls.

gre.s: The scientist did not merely question the theory; she set out to ____ it decisively, publishing data showing that its central prediction was simply false.
gre.clue: showing that its central prediction was simply false

rudimentary.story: Rudimentary. Very basic, or still in an early, simple form. When Robin moved to Japan for her master's degree, her Japanese was rudimentary: she could say hello, thank you, and one sentence about the weather. At the supermarket she pointed at everything. But she practised with her neighbours every evening, and by spring the old lady downstairs laughed at her jokes. Rudimentary shares a root with rude in its old sense of raw and unformed: rudimentary skills are still raw. So, what word describes knowledge that is very basic?... Rudimentary.
rudimentary.example: The first robots built by the school science club were rudimentary, able only to roll forward and stop at a wall.

gre.s: Although her grasp of statistics was only ____, the journalist managed to spot the fundamental flaw in the study's methodology.
gre.clue: managed to spot the fundamental flaw

sadistic.hook: SADISTIC: makes others SAD and enjoys it.
sadistic.story: Sadistic. Taking pleasure in causing pain or suffering to others. In some university hostels, seniors once forced new students to stand for hours or perform humiliating tasks at midnight, a practice called ragging. Most seniors joined in out of habit. But one clearly enjoyed it, smiling while a first-year student shook with fear. His behaviour was sadistic. When Barry, a new student, reported him, the university expelled the senior. The word comes from the Marquis de Sade, a French writer notorious for describing cruelty as pleasure. So, what word describes someone who enjoys causing others pain?... Sadistic.
sadistic.example: The novel's villain is a sadistic headmaster who canes boys for the smallest mistake and smiles as they cry.

gre.s: The guard was not merely strict but ____, devising humiliating punishments for minor offenses and visibly relishing the prisoners' suffering.
gre.clue: visibly relishing the prisoners' suffering

sever.story: Sever. To cut off completely; to end a connection. During one monsoon, the swollen river near Trisha's village tore at the only bridge. With a roar, the middle section collapsed, severing the road to town. For two weeks, villagers crossed by boat to reach the market and the clinic, and Trisha rowed with her father each morning to get to school. Countries can sever ties too, ending all contact. Sever comes from the same Latin root as separate: to sever is to separate completely. So, what verb means to cut something off completely?... Sever.
sever.example: The boatman severed the rope with one stroke of his knife, freeing the trawler before the current could drag it under.

gre.s: After the scandal, the university moved quickly to ____ all ties with the disgraced donor, returning his gifts and removing his name from its buildings.
gre.clue: returning his gifts and removing his name from its buildings

steadfast.hook: STEAD-FAST: holding FAST to your place (stead).
steadfast.story: Steadfast. Firmly loyal and unwavering. When Adam lost his job and his savings in the same year, many friends stopped calling. But his school friend Mark did not. He visited every week, lent him money without asking when it would come back, and helped him prepare for new interviews. When Adam finally found work, Mark was the first to hug him. He had been a steadfast friend. Stead means place and fast means firm: a steadfast person stays firmly in place beside you. So, what word describes a loyal, unwavering friend?... Steadfast.
steadfast.example: Throughout the long strike, the miners' families remained steadfast, running community kitchens so that no household went hungry.

gre.s: Through years of exile and imprisonment, she remained ____ in her commitment to democracy, refusing every offer of freedom that required her to renounce it.
gre.clue: refusing every offer of freedom

stoic.hook: STOIC: like a STONE, no visible emotion.
stoic.story: Stoic. Bearing pain or trouble calmly, without complaint. Julie's father, a rickshaw puller, broke his arm when a truck clipped his rickshaw. At the hospital, he sat still while the doctor set the bone, his jaw tight, saying only, "Do what you need to." Afterwards, he asked whether the rickshaw could be repaired. Julie marvelled at how stoic he was. The Stoics were Greek thinkers who taught at a painted porch in Athens and urged calm acceptance of hardship. So, what word describes someone who bears pain calmly, without complaint?... Stoic.
stoic.example: The goalkeeper stayed stoic after his error cost the match, shaking every opponent's hand before quietly leaving the field.

gre.s: The refugees remained ____ throughout their ordeal, enduring hunger and cold without a single complaint.
gre.clue: without a single complaint

tout.hook: TOUT: SHOUT about it, like a salesman.
tout.story: Tout. To praise something loudly, often to sell it. Outside the central bus stand, a man stood on a crate touting a herbal toothpaste. "Whitens teeth in one day! Cures toothache! Makes you smarter!" A small crowd gathered. Shelby, waiting for her bus, smiled at the last claim. The men who push bus tickets at terminals are also called touts. Tout rhymes with shout: to tout something is to shout its praises. So, what verb means to praise something loudly to sell it?... Tout.
tout.example: Property agents in Purbachal tout the new flats as lakeside living, though the lake is still a muddy pit.

gre.s: Although the company continues to ____ its new diet pill as a miracle cure, independent studies have found it no more effective than a placebo.
gre.clue: as a miracle cure

tranquil.story: Tranquil. Calm and peaceful, free from disturbance. After a month of exams, Lauren visited her uncle's tea estate in the hills. In the early morning, mist lay over the green rows, birds called from the shade trees, and the only other sound was the soft rustle of pickers' hands among the leaves. She sat on the veranda with a cup of tea and felt her mind settle. The estate was tranquil. A tranquilliser is a medicine that calms you; tranquil is that calm without the medicine. So, what word describes a place peaceful and free from noise?... Tranquil.
tranquil.example: The surgeon listened to tranquil sitar music while operating, saying it kept her hands steady during long procedures.

gre.s: The once ____ fishing village has been transformed by tourism into a noisy resort crowded with hotels and nightclubs.
gre.clue: transformed by tourism into a noisy resort

unravel.hook: UNRAVEL: pull the thread and the knitting comes apart.
unravel.story: Unravel. To solve something complicated; also, to fall apart. For weeks, Monica's grandfather's old ledger made no sense: numbers without names, names without dates. Then Monica noticed a pattern: each page matched a harvest season. One thread at a time, she unravelled the mystery, and found records of loans he had quietly forgiven. Think of a knitted sweater: pull one loose thread, and it unravels and comes apart. A plan can unravel too, when things go wrong. So, what verb means to untangle a mystery, or to fall apart?... Unravel.
unravel.example: The team's season began to unravel after the captain broke his wrist, and they lost six games in a row.

gre.s: It took investigators years to ____ the fraud, so intricately had the accountants tangled the money trail through dozens of shell companies.
gre.clue: so intricately had the accountants tangled the money trail

zenith.hook: ZENITH: the sun straight overhead, the top of the sky.
zenith.story: Zenith. The highest point; the peak of success. On a June day, Ian's science teacher took the class outside at noon and asked them to look at their shadows. They had almost disappeared, because the sun was near its zenith, nearly straight overhead. Years later, when Ian's band played to a packed stadium, his old teacher sent him a message: "This is your zenith." The word comes from an Arabic phrase for the path above your head. Its opposite is nadir, the lowest point. So, what word names the highest point of something?... Zenith.
zenith.example: Buddhist learning under the Pala kings reached its zenith at Somapura, one of the largest monasteries south of the Himalayas.

gre.s: At the ____ of his fame, the singer could fill any stadium in the country; a decade later, he was performing in near-empty halls.
gre.clue: could fill any stadium in the country

astute.hook: ASTUTE: A STUDENT who sees through everything.
astute.story: Astute. Clever at understanding situations and using them to your advantage. When a new supermarket opened next to her small grocery, Nancy did not panic. She noticed the big store closed at ten, so she stayed open until midnight. She learned the names of her regular customers' children and stocked the fresh fish the supermarket never had. She was astute. Astute sounds a little like a student: an astute person reads people and markets alike. So, what word describes someone who sharply understands a situation and gains from it?... Astute.
astute.example: An astute coach, Rahima noticed that the opposing bowler tired after five overs and told her batters to wait him out.

gre.s: The investor proved remarkably ____: while others panicked and sold, she quietly bought shares she knew were undervalued and tripled her money within a year.
gre.clue: while others panicked and sold

brazen.hook: BRAZEN: hard and shiny like BRASS, shameless.
brazen.story: Brazen. Bold and shameless, without any embarrassment. In the middle of a crowded town market, a man walked up to a vegetable stall, picked up three cauliflowers, and strolled away without paying, whistling. When the seller shouted, he turned around and waved. The seller simply stared. Russ, buying onions nearby, could hardly believe how brazen the man was. Brazen once meant made of brass: picture a face as hard and shiny as brass, unable to blush. So, what word describes someone boldly shameless?... Brazen.
brazen.example: In a brazen lie, the company called its river clean on the same day reporters filmed dead fish beside its outlet pipe.

gre.s: Rather than hiding the forgery, the art dealer made a ____ attempt to sell it at the very gallery that owned the original.
gre.clue: Rather than hiding the forgery

copious.hook: COPIOUS: so many COPIES that there's plenty for all.
copious.story: Copious. Abundant; existing in large amounts. During his first holiday at his in-laws' house by the sea, Mitch learned what hospitality means. Plates of spiced beef, fragrant rice, sweet noodles and three kinds of rice cakes kept arriving, and every time he emptied his plate, someone filled it again. By evening he begged for mercy, smiling. The food had been copious, and so was the love behind it. Copious comes from the Latin copia, plenty, which you also hear in cornucopia, the horn of plenty. So, what word describes something in very large amounts?... Copious.
copious.example: Copious rain in July filled the reservoirs around Rangamati, ending weeks of fear about a water shortage.

gre.s: Far from being sparse, the explorer's journals are ____, documenting every plant, river, and conversation she encountered.
gre.clue: Far from being sparse

cordial.hook: CORDIAL: from the HEART (cor, as in cardiac).
cordial.story: Cordial. Warm, friendly and polite. When Tamara moved into a new flat, she was nervous about her neighbours. On the first evening, the woman next door knocked with a plate of hot samosas and a smile. "If you need anything, just ring." The building's guard learned her name the same day. Everyone was so cordial that Tamara felt at home within a week. Cordial comes from the Latin cor, heart, the same root as courage: cordial greetings come from the heart. So, what word describes warm, friendly and polite behaviour?... Cordial.
cordial.example: Although the two former partners rarely agreed on business, their emails stayed cordial, always ending with good wishes for each other's families.

gre.s: Though the negotiations were tense, relations between the two delegations remained ____, and each side thanked the other warmly at the close.
gre.clue: each side thanked the other warmly

coy.hook: COY: playing it COOL and shy.
coy.story: Coy. Pretending to be shy; also, reluctant to give details. When the aunties at a wedding asked Rosie whether she had someone special in her life, she smiled, looked down at her bangles, and said, "Who knows?" Everyone saw her glance across the room at a young man in a blue suit. Her cousins nudged each other. She was being coy. Coy comes from an old French word for quiet, the same root as quiet itself: a coy person goes quiet on purpose. So, what word describes someone pretending to be shy or holding back details?... Coy.
coy.example: The author was coy about the ending of her next novel, saying only that readers should keep some tissues nearby.

gre.s: The minister was uncharacteristically ____ about her plans, deflecting every question about the coming election with a smile and a vague remark about the weather.
gre.clue: deflecting every question

dispense.hook: DISPENSE: like a water DISPENSER giving out water.
dispense.story: Dispense. To give out to many people; also, to provide a service. At a rural health clinic, nurse Fran starts work at eight. She checks each prescription, then dispenses tablets, syrup and oral saline to a long line of patients, explaining every dose slowly. She also dispenses something free: patience. Mothers trust her more than anyone in the district. Think of a water dispenser in an office, giving out cups of water one by one: to dispense is to hand things out. So, what verb means to give out or distribute?... Dispense.
dispense.example: Machines on every platform of the new metro dispense single-journey cards in less than ten seconds.

gre.s: Rather than stockpile the scarce grain, the village council chose to ____ it equally among all households, giving each family the same small ration.
gre.clue: giving each family the same small ration

dissident.story: Dissident. A person who opposes official policy, especially in a harsh, controlling state. In the nineteen sixties, under military rule, Steven's grandfather was a young poet in the capital who wrote verses criticising the government. He was arrested twice and his poems were banned, but students copied them by hand and passed them around. He was a dissident, and he never stopped writing. Dissident comes from the Latin for sitting apart: a dissident sits apart from those in power. So, what word names someone who openly opposes an authoritarian government?... Dissident.
dissident.example: After years in exile, the dissident novelist returned home to find her books finally sold openly in the capital's shops.

gre.s: The regime claimed to tolerate free speech, yet any ____ who criticized its policies in print could expect to be imprisoned or forced into exile.
gre.clue: who criticized its policies in print

egregious.hook: EGREGIOUS: so bad it stands out from the herd (e-greg = out of the flock).
egregious.story: Egregious. Outstandingly bad; shocking. When Janet's university published its final exam results, every student in her class had the same mark: forty-two. Even the students who had been absent. Someone had copied one number down the whole column. Students crowded the notice board in disbelief, and the registrar quickly apologised for such an egregious error. Egregious comes from the Latin for out of the flock, the same root as gregarious: an egregious mistake stands out from the herd. So, what word describes a mistake so bad it is shocking?... Egregious.
egregious.example: Attributing a famous quotation to the wrong president was an egregious slip for a history professor writing in a national newspaper.

gre.s: The auditors uncovered an ____ error in the accounts, a miscalculation so large that it had inflated profits by millions.
gre.clue: so large that it had inflated profits by millions

enigmatic.hook: ENIGMA = a riddle. ENIGMATIC = like a riddle.
enigmatic.story: Enigmatic. Mysterious and hard to understand or read. Every afternoon, an old man in a grey shawl sat on the same bench in the city park, feeding pigeons and writing in a small notebook. He never spoke to anyone. Some said he was a retired judge; others said a poet. Nadine, who jogged past daily, grew curious. One day he looked up, gave her an enigmatic smile, and went back to writing. An enigma is a riddle, so an enigmatic person is a living riddle. So, what word describes someone mysterious and hard to read?... Enigmatic.
enigmatic.example: The only clue was an enigmatic chalk symbol on the warehouse door, unlike anything the detectives had seen before.

gre.s: Scholars still debate the meaning of the poem's ____ final line, which seems to contradict everything that came before it.
gre.clue: Scholars still debate the meaning

exhilarating.story: Exhilarating. Making you feel very happy, excited and full of energy. On her first speedboat ride across the great river, Audrey stood at the front, wind whipping her hair, spray cooling her face, the river glittering in the sun. When the boat leapt over a wave, she grabbed the rail, then shouted with joy. It was the most exhilarating ten minutes of her year. Exhilarating shares a root with hilarious, from the Latin for cheerful: exhilarating moments fill you with bright joy. So, what word describes an experience that leaves you thrilled and full of energy?... Exhilarating.
exhilarating.example: Watching Bangladesh chase down a huge total in the final over was exhilarating for the packed crowd at Mirpur.

gre.s: For the young climbers, reaching the summit was ____, a moment of pure joy after weeks of exhausting effort.
gre.clue: a moment of pure joy

fickle.story: Fickle. Often changing your mind, likes or loyalties. In January, Freddie told everyone at the tea stall that he supported Argentina. By the World Cup quarter-finals, he was wearing a Brazil jersey. After Brazil lost, he appeared in a German cap. His friends started calling him the weather vane, turning with every wind. Freddie is a fickle fan, and he knows it. Fickle sounds like flicker: picture a candle flame flickering this way and that, never steady. So, what word describes someone whose loyalty keeps changing?... Fickle.
fickle.example: Mountain weather is fickle, so the guide packed rain jackets even though the morning sky was perfectly clear.

gre.s: Politicians who rely on the ____ support of voters soon learn that a single unpopular decision can turn yesterday's admirers into tomorrow's opponents.
gre.clue: turn yesterday's admirers into tomorrow's opponents

figurative.story: Figurative. Not literal; using figures of speech such as metaphors. When Cynthia's grandmother said, "My heart broke into a hundred pieces when you left for Australia," Cynthia's little brother looked worried and asked if she needed a doctor. Cynthia hugged him and explained that Grandma was speaking in a figurative way. Her heart was fine; she simply missed Cynthia very much. Figurative comes from figure, as in a figure of speech: words that paint a picture rather than state a fact. Its opposite is literal. So, what word describes language not meant literally?... Figurative.
figurative.example: Learners of English often stumble over figurative expressions such as 'break the ice', reading them word by word.

gre.s: Readers who interpret the poet's 'burning city' as an actual fire miss the point; the phrase is ____, describing the speaker's rage rather than any real blaze.
gre.clue: describing the speaker's rage rather than any real blaze

fledgling.hook: FLEDGLING: a baby bird just getting its feathers.
fledgling.story: Fledgling. New and inexperienced; also, a young bird just learning to fly. On their balcony, Robbie watched a baby myna hop to the edge of its nest, flap hard, and drop clumsily onto the railing. A day later it was flying short circles over the lane. That same month, Robbie started a fledgling business selling mangoes online, with three customers and a borrowed phone. To fledge is to grow the feathers you need to fly, so a fledgling is just getting its wings. So, what word describes something new and still learning to fly?... Fledgling.
fledgling.example: The fledgling theatre company in Rajshahi staged its first play in a school hall, with borrowed costumes and folding chairs.

gre.s: Like many ____ enterprises, the start-up struggled during its first year, lacking both the experience and the capital that established competitors enjoyed.
gre.clue: lacking both the experience and the capital that established competitors enjoyed

fraught.story: Fraught. Filled with something unwanted, such as danger or worry. For the whole month that Matthew's family waited to hear whether their visas to join his father in Italy would be approved, the house was fraught with tension. His mother cooked without speaking, his grandmother prayed longer than usual, and every phone call made them jump. Fraught means loaded, and it shares an old root with freight: a fraught situation is loaded with trouble, like a ship heavy with cargo. It usually comes with with: fraught with danger. So, what word describes a situation loaded with worry?... Fraught.
fraught.example: Moving their parents to Dhaka was a decision fraught with guilt for the siblings, who had once promised never to leave the village.

gre.s: The negotiations were ____ with danger from the start: a single careless word from either side could have reignited a war that had only just ended.
gre.clue: a single careless word from either side could have reignited a war

gullible.hook: GULLIBLE: like a sea GULL that swallows anything thrown at it.
gullible.story: Gullible. Quick to believe things, and so easily fooled. Olivia's uncle received a message saying he had won a lottery in London. All he had to do was send five hundred dollars for processing fees. He was on his way to the mobile banking shop when Olivia grabbed his phone. "Uncle, you never bought a ticket!" Her uncle laughed nervously. He was kind, but gullible. Picture a seagull swallowing anything thrown into the water: a gullible person swallows any story. So, what word describes someone easily fooled?... Gullible.
gullible.example: Fake websites selling cheap concert tickets target gullible teenagers, who often discover the fraud only at the stadium gate.

gre.s: Far from being ____, the investigator questioned every claim the witness made, insisting on documents for even the most trivial details.
gre.clue: questioned every claim the witness made

incite.hook: INCITE: light a fire INSIDE the crowd.
incite.story: Incite. To stir people up to violence or law-breaking. After a minor car accident on a busy highway, a crowd gathered. One man began shouting false claims that the driver had done it on purpose, urging people to smash the car. Shawn, a schoolteacher, stepped between them and calmly asked everyone to look at the facts. The crowd cooled, and the man who had tried to incite them slipped away. Incite shares a root with excite: to incite a crowd is to excite it toward harm. So, what verb means to stir people up to violence?... Incite.
incite.example: The club banned a group of supporters for using social media to incite fights with rival fans after matches.

gre.s: Prosecutors argued that the pamphlets were written not merely to criticize the government but to ____ riots, pointing to passages that urged readers to burn public buildings.
gre.clue: urged readers to burn public buildings

jeopardize.story: Jeopardize. To put someone or something in danger. Lydia had a scholarship offer from a university in Canada, but she still needed to finish her final project. Two weeks before the deadline, her friends invited her on a long trip to the beach. She thought it over and stayed home. Missing the deadline would jeopardize everything she had worked for. Jeopardize comes from jeopardy, from an old French phrase for a divided game, where the result could go either way. So, what verb means to put something at risk?... Jeopardize.
jeopardize.example: Leaking the exam questions could jeopardize the careers of every teacher at the school, even those who knew nothing about it.

gre.s: Officials warned that any further delay would ____ the entire bridge project, since the foreign loan would be withdrawn if construction had not begun by March.
gre.clue: since the foreign loan would be withdrawn

loathe.hook: LOATHE: 'LOW-THE' — so low in your opinion that you hate it.
loathe.story: Loathe. To hate something very strongly. Toby loathes the traffic jam at the big junction. Every morning his bus sits there for an hour while horns scream and the air turns grey. He checks the time again and again and counts the minutes he will never get back. Do not confuse loathe with loath, without the e, which means unwilling: Toby is loath to leave home any earlier, but he truly loathes the traffic. So, what verb means to hate something intensely?... Loathe.
loathe.example: Most cats loathe water, which is why bathing them usually ends with scratched arms and a soaked bathroom floor.

gre.s: Though he came to ____ the city's noise and crowds, the poet found he could not write anywhere else.
gre.clue: Though he came to

mediate.story: Mediate. To step in and help settle a dispute. Two neighbours in Mitchell's village had argued for months about a goat that kept eating the other's vegetables. Shouting turned to threats. Then the village schoolmaster invited both men to his veranda for tea. He listened to each side and suggested a bamboo fence paid for by both. Soon the two were arguing only about who would bring the bamboo. He had mediated the quarrel. Mediate comes from the Latin for middle: a mediator stands in the middle. So, what verb means to help two sides settle a dispute?... Mediate.
mediate.example: A retired judge was asked to mediate between the garment workers' union and the factory owners after wage talks collapsed.

gre.s: Because neither side trusted the other enough to negotiate directly, both agreed to let a neutral diplomat ____ the dispute over the contested border.
gre.clue: neither side trusted the other enough to negotiate directly

metaphorical.story: Metaphorical. Not literal; using one thing to stand for another. When Andrea's teacher said that the new river bridge was a golden thread tying the country together, a boy in the front row asked whether it was really made of gold. Andrea explained that the teacher was being metaphorical. The bridge is concrete and steel; the golden thread meant how it joins the southwest to the rest of the nation. Metaphor comes from the Greek for carry across: metaphorical words carry meaning from one thing to another. So, what word describes language that uses one thing to represent another?... Metaphorical.
metaphorical.example: The shattered mirror in the film's last scene is metaphorical, standing for the family that has broken apart.

gre.s: When the poet describes the city as a cage, she is speaking in ____ terms, not complaining about any actual bars.
gre.clue: not complaining about any actual bars

neutralize.hook: NEUTRALIZE: make NEUTRAL, neither acid nor base.
neutralize.story: Neutralize. To cancel the effect of something and make it harmless. After a plate of spicy street snacks with extra tamarind water, Randy's stomach burned all evening. His mother handed him an antacid tablet, and within minutes the burning eased: the tablet had neutralized the acid. In chemistry class the next day, his teacher showed how a base neutralizes an acid until the mixture is neither. Neutralize simply means to make neutral, taking neither side. So, what verb means to cancel out the effect of something?... Neutralize.
neutralize.example: Farmers add lime to their fields to neutralize soil that has grown too acidic after years of heavy fertiliser use.

gre.s: Her rivals hoped the scandal would sink the senator's campaign, but her swift and candid apology served to ____ its effects almost entirely.
gre.clue: swift and candid apology

reiterate.hook: RE-ITERATE: say it again and again (iterate).
reiterate.story: Reiterate. To repeat something already said, usually to stress it. Before a field trip into the mangrove forest, the forest guide gathered Neil's class on the boat. "Stay with the group. Do not touch the water. Do not wander into the forest." Then, as the boat docked, he reiterated every rule, more slowly. When they spotted a fresh tiger pawprint in the mud, nobody needed the rules reiterated a third time. Iterate means to repeat, and re means again: to reiterate is to say it again, for emphasis. So, what verb means to repeat something to stress it?... Reiterate.
reiterate.example: At the press conference, the captain reiterated that he would retire after the World Cup, ending weeks of rumours.

gre.s: Because so many students had ignored the first notice, the principal felt obliged to ____ the warning in a second, more strongly worded letter.
gre.clue: Because so many students had ignored the first notice

relinquish.story: Relinquish. To voluntarily give up or let go. For thirty years, Sabrina's grandfather ran the family sweet shop, famous for its syrupy sweets. At seventy-five, he finally handed the keys to his granddaughter. His hands shook as he gave them over, but he smiled. Relinquishing the shop was hard, yet he knew it was time. Relinquish shares its Latin root with relic: both are about something left behind. To relinquish is to leave something behind willingly. So, what verb means to give up something willingly?... Relinquish.
relinquish.example: The champion boxer chose to relinquish his title rather than fight an opponent he believed had been doping.

gre.s: The aging dictator refused to ____ power, even after losing an election by an overwhelming margin.
gre.clue: even after losing an election by an overwhelming margin

resolute.story: Resolute. Firmly determined, refusing to be turned aside. When Emma decided to become the first woman in her village to study engineering, relatives told her it was impossible, and her uncle said girls should marry early. She ignored them, woke at five every morning to study, and walked an hour to the coaching centre. When she won a seat at a top engineering university, the same uncle brought sweets for the whole village. She had been resolute. Resolute comes from resolve: a resolute person makes a firm decision and keeps it. So, what word describes someone firmly determined?... Resolute.
resolute.example: Resolute in her plan to swim the English Channel, Shabnam trained every dawn in the choppy sea off Cox's Bazar.

gre.s: Despite years of threats and imprisonment, the activist remained ____ in her demands for reform, refusing every offer of compromise from the government.
gre.clue: refusing every offer of compromise from the government

retaliate.hook: RETALIATE: return the TALLY, an eye for an eye.
retaliate.story: Retaliate. To strike back after an attack or insult. In a lane cricket match in the old city, Sam bowled a tennis-ball bouncer that knocked off his friend's cap. The very next over, his friend grabbed the ball and bowled one straight back at Sam's head. The other boys shouted, "Revenge!" His friend had retaliated. Retaliate comes from the old Roman idea of talio, paying back like for like, the law of an eye for an eye. When someone hits you and you hit back, you retaliate. So, what verb means to strike back after being attacked?... Retaliate.
retaliate.example: When the neighbour's goat ate her spinach for the third time, Nanu retaliated by planting chillies all along the fence.

gre.s: Fearing that the rival nation would ____ with punishing tariffs of its own, the government hesitated to impose new taxes on imported goods.
gre.clue: with punishing tariffs of its own

scant.story: Scant. Hardly enough; only a small amount. In the last week before payday, Meredith's family lived on scant supplies: a little rice, a few potatoes and one bottle of oil. Her mother made every meal stretch, frying the potato peels until they were crisp. Nobody complained. Scant can also describe attention or evidence: a report with scant proof has barely any. Scant is the root of scanty, and it is the opposite of copious. So, what word means hardly enough?... Scant.
scant.example: The rescue team had scant information about the missing hikers, knowing only which valley they had entered.

gre.s: The theory has attracted wide popular attention despite ____ evidence, resting on a single study that has never been replicated.
gre.clue: resting on a single study that has never been replicated

scorn.story: Scorn. Strong contempt; to reject with contempt. When Bruce said he wanted to quit his bank job and become a potter, his cousins treated the idea with scorn. "Playing with mud at your age?" Bruce did not argue. He bought a wheel and worked every evening. Five years later, his clay pots sold in shops across the city, and the same cousins asked him for discounts. Scorn sounds a little like score zero: when you scorn someone, you give them zero respect. So, what word names a strong feeling of contempt?... Scorn.
scorn.example: The veteran critic poured scorn on the sequel, calling it a lazy copy stitched together from leftover scenes.

gre.s: Purists tend to ____ any adaptation of a classic novel, dismissing even the most faithful film versions as cheap imitations.
gre.clue: dismissing even the most faithful film versions as cheap imitations

shrewd.hook: SHREWD: sharp as a SHREW's teeth.
shrewd.story: Shrewd. Showing sharp judgment, especially in practical matters. At the big cattle market before the holiday, Tyler's grandfather walked slowly between the cows, checking teeth, eyes and legs. One seller demanded a high price. The old man shrugged, walked away, and returned an hour later, when it was getting dark and the seller was nervous. He bought the best cow for far less. He was shrewd. Shrewd grew from shrew, the tiny sharp-nosed animal: picture its sharp little eyes missing nothing. So, what word describes someone with sharp, practical judgment?... Shrewd.
shrewd.example: A shrewd judge of character, the old headmaster could tell within a minute whether a new teacher would last the year.

gre.s: A ____ investor, she sold her shares months before the crash, having recognized warning signs that most analysts had dismissed as insignificant.
gre.clue: having recognized warning signs that most analysts had dismissed

transcend.story: Transcend. To go beyond the limits of something. Sophie and Fred, two students from neighbouring countries, met at a music evening in London. When the singer began a Tagore song, both of them sang along, word for word, and then looked at each other in surprise. Tagore wrote the national anthems of both their countries, and his songs transcend borders. Trans means across, and scend means climb, as in ascend: to transcend is to climb across a limit. So, what verb means to go beyond the limits of something?... Transcend.
transcend.example: Great children's books transcend their intended age group, delighting grandparents as much as the grandchildren they read to.

gre.s: The finest translations ____ the limits of a word-for-word rendering; rather than merely copying sentences, they recreate the spirit of the original.
gre.clue: rather than merely copying sentences

understated.hook: UNDER-STATED: stated less loudly than it could be.
understated.story: Understated. Quietly simple and tasteful rather than showy. At a wedding full of glittering gowns and heavy gold, Madeline wore a plain cream silk sari, small pearl earrings, and a single white flower in her hair. Yet by the end of the night, every aunty had asked where she bought the sari. Her style was understated, quiet but impossible to forget. Understated means stated below its full volume: an understated look whispers instead of shouting. So, what word describes style that is simple and tasteful, not showy?... Understated.
understated.example: The actor's understated performance, built almost entirely from glances and silences, moved audiences more than any tearful speech.

gre.s: Unlike the flashy designs of her rivals, the architect's ____ buildings blend quietly into their surroundings.
gre.clue: blend quietly into their surroundings

abstain.hook: ABS-TAIN: to keep your ABS, you abstain from sweets.
abstain.story: Abstain. To deliberately hold back from doing or enjoying something, or to choose not to vote. Every year during his month of fasting, Felix's grandfather abstains from food and water from dawn to sunset, even in the April heat. This year Felix, aged twelve, tried a full fast too. At the sunset call to prayer, the family broke their fast with dates and cold lemonade. Felix drank slowly, proud that he had managed to abstain all day. Abs means away, and tain means hold: to abstain is to hold yourself away. So, what verb means to hold back on purpose?... Abstain.
abstain.example: Three council members abstained in the vote on the new bus routes, saying they needed more time to study the plan.

gre.s: Although he enjoyed rich food, the athlete chose to ____ from sweets for the entire season, convinced that discipline would sharpen his game.
gre.clue: convinced that discipline would sharpen his game

apprehension.hook: APPREHENSION: feeling like you're about to be APPREHENDED (arrested).
apprehension.story: Apprehension. Anxiety or fear that something bad will happen. The night before her viva at the university, Maggie lay awake under the slow ceiling fan. She kept picturing the examiners frowning and her voice cracking on the first question. By morning her hands were cold and her stomach was tight with apprehension. Then the first examiner smiled kindly, and her apprehension melted away. The trick: to apprehend a thief is to seize him, and apprehension is the dread that seizes you before trouble arrives. So, what word names the uneasy fear that something will go wrong?... Apprehension.
apprehension.example: Despite her apprehension about flying for the first time, Nanu smiled through the whole journey from Dhaka to Jeddah.

gre.s: Although the villagers greeted the new dam with ____, fearing floods and lost farmland, their worries proved unfounded when the first monsoon passed without incident.
gre.clue: fearing floods and lost farmland

auspicious.hook: AUSPICIOUS: AUSPICES were bird signs Romans read for good luck.
auspicious.story: Auspicious. Suggesting that things will go well; a good sign. On the first morning of his small tea stall near the city college, Kevin was nervous. Before he had even boiled the milk, a professor stopped, ordered ten cups for his whole department, and promised to come back every day. Kevin grinned with relief. What an auspicious start. In ancient Rome, a priest called an auspex watched the flight of birds for signs, and good signs were called auspicious. So, what word describes a beginning that promises success?... Auspicious.
auspicious.example: Three wide-margin wins in its first week were an auspicious beginning for the newly formed university cricket team.

gre.s: The campaign's opening day was hardly ____: the candidate's car broke down on the way, and a sudden storm emptied the rally ground before she could speak.
gre.clue: the candidate's car broke down on the way

banish.story: Banish. To send someone away officially as punishment; also, to get rid of something. On the train home, Toby reached a sad page in his history book. After the revolt of eighteen fifty-seven, the British banished the last Mughal emperor, an old poet king, to Rangoon. The old poet wrote of longing for Delhi and never saw it again. Toby closed the book and watched the fields for a long time. Banish rhymes with vanish: to banish someone is to make them vanish from the land. So, what verb means to send someone out of their country as punishment?... Banish.
banish.example: A brisk walk along the river and a cup of strong tea were usually enough to banish Rokeya's morning gloom.

gre.s: Determined to ____ every trace of the old regime, the new government renamed streets, toppled statues, and rewrote textbooks.
gre.clue: renamed streets, toppled statues, and rewrote textbooks

callous.hook: CALLOUS: hardened like a CALLUS on the skin.
callous.story: Callous. Cruelly uncaring about other people's pain. On a hot city afternoon, an old rickshaw puller slipped and fell under a heavy load of rice sacks. A man in a shiny car honked at him to move, then drove around without a glance. A student named Jill ran to help him up shaking with anger at such callous behaviour. The trick: a callus is hard skin on a working hand, and a callous heart has grown just as hard, so others' pain cannot reach it. So, what word describes someone who does not care when others suffer?... Callous.
callous.example: The company's callous decision to fire injured workers by text message, with no compensation, sparked protests outside its headquarters.

gre.s: The official's ____ response to the flood victims, whom he dismissed as careless people who deserved their fate, provoked outrage across the country.
gre.clue: dismissed as careless people who deserved their fate

dichotomy.hook: DI-CHOTOMY: cutting in two (di = two, tomy = cut).
dichotomy.story: Dichotomy. A sharp split separating two opposite ideas or groups. From the window of a glass tower, Sally could see both shores of the lake at once. On one side stood glass buildings and rooftop gardens. On the other lay the tin roofs of the slum, packed so tightly they almost touched. The dichotomy between the two shores stayed with her all evening. The first part means in two, and tomy means cutting: a dichotomy cuts something cleanly in two. A false dichotomy offers only two choices when more exist. So, what word names a sharp split between two opposite sides?... Dichotomy.
dichotomy.example: Many medical students feel a dichotomy between the science they learn in lectures and the folk remedies their grandparents swear by.

gre.s: The author rejects the traditional ____ between reason and emotion, arguing that the two are deeply intertwined in every decision.
gre.clue: arguing that the two are deeply intertwined

diminutive.story: Diminutive. Extremely or unusually small. Paula's headmistress was barely taller than the girls in class six. Yet when she walked into the morning assembly and raised one small hand, eight hundred students fell silent at once. Paula, standing in the back row, always smiled at the sight. That diminutive woman ran the whole school like a general, and everyone loved her for it. Diminutive shares its root with diminish, to make smaller, so a diminutive thing looks as if it has been diminished. So, what word describes someone or something unusually tiny?... Diminutive.
diminutive.example: The diminutive hummingbird beats its wings so fast that they blur into a faint hum.

gre.s: Despite his ____ stature, the jockey controlled the enormous stallion with remarkable strength and confidence.
gre.clue: controlled the enormous stallion

distort.story: Distort. To bend something out of its normal shape, or to present facts falsely. At the children's park funfair, Aaron grinned at himself in a curved mirror that made him tall and wobbly. A newspaper printed only half of his uncle's speech, and suddenly the kind man seemed to be insulting farmers. The mirror had distorted his body; the paper had distorted his uncle's words. Tort comes from the Latin for twist, as in torture: to distort is to twist out of shape. So, what verb means to twist facts until they become false?... Distort.
distort.example: Cheap speakers distort the bass, so the drums on the recording sounded like someone banging on a tin box.

gre.s: By quoting only fragments of her speech, the article managed to ____ her position, making her appear to support a policy she had criticized.
gre.clue: making her appear to support a policy she had criticized

dwindling.hook: DWINDLE: shrinking like a candle's WICK.
dwindling.story: Dwindling. Gradually becoming smaller or fewer. When Ian moved into a city dorm, his father gave him four hundred dollars to last the month. Books, rickshaw fares and late-night tea each took their share. By the third week the bundle in his drawer was dwindling fast, and he was eating rice and egg every night. Each time he counted it, the dwindling pile felt thinner. Dwindling rhymes with kindling: like a small fire of kindling, it burns lower and lower until little is left. So, what word describes a supply that is slowly shrinking away?... Dwindling.
dwindling.example: With dwindling daylight and no torch, the hikers gave up on reaching the waterfall and turned back toward the village.

gre.s: Conservationists warn that the species' ____ population, now fewer than two hundred animals, may not survive another decade.
gre.clue: now fewer than two hundred animals

elitist.hook: ELITIST: thinks only the ELITE matter.
elitist.story: Elitist. Believing that a select group is superior and deserves special treatment. Heather joined a debate club where the senior members listened only to students from three expensive English-medium schools. When a brilliant girl from a village college stood up to speak, two of them rolled their eyes. Heather felt ashamed, and she left the club the next week. Its attitude was openly elitist. The trick: an elitist believes only the elite matter, and the opposite is egalitarian, believing everyone is equal. So, what word describes someone who thinks a privileged few deserve special treatment?... Elitist.
elitist.example: Some readers dismiss literary prizes as elitist, arguing that the judges reward books ordinary people find dull.

gre.s: The university's admissions policy was attacked as ____, since it effectively excluded applicants who could not afford expensive private tutoring.
gre.clue: effectively excluded applicants who could not afford expensive private tutoring

harrowing.hook: HARROWING: like a HARROW (farm tool) tearing through your heart.
harrowing.story: Harrowing. Deeply upsetting and painful to live through or hear about. Annie's grandfather rarely spoke about nineteen seventy-one. One winter evening he told the family how he hid for nine days in a flooded jute field, listening to soldiers search the village, with only raw rice to eat. No one moved. Annie held his hand as he finished his harrowing story. A harrow is a farm tool that tears through the soil, and a harrowing experience tears through the heart in the same way. So, what word describes an experience so painful it is hard even to hear?... Harrowing.
harrowing.example: The film's harrowing portrayal of the 1943 famine left many viewers sitting in silence long after the credits rolled.

gre.s: Survivors of the shipwreck gave ____ accounts of the night they spent clinging to wreckage in freezing water, many of them watching companions drown beside them.
gre.clue: watching companions drown beside them

heterogeneous.hook: HETERO = different, GENE = kind. Different kinds mixed.
heterogeneous.story: Heterogeneous. Consisting of many different kinds of things. Sarah's GRE coaching batch downtown was a surprising mix: a young doctor, a banker, a fresh graduate, a fifty-year-old engineer and a cricket coach from the south. They had different ages, accents and dreams. Every discussion went somewhere new, and Sarah looked forward to each class. Such a heterogeneous group taught her more than any textbook. Hetero means other or different, and gen means kind: different kinds mixed together. Its opposite is homogeneous, all of one kind. So, what word describes a group made of many different kinds?... Heterogeneous.
heterogeneous.example: Granite looks smooth from a distance, but up close it is heterogeneous, speckled with grains of quartz, feldspar and mica.

gre.s: Far from being uniform, the region's population is remarkably ____, comprising dozens of languages, religions, and ethnic groups.
gre.clue: Far from being uniform

impenetrable.story: Impenetrable. Too dense to get through, or too difficult to understand. On a boat in the mangrove forest, Reid stared at the wall of mangrove roots along the bank, twisted so tightly that not even a monkey could squeeze through. "Impenetrable," the guide said. Back in his dorm, Reid opened a philosophy book so full of jargon that it felt just as impenetrable. Im means not, so impenetrable means it cannot be penetrated, whether it is a forest or an idea. So, what word describes a forest you cannot enter, or a text you cannot understand?... Impenetrable.
impenetrable.example: Thick fog made the mountain pass impenetrable, and the convoy waited until noon for it to lift.

gre.s: Although the theorist claimed to be writing for a general audience, her prose proved virtually ____, so dense with jargon that even specialists struggled to follow it.
gre.clue: even specialists struggled to follow it

ingrained.hook: INGRAINED: deep IN the GRAIN of the wood.
ingrained.story: Ingrained. Fixed so deeply in a person or culture it rarely changes. Raymond left his village twenty years ago for a glass office downtown. Yet he still wakes before dawn without an alarm, still takes off his shoes at every door, and still stands up when an elder enters the room. His colleagues tease him gently, but these habits are ingrained. Picture a stain soaked deep into the grain of a wooden table: no scrubbing can remove what is in the grain. So, what word describes a habit fixed so deep it rarely changes?... Ingrained.
ingrained.example: Checking his phone first thing every morning was so ingrained that Imran did it even on holiday at the beach.

gre.s: Prejudices that are ____ in a culture rarely vanish with the passage of a single law; they persist for generations, handed down quietly from parents to children.
gre.clue: they persist for generations

lull.hook: LULL: a LULLABY puts you to sleep.
lull.story: Lull. A temporary period of calm; as a verb, to calm someone or send them to sleep. All afternoon a storm pounded the tin roof of Josie's house. Then, near sunset, the wind dropped and the rain stopped. Her father hurried out to tie up the goats. In that short lull, Josie's mother sat on the bed, humming softly, and lulled the baby to sleep. Lull is hidden inside lullaby, the soft song that lulls a child to sleep. So, what word names a short, quiet pause in a storm?... Lull.
lull.example: The gentle rocking of the launch on the Meghna soon lulled the children to sleep.

gre.s: After weeks of relentless fighting, a brief ____ allowed aid workers to deliver food to the city, though the shelling resumed within two days.
gre.clue: allowed aid workers to deliver food

momentary.story: Momentary. Over almost as soon as it begins. The teacher held up the results sheet in front of class ten and paused. In that momentary silence, Isla could hear the ceiling fan creak and her own heart pounding. Then the teacher read out her name. Isla covered her mouth as the room burst into cheers. Her fear had been momentary; her joy lasted all week. Momentary lasts only a moment, so do not confuse it with momentous, which means hugely important. So, what word describes a silence that lasts only a moment?... Momentary.
momentary.example: A momentary gap in the clouds let the astronomers photograph the comet before the sky closed over again.

gre.s: The pilot's ____ lapse in concentration lasted only a second, but it was long enough to put the plane dangerously off course.
gre.clue: lasted only a second

nascent.hook: NASCENT: newly born (natal), like a newborn.
nascent.story: Nascent. Just beginning to exist, and showing signs of future potential. Sabrina and her friend started selling handmade jute bags from a tiny city room, with one sewing machine and a Facebook page. In the first month they sold only eleven bags, but every buyer came back for more. Their business was nascent, small and fragile, yet clearly growing. Sabrina packed each order herself, as carefully as if it were a gift. Nascent comes from the Latin for being born, the same root as native. So, what word describes something newly born and just starting to grow?... Nascent.
nascent.example: Bangladesh's nascent space programme reached a milestone in 2018, when the country's first communications satellite was launched.

gre.s: Investors hesitated to fund the ____ industry, since it was still in its infancy and no company had yet proved it could earn a profit.
gre.clue: still in its infancy

nimble.hook: NIMBLE: as quick as a NIMBLE squirrel.
nimble.story: Nimble. Moving quickly and easily; also quick in thinking. In the crowded city market, a young porter carried a basket of vegetables on his head, weaving between rickshaws, buses and shoppers without bumping a single person. Terry watched from a tea stall, amazed by those nimble feet. That evening, at a university debate, he saw a girl answer every tricky question in a flash; her mind was just as nimble. Remember the old rhyme, Jack be nimble, Jack be quick: nimble simply means quick and light. So, what word describes someone light and quick on their feet?... Nimble.
nimble.example: A nimble debater, Faria turned every attack from her opponent into a point in her own favour.

gre.s: Though the old pianist's body had grown frail, his fingers remained astonishingly ____, racing through the most difficult passages without a single error.
gre.clue: racing through the most difficult passages

omit.story: Omit. To leave out or fail to include. Colin filled in his visa form late at night and submitted it, relieved to be done. A week later it came back. He had omitted his middle name, which was printed clearly in his passport. One missing word, and the whole application stopped. Now he reads every form twice, so he never omits a thing. Omit sounds a little like oh, missed it, which is exactly what you say when you omit something. The noun is omission. So, what verb means to leave something out?... Omit.
omit.example: The recipe card omitted the salt, so Babli's first batch of pitha tasted strangely flat.

gre.s: In order to keep the report brief, the authors chose to ____ several minor findings, mentioning only those results directly relevant to the policy debate.
gre.clue: mentioning only those results directly relevant to the policy debate

opportunistic.hook: OPPORTUNISTIC: grabs every OPPORTUNITY, ethical or not.
opportunistic.story: Opportunistic. Grabbing any chance for gain, even against one's principles. When a rumour spread that salt would run out, worried families in the old city rushed to the shops. A few traders hid their stock and sold it at five times the usual price. They had not started the rumour, but they hurried to profit from other people's fear. Their neighbours never fully trusted them again after such opportunistic greed. An opportunist grabs every opportunity, fair or unfair. So, what word describes someone who seizes any chance for profit, whatever it costs their principles?... Opportunistic.
opportunistic.example: Opportunistic scammers posted fake relief appeals within hours of the cyclone, hoping to steal donations meant for survivors.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the politician's sudden embrace of environmental causes as ____, noting that he had opposed every green initiative until polls showed voters cared about them.
gre.clue: until polls showed voters cared about them

outlandish.hook: OUT-LANDISH: from an OUTside LAND, totally foreign and weird.
outlandish.story: Outlandish. Bizarrely strange or unusual. On a country bus, a seller stood up with a bottle of yellow oil. It could cure toothache, baldness, back pain and even bad luck, he said, all for two dollars. Freddy's grandmother leaned over and whispered that if it really worked, the seller would surely have a full head of hair himself. Such outlandish claims never fooled her. Outlandish once meant foreign, from an outside land, so anything outlandish seems to come from somewhere very strange. So, what word describes a claim so bizarre that it is hard to believe?... Outlandish.
outlandish.example: The student's outlandish excuse, that a monkey had stolen her assignment from the rooftop, turned out to be completely true.

gre.s: The theory that the pyramids were built by visitors from another planet is so ____ that serious archaeologists refuse even to debate it.
gre.clue: serious archaeologists refuse even to debate it

propagate.story: Propagate. To spread widely, or to breed and multiply. Every monsoon, Iris's mother cut small stems from her rose bushes, planted them in clay pots, and gave the new plants to neighbours. Within a few years, roses bloomed on half the balconies of the lane. She had propagated them, one cutting at a time. Ideas propagate the same way, passed from hand to hand. The word shares a root with propaganda, which is something spread on purpose. So, what verb means to breed something and spread it widely?... Propagate.
propagate.example: Early printing presses helped propagate the reformers' ideas across Europe far faster than handwritten copies ever could.

gre.s: Rather than suppress the rumour, the agency's clumsy denial served only to ____ it, as thousands of users shared the statement with mocking comments.
gre.clue: as thousands of users shared the statement

remedial.story: Remedial. Intended to correct or improve something, especially weak skills. After his first GRE practice test, Steve stared at his quant score and felt his face go hot. He had forgotten fractions and basic geometry since school. So he joined a remedial maths class downtown every evening, rebuilding the basics one step at a time. Eight weeks later his score jumped, and he called his mother from the street to tell her. Remedial comes from remedy: a remedial class is a remedy for weak skills. So, what word describes lessons meant to fix what you never learned properly?... Remedial.
remedial.example: After the audit, the bank took remedial steps, retraining its cashiers and installing software to catch suspicious transfers.

gre.s: Because so many incoming students lacked basic writing skills, the university introduced ____ courses designed to correct these deficiencies before regular classes began.
gre.clue: designed to correct these deficiencies

resourceful.hook: RESOURCEFUL: full of RESOURCES in your mind.
resourceful.story: Resourceful. Good at finding clever ways to solve problems. A storm cut the power in Tess's village an hour before her online university interview, and her phone was nearly dead. She ran to a neighbour's house, charged it from their small solar panel, then climbed onto the cowshed roof for a better signal. She logged in, with two minutes to spare. Later the interviewer said that was exactly the kind of resourceful student they wanted. A resourceful person is full of resources, especially inner ones like wit and courage. So, what word describes someone who always finds a way?... Resourceful.
resourceful.example: Resourceful as ever, Grandmother turned the leftover rice into crispy fritters that the children liked better than dinner.

gre.s: Stranded without tools when their car broke down in the desert, the ____ travelers repaired the fan belt with a pair of nylon stockings and reached the next town by nightfall.
gre.clue: repaired the fan belt with a pair of nylon stockings

self-indulgent.hook: SELF-INDULGENT: INDULGING the SELF too much.
self-indulgent.story: Self-indulgent. Excessively indulging one's own desires. After his exams ended, Zane bought a whole box of syrup sweets and ate every single one alone on the rooftop. Then he slept until noon, skipped his cousin's birthday, and spent the evening watching films. By night he felt sick and a little guilty. One self-indulgent day is fine, his mother said gently, but a self-indulgent life is not. To indulge is to give in to a desire, so to be self-indulgent is to give in to your own. So, what word describes giving in too much to your own wants?... Self-indulgent.
self-indulgent.example: The singer's self-indulgent twenty-minute guitar solo emptied half the auditorium before the final song.

gre.s: The editor urged the novelist to cut her lengthy digressions about her own childhood, which, however satisfying to write, struck readers as ____ and irrelevant to the plot.
gre.clue: however satisfying to write

tact.hook: TACT: a gentle TACTILE touch with words.
tact.story: Tact. Knowing what to say so that you do not upset others. Nora's aunt served a biryani that was far too salty, and the table went quiet. Nora sipped some water and said, "The meat is so tender, Auntie. You must teach me how you cook it." It was true, and her aunt beamed with pride. That was tact: honest kindness without a sharp edge. The word comes from the Latin for touch, as in tactile, so tact is a gentle touch with words. So, what word names the skill of speaking without hurting feelings?... Tact.
tact.example: Breaking the news of the cancelled trip to forty excited schoolchildren required more tact than the young teacher possessed.

gre.s: The ambassador's ____ in handling the dispute, defusing tensions without insulting either party, won her praise from both governments.
gre.clue: defusing tensions without insulting either party

undercut.hook: UNDER-CUT: CUT the price UNDER theirs, or cut UNDER the foundation.
undercut.story: Undercut. To offer lower prices than a competitor; also, to weaken or undermine. When a big grocery app arrived in the neighbourhood with cheaper rice and lentils, Rick's small corner shop lost half its customers. The app had undercut him. But Rick knew every family by name, gave credit when times were hard, and remembered which child liked which biscuit. Slowly, people returned. No app could undercut that trust. Picture cutting under a wall until it falls, or cutting your price under someone else's. So, what verb means to sell more cheaply than a rival, or to weaken them?... Undercut.
undercut.example: Cheap imported toys undercut the craftsmen of Sonargaon, who could not match prices made possible by mass production.

gre.s: The witness's repeated contradictions served only to ____ the credibility of the defense, which had built its entire case on his reliability.
gre.clue: repeated contradictions

wayward.hook: WAYWARD: going AWAY from the right path.
wayward.story: Wayward. Hard to control and inclined to go its own way. During the winter kite festival on the rooftops of the old city, Mike's kite caught a gust and refused to obey him. It swooped, spun and drifted toward the neighbour's water tank. Mike tugged the string, but the wayward kite went wherever it pleased. His grandfather said Mike had been just as wayward as a little boy. Wayward is a shortened form of awayward, turned away from the path you are meant to follow. So, what word describes something that refuses to be controlled and goes its own way?... Wayward.
wayward.example: A wayward kite drifted across the rooftops of Old Dhaka during the Shakrain festival before tangling in a coconut tree.

gre.s: The novel follows a ____ teenager who drifts from one reckless adventure to another before finally finding purpose.
gre.clue: drifts from one reckless adventure to another

whimsical.story: Whimsical. Playfully quaint or fanciful; acting on sudden impulses. Lila's art teacher painted the classroom ceiling with flying fish, umbrellas growing like flowers, and a cat riding a rickshaw through the clouds. The students loved every corner of it.
