He found all three. His knowledge of books is encyclopedic. Like an encyclopedia, an encyclopedic mind covers nearly everything in its field. So, what word describes knowledge that is broad and thorough?... Encyclopedic.
encyclopedic.example: Professor Haque's encyclopedic grasp of Bengali folk music lets him name the district where almost any song began.

gre.s: The guide's ____ knowledge of the city, extending from medieval architecture to the history of every street name, delighted the tourists.
gre.clue: extending from medieval architecture to the history of every street name

extenuating.hook: EXTENUATING: makes the guilt more TENUOUS (thin).
extenuating.story: Extenuating. Making a wrong seem less serious; partly excusing it. Shelby submitted her term paper two days late, and her department's rule was strict: late work gets zero. But on the due date, the river near her village had broken its embankment, and she had spent two days helping her family carry their belongings to higher ground. Her professor listened quietly, then accepted the paper. These were extenuating circumstances. Extenuating comes from the Latin for making thin, like tenuous: extenuating facts thin out the blame. So, what word describes circumstances that partly excuse a wrong?... Extenuating.
extenuating.example: The school accepted that a burst water pipe in the exam hall was an extenuating factor and allowed the students to resit.

gre.s: Although the judge acknowledged that the defendant had stolen the medicine, she cited ____ circumstances, noting that he had done so to save his dying child.
gre.clue: he had done so to save his dying child

facetious.hook: FACETIOUS: makes funny FACES at serious things.
facetious.story: Facetious. Joking at the wrong moment about something serious. Spencer's family sat in the living room after his father's blood pressure report came back high. Everyone was worried. Spencer tried to lighten the mood. "Good news," he said, "now Dad has an excuse to skip the wedding feasts." Nobody laughed. His mother gave him a long, tired look. His facetious joke had fallen flat. A handy trick: facetious contains the vowels a, e, i, o, u in order. So, what word describes a joke made at the wrong time about something serious?... Facetious.
facetious.example: Asked how the company would repay its debts, the chief executive gave a facetious reply about winning the lottery.

gre.s: The minister's ____ remark about the flood victims, which he apparently intended as a joke, provoked outrage among families who had lost everything.
gre.clue: which he apparently intended as a joke

fallible.hook: FALLIBLE: able to FALL into error.
fallible.story: Fallible. Not perfect, and so sometimes wrong or mistaken. Mason's cricket coach was a local legend, and the boys trusted his every word. One season he moved Mason down the batting order, and Mason's scores fell. After a month, the coach called him aside. "I was wrong. Go back to opening." Mason was stunned, but he respected the coach more than ever. Even the best coaches are fallible, and the wise ones admit it. Fallible shares its root with false and fail; its opposite, infallible, means never wrong. So, what word describes anyone capable of making mistakes?... Fallible.
fallible.example: Even the most advanced weather models are fallible, so farmers in Rangpur still watch the sky before sowing.

gre.s: Eyewitness testimony, once treated as nearly conclusive, is now known to be highly ____, since memories can be distorted by stress, suggestion, and the passage of time.
gre.clue: memories can be distorted by stress, suggestion, and the passage of time

feint.hook: FEINT: a FAKE move. Sounds like FAINT but means FAKE.
feint.story: Feint. A deceptive movement meant to distract an opponent. In a village kabaddi match, Tanner crossed into the other team's half, chanting under his breath. He lunged left as if to touch the nearest defender. Three defenders shifted left to trap him. In that instant he spun right, tagged the last player, and dashed home. The crowd roared. His lunge had been a feint. Feint sounds exactly like faint, but think of a fake: a feint is a fake move, made to fool. So, what word names a fake move that tricks an opponent?... Feint.
feint.example: The chess master's queen move looked like an attack but was only a feint to pull the defending pieces out of position.

gre.s: The general's apparent retreat was merely a ____: while the enemy rushed to pursue, his main force circled behind them and attacked their unguarded camp.
gre.clue: while the enemy rushed to pursue, his main force circled behind them

gauche.hook: GAUCHE: French for LEFT, as in left-handed and clumsy.
gauche.story: Gauche. Socially awkward; lacking grace or tact. The first time Frank met his fiancée's family in the old city, he wanted so badly to impress them. Instead, he knocked over a glass of spiced yogurt drink, called her grandmother by the wrong name, and asked her uncle how much his house had cost. Everyone smiled politely. Later, in the rickshaw, Frank groaned at how gauche he had been. Gauche is French for left, from an old belief that the left hand is clumsy; its opposite, adroit, comes from the French for right. So, what word describes someone socially clumsy and tactless?... Gauche.
gauche.example: As a gauche teenager, I once congratulated a guest on her pregnancy when she was simply wearing a loose dress.

gre.s: Though brilliant in the laboratory, the young chemist was painfully ____ at receptions, blurting out tactless remarks and forgetting the names of her hosts.
gre.clue: blurting out tactless remarks

glum.story: Glum. Looking or feeling sad and gloomy. Rain had been falling on the port city for three days, and the school picnic to the beach was cancelled. Little Sadie sat by the window with her chin in her hands. She would not eat her lunch, and she would not talk. Her father sat beside her quietly for a while, then gently asked, "Why so glum?" Glum sounds like a short, heavy cousin of gloom, and it means the same heavy mood. So, what word describes a face that is sad and gloomy?... Glum.
glum.example: The glum faces of the waiting passengers told me that the flight to Cox's Bazar had been delayed yet again.

gre.s: Despite the company's record profits, the shareholders' meeting was strangely ____, since everyone knew the beloved founder would announce his resignation.
gre.clue: since everyone knew the beloved founder would announce his resignation

impertinent.hook: IM-PERTINENT: not pertinent (relevant), and rude to boot.
impertinent.story: Impertinent. Rude and disrespectful; not showing proper respect. At a family dinner, Nora's teenage cousin was asked by their grandfather about his exam results. The boy did not even look up from his phone. "You would not understand my results anyway." The table fell silent. His mother's face went red, and the grandfather slowly set down his glass. It was an impertinent answer. Impertinent literally means not pertinent: an impertinent remark has no place in the conversation, and it is rude besides. So, what word describes a cheeky, disrespectful reply to an elder?... Impertinent.
impertinent.example: The impertinent customer told the elderly tailor that he was far too old to understand modern fashion.

gre.s: The young reporter's ____ questions about the senator's private life drew a sharp rebuke from the press secretary.
gre.clue: drew a sharp rebuke

indefatigable.story: Indefatigable. Never tiring; persistently energetic. In a southern fishing village, a retired teacher named Rose runs free evening classes for children. After teaching, she visits families who keep their girls at home, walks miles along sandy paths, and returns the next day to try again. Volunteers half her age struggle to keep up. "Where does she get the energy?" they whisper. She is indefatigable. Break it apart: in means not, and fatigable means able to be fatigued, so an indefatigable person can never be worn out. So, what word describes someone who never tires?... Indefatigable.
indefatigable.example: The indefatigable archivist spent twelve years cataloguing every letter in the old zamindar family's collection.

gre.s: Even in her nineties, the ____ activist continued to march at every protest, outlasting colleagues half her age.
gre.clue: outlasting colleagues half her age

inscrutable.story: Inscrutable. Impossible to understand or interpret. Every Friday, Tessa's grandfather plays chess with his oldest friend under the banyan tree near the church. Tessa watches the friend's face for clues, but it never changes: no smile, no frown, not even a blink before a winning move. Is he worried? Is he about to win? Nobody can tell. Grandfather calls him the sphinx. His face is truly inscrutable. Scrutiny means close examination, so something inscrutable stays a mystery no matter how closely you examine it. So, what word describes a face that no one can read?... Inscrutable.
inscrutable.example: The ancient Indus script remains inscrutable, since no one has yet found a bilingual inscription that would help decode it.

gre.s: The cat's ____ expression gave no hint of whether it was about to purr contentedly or lash out with its claws.
gre.clue: gave no hint

jettison.hook: JETTISON: a JET dumping fuel to lighten its load.
jettison.story: Jettison. To throw away or abandon something unwanted. Halfway across a wide river, a small trawler began to take on water in the rising waves. The boatman shouted, and the passengers worked fast, heaving sacks of potatoes and empty drums over the side. The boat rode higher, and everyone reached the bank safely. They had jettisoned the cargo to save themselves. In the same way, a company can jettison a failing plan. Picture a jet dumping fuel to lighten its load before an emergency landing. So, what verb means to throw away what you no longer want?... Jettison.
jettison.example: The design team jettisoned their original logo after customers said it looked like a broken umbrella.

gre.s: Faced with mounting losses, the company decided to ____ its least profitable divisions so that it could focus its resources on its core business.
gre.clue: so that it could focus its resources on its core business

languid.story: Languid. Lacking energy; relaxed and slow. It is a hot Friday afternoon in May. After a heavy lunch of rice and fish curry, Ian's whole family lies on the cool floor under the ceiling fan. Nobody talks. The cat stretches, yawns, and closes its eyes. Even the street outside is quiet, except for one far-off crow. Ian thinks he has never felt so languid. Languid and languish share a Latin root meaning to be faint or weak, and a languid afternoon moves at half speed. So, what word describes a slow, lazy, low-energy mood?... Languid.
languid.example: The cat stretched languidly across the warm windowsill, ignoring the pigeons that strutted just outside the glass.

gre.s: The afternoon heat made everyone ____: even the usually restless children lay on the cool floor, too sluggish to play or even talk.
gre.clue: too sluggish to play or even talk

languish.hook: LANGUISH: become LANGUID, weak and fading.
languish.story: Languish. To lose strength; to suffer from being in an unpleasant situation. When Tina's family moved to a small city flat, her grandmother's basil plant came too. On a dark balcony with no sun, it began to languish, its leaves pale and drooping. Her grandmother was languishing too; she missed her village courtyard. One weekend, Tina carried the plant up to the rooftop, and took her grandmother up with it. Both seemed to come alive again. Languish shares its root with languid. So, what verb means to grow weak while stuck in a bad situation?... Languish.
languish.example: Plans for the new metro line languished in government files for twenty years before construction finally began.

gre.s: Without fresh investment, the once thriving port continued to ____, its warehouses empty and its docks slowly crumbling into the harbor.
gre.clue: its warehouses empty and its docks slowly crumbling

libertine.hook: LIBERTINE: takes too many LIBERTIES with morality.
libertine.story: Libertine. A person who freely indulges in pleasures, ignoring moral restraints. In an old novel that Nadia reads for her literature class, a landlord's son wastes his father's fortune on card games, wine and parties that last until dawn. He laughs at every warning, breaks every promise, and answers to no one. His mother watches the estate slowly crumble. In the margin, Nadia writes one word: libertine. Libertine shares a root with liberty, but a libertine takes liberty too far, with no self-control at all. So, what do you call a person who chases pleasure and ignores morals?... Libertine.
libertine.example: Lord Byron was known in London society as a libertine whose love affairs and debts fed endless gossip.

gre.s: Unlike his brother, a notorious ____ who squandered his fortune on drink and gambling, the younger prince lived a life of strict self-discipline.
gre.clue: squandered his fortune on drink and gambling

pastiche.hook: PASTICHE: a PASTE of different styles glued together.
pastiche.story: Pastiche. An artistic work that imitates the styles of other works; a medley. At a university cultural night, Sam's band played one song that began like an old folk tune, slid into a classic ballad, and ended with a roaring rock guitar solo. The audience cheered and clapped along. A music teacher in the front row smiled and called it a clever pastiche. Pastiche comes from the Italian pasticcio, a pie that mixes many ingredients, so picture a pie baked from borrowed styles. So, what word names a work stitched together by imitating other styles?... Pastiche.
pastiche.example: The new shopping mall is an odd pastiche of Greek columns, Mughal domes and mirrored glass towers.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the film as a mere ____, cobbled together from scenes borrowed from a dozen earlier thrillers and lacking any style of its own.
gre.clue: cobbled together from scenes borrowed from a dozen earlier thrillers

predilection.story: Predilection. A particular fondness for something over other things. Every evening, when the snack seller rings his bell, Tessa runs downstairs. She has tried every new café in the area, but nothing beats spicy street snacks with extra tamarind water and a pinch of green chilli. Her friends tease her, but she just orders another plate. Her predilection for street snacks is famous in the family. Predilection comes from Latin roots meaning to choose before others: a predilection is the thing you pick first, every time. So, what word means a special fondness for one thing over others?... Predilection.
predilection.example: The physicist had a predilection for old detective novels, which she read on every long flight to conferences.

gre.s: The collector's ____ for small Dutch landscapes was well known, and dealers saved such paintings especially for him.
gre.clue: dealers saved such paintings especially for him

relent.story: Relent. To finally agree after refusing; also, to become less severe. For a week, Jody begged to join her university trip to the hills, and every day her mother said no. Then on Thursday evening, the heavy rain that had drummed on their roof all week finally relented, and so did her mother. "Go," she said, "but call me every night." Jody hugged her so hard they both nearly fell over. Do not confuse relent with relentless, which means never easing up; to relent is the opposite, to soften. So, what verb means to give in after refusing?... Relent.
relent.example: The heavy rain finally relented around noon, and the groundsmen hurried to pull the covers off the pitch.

gre.s: The authorities refused for months to release the detained journalist, but mounting international pressure eventually forced them to ____.
gre.clue: refused for months

sinuous.story: Sinuous. Curving and bending, often in a smooth, graceful way. On her first flight south over the delta, Annie pressed her face to the window. Below, the rivers wound across the green land in great silver loops, bending back on themselves like ribbons. She had never seen anything so beautiful. At a dance recital later, she noticed the same sinuous grace in a dancer's arms. Sinuous comes from the Latin sinus, a curve or fold; do not confuse it with sinewy, which means tough and muscular. So, what word describes a river that winds in smooth curves?... Sinuous.
sinuous.example: The dancer's sinuous arm movements made the old Manipuri dance look as smooth as flowing water.

gre.s: Unlike the straight highways of the plains, the mountain road was ____, twisting back on itself so many times that several passengers grew carsick.
gre.clue: twisting back on itself so many times

supplant.hook: SUP-PLANT: uproot one PLANT and put another in its place.
supplant.story: Supplant. To take someone's place, often by plotting or force. Nadia's grandmother often tells a story from her father's old office in a river port town. A charming young clerk joined, helpful to everyone. But behind the manager's back, he whispered to the owner, took credit for others' work, and slowly won the owner's trust. Within a year, he had supplanted the loyal old manager entirely. The Latin root means to trip someone up by the sole of the foot, and that is exactly how a schemer supplants a rival. So, what verb means to push someone out and take their place?... Supplant.
supplant.example: The young striker gradually supplanted the veteran captain in the starting eleven, scoring in nine straight matches.

gre.s: The ambitious deputy spent years flattering the board and quietly undermining his superior, plotting all the while to ____ her as head of the company.
gre.clue: quietly undermining his superior

vacuous.hook: VACUOUS: like a VACUUM, empty inside.
vacuous.story: Vacuous. Empty of real ideas or intelligence; blank. On a television talk show, a young politician was asked how he would fix the city's traffic. He smiled widely. "Traffic is a big problem, and we will solve it with solutions. The future is very bright." Then he said nothing more. Fiona, watching at home, turned to her father in disbelief. He shook his head. "What a vacuous answer." Vacuous shares its root with vacuum and vacant: nothing inside. So, what word describes an answer, or a stare, that is empty of thought?... Vacuous.
vacuous.example: The quiz contestant gave a vacuous grin when asked to name the capital of Australia.

gre.s: The candidate's speeches, full of rousing slogans but devoid of any concrete policy proposals, struck most serious analysts as ____.
gre.clue: devoid of any concrete policy proposals

vapid.story: Vapid. Offering nothing stimulating or challenging; dull and empty. Matt's cousin forwarded him a famous motivational video. Twenty minutes of slow piano music and lines like "Believe in yourself" and "Dreams come true." Not one useful idea. Matt yawned and closed it halfway. Later, his cousin asked what he thought. Matt searched for a polite word, but the only honest one was vapid. Vapid comes from the Latin for flat, the way wine tastes when it has lost its flavour. A vapid talk is flat. So, what word describes talk that is flat, dull and empty?... Vapid.
vapid.example: The award show's vapid speeches, all thanks and no ideas, sent half the audience back to their phones.

gre.s: The critic dismissed the pop song's lyrics as ____, a string of empty phrases that said nothing at all about love.
gre.clue: a string of empty phrases that said nothing at all

acquiesce.story: Acquiesce. To accept something reluctantly, but without protest. Nadia had planned a quiet wedding with twenty guests. Her mother had other plans: a big community centre, four hundred guests, and a henna night with a live band. Nadia opened her mouth to argue, looked at her mother's shining eyes, and closed it again. She acquiesced. Inside acquiesce is the Latin quies, meaning rest, the same root as quiet: to acquiesce is to accept quietly, without a fight. So, what verb means to go along with something you would not have chosen, without protest?... Acquiesce.
acquiesce.example: Tired of arguing, the residents' committee acquiesced to the developer's plan to cut down two old mango trees.

gre.s: Although she privately opposed the merger, the director chose to ____ rather than risk a damaging public battle with the board.
gre.clue: rather than risk a damaging public battle

anoint.hook: ANOINT: kings were 'A-OIL-ed' — oil on the head at coronation.
anoint.story: Anoint. To choose someone ceremonially for an important role; also, to put oil on someone in a religious ceremony. When Grandpa Harold turned eighty, he gathered the whole family in his famous sweet shop. Everyone expected his eldest son to take over. Instead, he placed his old brass ladle in the hands of his granddaughter Mallory. He had anointed her, just as kings were once anointed with holy oil. Anoint shares its root with ointment, an oily cream rubbed on the skin. So, what verb means to formally choose someone as the next leader?... Anoint.
anoint.example: Critics were quick to anoint the young Rajshahi novelist as the most important new voice of her generation.

gre.s: Although many party insiders expected an open contest, the retiring leader chose to ____ his deputy as successor, effectively ending the race before it began.
gre.clue: effectively ending the race before it began

aphorism.hook: APHORISM: a short AFFIRMATION of truth.
aphorism.story: Aphorism. A brief, clever saying that sums up a broad truth. Whenever Nate wasted an afternoon on his phone, his grandmother would say one old line: an idle mind is the devil's workshop. As a boy, Nate rolled his eyes at her aphorisms. But years later, during his GRE preparation, he caught himself whispering that same line whenever he felt lazy. Aphorism comes from a Greek word meaning to mark off or define: an aphorism defines a big truth in a few words. So, what word names a short, wise saying that captures a broad truth?... Aphorism.
aphorism.example: Sticky notes bearing Tania's favourite aphorism, done is better than perfect, lined the edge of her computer monitor.

gre.s: The essay closes with a single pithy ____, "Certainty ages a face faster than doubt," which has been quoted far more often than any of the arguments that precede it.
gre.clue: a single pithy

befuddled.hook: BE-FUDDLED: a brain in a MUDDLE.
befuddled.story: Befuddled. So confused that you cannot think clearly. Ricky's grandfather got his first smartphone last holiday. He pressed one button, and the screen turned sideways. He pressed another, and a video of a dancing cat began to play, loudly, in the middle of dinner. He held the phone at arm's length, completely befuddled, while the grandchildren rushed to help. Befuddled rhymes with muddled, and a befuddled mind is exactly that: a muddle where no clear thought can get through. So, what word describes someone so confused they cannot think straight?... Befuddled.
befuddled.example: Jet lag left the visiting scientist so befuddled that she gave her keynote talk with the slides in the wrong order.

gre.s: Students left the lecture thoroughly ____, as the professor had jumped between unrelated theories without explaining any of them.
gre.clue: without explaining any of them

belie.hook: BE-LIE: the appearance tells a LIE about what's underneath.
belie.story: Belie. To give a false impression of something; to hide the truth behind an appearance. At her thesis defence, Alice answered every question in a calm, steady voice. The examiners nodded, impressed. Only her best friend, in the back row, could see her fingers twisting the end of her scarf under the table. Alice's calm voice belied her racing heart. The trick is in the word itself: be plus lie. When an appearance belies the truth, it tells a lie about what is underneath. So, what verb means to give a false impression of what is really there?... Belie.
belie.example: The bakery's tiny, shabby storefront belies the remarkable quality of the pastries made inside.

gre.s: The pianist's relaxed, almost careless stage manners ____ the punishing hours of practice that lie behind every performance.
gre.clue: relaxed, almost careless

blithe.story: Blithe. Cheerfully carefree; also, casually unconcerned about something serious. Every morning, Zack's cousin rides his motorbike through city traffic without a helmet, humming a song and waving at friends. When his mother begs him to be careful, he only grins. "Nothing will happen to me, Mom." His blithe confidence makes her stomach twist. Blithe can be sweet, like a child's blithe laughter, but on the GRE it often means not worrying when you should. Blithe and bliss are old relatives: a blithe person floats along in blissful unconcern. So, what word describes someone carelessly cheerful about a real danger?... Blithe.
blithe.example: Some commuters in Dhaka cross the busy road with blithe disregard for the buses roaring toward them.

gre.s: The CEO's ____ dismissal of the auditors' warnings, delivered with a cheerful wave of the hand, alarmed investors who knew how serious the losses were.
gre.clue: delivered with a cheerful wave of the hand

circumspect.hook: CIRCUM-SPECT: looking (spect) all around (circum) before acting.
circumspect.story: Circumspect. Cautious; carefully considering everything before acting. When a stranger on Facebook offered Isaac a well-paid job in Dubai, his friends told him to grab it. Isaac was more circumspect. He called the company, asked for its licence, and requested a cousin in Dubai to visit the address. There was no office there at all. Being circumspect had saved him. Circum means around, and spect means look, as in spectacles: a circumspect person looks all around before taking a step. So, what word describes someone careful to consider everything before acting?... Circumspect.
circumspect.example: Journalists covering the election learned to be circumspect on the phone, assuming that every call might be monitored.

gre.s: Having been burned by a previous scandal, the senator was ____ in her public statements, weighing every word before she spoke.
gre.clue: weighing every word before she spoke

collude.story: Collude. To cooperate secretly for a dishonest purpose. In a northern market town, rice prices jumped in every shop on the same morning. Ruby's father, a schoolteacher, found it strange. A local reporter dug deeper and discovered that the three biggest wholesalers had met at night and agreed to hold back their stock together. They had colluded to squeeze every family in town. Collude comes from the Latin for playing together, the same root as ludicrous: those who collude play a secret game against everyone else. So, what verb means to work together secretly to cheat others?... Collude.
collude.example: Officials found that several exam invigilators had colluded with a printing press to leak the question papers.

gre.s: Investigators suspected that the two rival bidders had secretly agreed to ____, inflating their offers so that the government would pay far more than the project was worth.
gre.clue: secretly agreed

contrite.hook: CONTRITE: sounds like 'contrition' — a confession full of regret.
contrite.story: Contrite. Feeling deep regret and guilt for having done wrong. Playing cricket in the lane, eleven-year-old Shane hit a six straight through old Grandma Rose's window. The other boys ran. Shane did not. He knocked on her door, eyes on the floor, holding out the ball and his whole month's pocket money. "I am really sorry, Grandma Rose." His voice shook. She looked at the contrite boy, and offered him a biscuit. Contrite comes from the Latin for crushed: a contrite heart feels crushed by guilt. So, what word describes someone full of genuine regret for a wrong?... Contrite.
contrite.example: The contrite striker visited the injured defender in hospital and apologized for his reckless tackle.

gre.s: The defendant's ____ statement, in which he tearfully apologized to the victims, persuaded the judge to reduce his sentence.
gre.clue: tearfully apologized to the victims

dictum.story: Dictum. A formal, authoritative statement; also, a short saying. At Ross's school, the headmaster had one famous dictum, painted above the gate: "Discipline is the bridge between goals and success." Every morning for ten years, students walked under it. Today, as a busy doctor, Ross repeats that dictum to his young interns, and they roll their eyes exactly the way he once did. Dictum comes from the Latin dicere, to say, as in dictate and dictionary: a dictum is something said with authority. So, what word names an authoritative statement or principle?... Dictum.
dictum.example: Architects still quote the famous dictum that form follows function, though few of their buildings actually obey it.

gre.s: The founder's ____ that the customer is always right was treated by her managers as an unquestionable law, though she herself frequently ignored it.
gre.clue: treated by her managers as an unquestionable law

distill.hook: DISTILL: boil it down to the pure essence.
distill.story: Distill. To extract the essential meaning of something; also, to purify a liquid by heating and cooling it. In chemistry lab, Paige watched muddy water boil in a flask, while clean drops slowly gathered in a cool glass tube on the other side. Years later, her boss handed her a two-hundred-page report and asked for one page by morning. She worked all night and distilled it to its pure essence. It felt just like the lab: boil away everything else and keep only what matters. So, what verb means to boil something down to its essential meaning?... Distill.
distill.example: Before kickoff, the coach distilled the whole match plan into three words on the whiteboard: press, pass, shoot.

gre.s: In just a few pages, the author manages to ____ decades of complex research into a handful of clear principles that any reader can grasp.
gre.clue: into a handful of clear principles

encroach.hook: EN-CROACH: like a COCKROACH creeping into your space.
encroach.story: Encroach. To gradually intrude beyond proper limits. When Kyle's grandfather was young, the canal behind their city neighbourhood was wide enough for boats. Then, year by year, people began to encroach on it: first a bamboo platform, then a tin shed, then a concrete wall. Today the canal is a thin, black drain, and the old man still points to where the water once shone. Encroach comes from an old French word for hook: those who encroach hook a little more space each time. So, what verb means to creep beyond your proper limits?... Encroach.
encroach.example: Long working hours began to encroach on the evenings Babul had promised to spend with his children.

gre.s: Residents worried that the expanding city would gradually ____ on the surrounding farmland, swallowing a few more fields each year until none remained.
gre.clue: swallowing a few more fields each year

feckless.hook: FECK-LESS: 'feck' is old Scottish for effect. No effect at all.
feckless.story: Feckless. Lacking initiative or strength of character; irresponsible and ineffective. Rosa's uncle has started six businesses in ten years, from a phone shop to a poultry farm. Each one failed within months, because he slept till noon and let his friends run up unpaid bills. Now he asks Rosa's father for money again, smiling as if nothing happened. The family loves him, but everyone agrees he is feckless. Feck is an old Scottish word for effect, so a feckless person is one without effect, achieving nothing. So, what word describes someone weak-willed and irresponsible?... Feckless.
feckless.example: Her feckless brother borrowed money to start a new business every year and lost it within months.

gre.s: Voters grew frustrated with the ____ government, which announced ambitious plans every year but never carried any of them out.
gre.clue: never carried any of them out

finicky.story: Finicky. Fussy and hard to please; also, needing great attention to detail. Seven-year-old Archie will eat rice only if the dal does not touch it. His egg must be fried, never boiled, and the onion must be invisible. If a single curry leaf appears on his plate, he pushes it away with one finger, and his mother picks it out, every time. Archie is the most finicky eater in the family. Finicky sounds like fine plus picky, and a finicky person fusses over every fine detail. So, what word describes someone fussy and hard to please?... Finicky.
finicky.example: Orchids are finicky plants, so my aunt in Mymensingh checks the humidity in her greenhouse twice a day.

gre.s: The critic was notoriously ____ about food, sending back dishes whose sauce was a few degrees too cool or whose garnish sat slightly off centre.
gre.clue: sending back dishes whose sauce was a few degrees too cool

furtive.hook: FURTIVE: like a FERRET, sneaking around quietly.
furtive.story: Furtive. Secretive and sly, as if trying to avoid notice. In the exam hall, the invigilator walked slowly between the rows. One boy near the window kept stealing quick, furtive glances at his left sleeve, then back at his paper, then at the invigilator. The invigilator stopped beside him, gently turned back the sleeve, and found tiny notes written in ink. The boy's face went pale. Furtive comes from the Latin fur, meaning thief: a furtive look is the quick glance of a thief. So, what word describes a secretive glance meant to avoid notice?... Furtive.
furtive.example: The two lovers exchanged furtive smiles across the crowded wedding hall, careful that no relative noticed.

gre.s: The thief cast ____ glances around the gallery before slipping the small sculpture into his coat.
gre.clue: before slipping the small sculpture into his coat

impudent.story: Impudent. Rude and cheeky in a bold, shameless way. In a long downtown bank queue, a young man walked straight to the counter and pushed his cheque in front of an old woman. When the clerk asked him to wait his turn, he smirked. "Make me." Shauna, standing behind the old woman, could hardly believe such impudent behaviour. The whole queue stared until he stepped back. Inside impudent is the Latin pudor, shame, and im means without: an impudent person has no shame at all. So, what word describes someone rude and shamelessly bold?... Impudent.
impudent.example: An impudent post from the club's official account mocked the referee and earned the team a heavy fine.

gre.s: The ____ student not only ignored the teacher's warning but mimicked her voice in front of the whole class, apparently without the slightest shame.
gre.clue: apparently without the slightest shame

incontrovertible.story: Incontrovertible. So clearly true that no one can argue against it. Two city neighbours argued for a week about who had scratched a new car in their garage. Each blamed the other's driver. Then the building guard quietly brought the security camera footage. On the screen, clear as day, a delivery van backed into the car and drove away. The argument ended in an instant. The video was incontrovertible proof. Break it apart: in means not, and controvert means argue against, as in controversy, so incontrovertible means beyond argument. So, what word describes evidence no one can dispute?... Incontrovertible.
incontrovertible.example: Carbon dating of the paper gave the museum incontrovertible proof that its prized manuscript was a modern forgery.

gre.s: Although the theory was once fiercely contested, the satellite data now provide ____ proof, leaving even the most skeptical scientists with no grounds for doubt.
gre.clue: leaving even the most skeptical scientists with no grounds for doubt

magisterial.hook: MAGISTERIAL: like a MAGISTRATE in court.
magisterial.story: Magisterial. Having or showing great authority; sometimes domineering. When the family gathered to settle a quarrel over land, nobody spoke until Nolan's grandmother entered. She sat at the head of the table, adjusted her glasses, and listened to each son in turn. Then she gave her decision in three calm sentences. No one argued. Her magisterial presence filled the room, and even her silence was magisterial. Think of a magistrate in court: magisterial and magistrate both come from the Latin magister, meaning master. So, what word describes a manner full of commanding authority?... Magisterial.
magisterial.example: The retired judge gave a magisterial lecture on the constitution, speaking for two hours without a single note.

gre.s: The historian's ____ survey of the empire, which drew on sources in twelve languages, is still regarded as the definitive work on the subject.
gre.clue: is still regarded as the definitive work

perfunctory.hook: PERFUNCTORY: done just to PERFORM the FUNCTION, nothing more.
perfunctory.story: Perfunctory. Done with minimal effort, routinely and without real interest. At the entrance of a big city shopping mall, a security guard waves a metal detector near each visitor's bag. The detector beeps for everyone, and he waves everyone through anyway. Rafe whispers that a tiger could walk past. The check is perfunctory, done only to say it was done. Perfunctory comes from a Latin word for getting a duty over with: a perfunctory task is simply got through, nothing more. So, what word describes a task done routinely, with no real care?... Perfunctory.
perfunctory.example: The waiter's perfunctory smile vanished the moment he turned away from our table.

gre.s: The manager gave the report only a ____ glance before signing it, a carelessness that allowed several glaring errors to slip through.
gre.clue: allowed several glaring errors to slip through

perpetrate.story: Perpetrate. To be the one who commits a crime or a wrong. For weeks, people in a northern town received calls from a man claiming to work for their mobile banking company, asking for their secret code. Many lost their savings. Then police traced the calls to one small rented room, where two young men sat with a pile of phones. They had perpetrated the entire fraud. Perpetrate comes from a Latin word for carrying out an act, and the one who perpetrates a crime is the perpetrator. So, what verb means to be the one who carries out a wrong?... Perpetrate.
perpetrate.example: The bank's own IT manager perpetrated the fraud, quietly moving small sums into hidden accounts for six years.

gre.s: Although the soldiers claimed they were only following orders, the tribunal held that those who ____ such atrocities bear personal responsibility for them.
gre.clue: the soldiers claimed they were only following orders

plaintive.hook: PLAINTIVE: like a PLAINT, a sad complaint.
plaintive.story: Plaintive. Having a sad, longing sound, like a cry or a lament. On a ferry crossing the great river at dusk, Iris heard an old boatman singing an old river song as he rowed past. His voice rose and fell over the water, slow and aching, a song about a far-off home. Even the children stopped playing to listen. It was the most plaintive sound she had ever heard. Plaintive comes from plaint, an old word for a lament, the same root as complaint. So, what word describes a sad, longing sound, like a boatman's song at dusk?... Plaintive.
plaintive.example: Through the thin wall we heard the plaintive mewing of the neighbour's kitten, which had been shut out of the kitchen.

gre.s: From the abandoned house drifted the ____ notes of a flute, so sorrowful that passers-by stopped in the street and fell silent.
gre.clue: so sorrowful that passers-by stopped in the street and fell silent

polemical.hook: POLEMICAL: POLE-vaulting into a fight; aggressive argument.
polemical.story: Polemical. Strongly critical or controversial in argument. Every Friday, a well-known columnist in a city newspaper writes a fierce attack on someone: a minister, a cricket board, a famous writer. His words are sharp, his tone furious, and readers either cheer or send angry letters. Rob's father reads each column aloud at breakfast, shaking his head. "Polemical again." Polemical writing goes to war with words, and that is exactly its origin: polemos is the Greek word for war. So, what word describes writing that attacks fiercely and stirs controversy?... Polemical.
polemical.example: The scientist's polemical blog posts against homeopathy won her many fans and a few angry lawsuits.

gre.s: Although the book's ____ tone alienated some readers, its fierce attack on the policy succeeded in sparking a national debate.
gre.clue: its fierce attack on the policy

ponderous.hook: PONDEROUS: as heavy as a POUND of lead.
ponderous.story: Ponderous. Slow and clumsy because of great weight; also, dull and laborious. At the river port, Rex watched an old cargo ship pull away, loaded to the edge with sand. It moved so slowly that a boy on the bank walked faster. That evening, his GRE reading passage felt the same: endless clauses, no life at all. Both were ponderous. Ponderous comes from the Latin pondus, weight, the same root as ponder, to weigh a thought in your mind. So, what word describes something slow and heavy, or dull and laborious?... Ponderous.
ponderous.example: Freight trains made a ponderous climb up the hill outside Srimangal, crawling past the tea gardens at walking speed.

gre.s: The biography's ____ prose, weighed down by endless digressions and dense footnotes, made it a chore to read despite the fascinating life it described.
gre.clue: weighed down by endless digressions and dense footnotes

relegate.hook: RELEGATE: sent back to the LEAGUE below.
relegate.story: Relegate. To push someone or something down to a lesser place. For thirty years, Grandfather's wooden radio stood proudly in the middle of the drawing room. The whole family gathered around it for news and cricket commentary. Then a big flat television arrived, and the radio was relegated to a dusty shelf in the storeroom. But every evening, Grandfather quietly carries it back to his room to listen to old songs. In football, a weak team is relegated, sent down to a lower league. So, what verb means to move something to a lower, less important position?... Relegate.
relegate.example: Once the new laptops arrived, the old desktop computers were relegated to a dusty storeroom behind the canteen.

gre.s: Although she was once celebrated as a pioneer, younger scholars now tend to ____ her work to footnotes, considering her methods hopelessly outdated.
gre.clue: considering her methods hopelessly outdated

repudiate.story: Repudiate. To refuse to accept or be associated with something; to reject it. One morning, Professor Hayes found a fake quote, printed beside his photo, spreading across social media. It praised a scheme he had never heard of. By noon he had posted a firm statement: he had never said those words, and he rejected everything they stood for. He had publicly repudiated the quote. In ancient Rome, to repudiate meant to divorce: to cast someone off and refuse all connection. So, what verb means to reject something and refuse any connection with it?... Repudiate.
repudiate.example: In later life, the philosopher repudiated many ideas from his first book, calling them the errors of youth.

gre.s: Hoping to save his career, the candidate was quick to ____ the extremist group that had endorsed him, insisting he shared none of its views.
gre.clue: insisting he shared none of its views

soliloquy.story: Soliloquy. A speech in a play where one character, alone on stage, thinks aloud. At a city drama festival, the lights dimmed until only one spotlight remained. Tim stood in it, alone, playing Hamlet. He spoke softly, as if to himself: "To be, or not to be." The hall was so quiet you could hear the fans. When the soliloquy ended, the audience burst into applause. Soli means alone, as in solo, and loquy means speaking, as in eloquent: a soliloquy is speaking alone. So, what do you call a speech a character makes alone, thinking aloud?... Soliloquy.
soliloquy.example: In Macbeth's dagger soliloquy, the audience watches a man wrestle aloud with his own conscience on the eve of murder.

gre.s: Unlike a dialogue, in which characters respond to one another, a ____ lets the audience overhear a character's private reflections while he stands alone on stage.
gre.clue: while he stands alone on stage

specious.hook: SPECIOUS: looks SPECIAL on the surface, but it's wrong underneath.
specious.story: Specious. Seeming true or reasonable on the surface, but actually false. Tanner told his mother he should skip his maths tuition. "Einstein failed maths at school, and look how he turned out." It sounded clever. His mother looked up from her sewing. "Einstein never failed maths. That story is a myth." Tanner had no answer. His argument was specious: attractive on the surface, hollow inside. Specious comes from the Latin species, meaning appearance; a specious claim only looks right. So, what word describes reasoning that looks sound but is actually false?... Specious.
specious.example: The salesman's specious claim that the filter removed every virus fell apart as soon as a chemist tested it.

gre.s: The argument appeared persuasive at first, but on closer inspection its reasoning proved ____, resting on a statistic that had been misread.
gre.clue: resting on a statistic that had been misread

tempestuous.story: Tempestuous. Full of strong, turbulent emotions; stormy. Every spring, the spring storm rolls over the villages of the delta: black clouds, sudden wind, mango branches cracking. Then, just as fast, the sky clears. Mona's friendship with her cousin Rita is just like that. They fight, cry, and refuse to speak for days, then share a plate of street snacks as if nothing happened. Their friendship is tempestuous. Tempestuous comes from tempest, a violent storm, and a tempestuous bond blows hot and cold just as suddenly. So, what word describes a relationship full of stormy emotions?... Tempestuous.
tempestuous.example: The tempestuous final session of parliament ended with members shouting and tearing up copies of the budget.

gre.s: The composer's ____ relationship with his patron, marked by violent quarrels and tearful reconciliations, inspired several of his most passionate works.
gre.clue: marked by violent quarrels and tearful reconciliations

urbane.story: Urbane. Polished, sophisticated and courteous. At a crowded wedding reception, Uncle Charles, a retired diplomat, moved through the hall greeting everyone by name. He chatted easily with the cooks, spoke smooth English with the foreign guests. When a nervous waiter spilled tea on his sleeve, he only smiled and put the boy at ease. Everyone agreed he was the most urbane man in the room. Urbane and urban come from the same Latin word for city: urbane manners are the polish of city life. So, what word describes someone smooth, polished and courteous?... Urbane.
urbane.example: The urbane museum director chatted in French with the visiting minister and then in Bangla with the guards.

gre.s: The ____ host, polished and witty, put even his most awkward guests at ease.
gre.clue: polished and witty

vestigial.story: Vestigial. Remaining as a small trace of something that was once larger or more important. In biology class, Ariel's teacher pointed to the base of a human skeleton. "This small bone is the tailbone, a vestigial tail left from our distant ancestors." The class stared in wonder. Walking home past the crumbling gate of an old landlord's palace, Ariel thought the gate was vestigial too, all that remained of a vanished estate. A vestige is a trace or remnant, so something vestigial is a leftover trace. So, what word describes a small leftover trace of something once larger?... Vestigial.
vestigial.example: The town's vestigial city wall, now a few crumbling stretches, still marks where the medieval market once stood.

gre.s: Although the office of governor-general still exists, its powers are now largely ____: the post survives as a ceremonial remnant of an era when it truly governed.
gre.clue: survives as a ceremonial remnant

abet.hook: ABET: placing A BET on the criminal and helping him win.
abet.story: Abet. To encourage or help someone in doing something wrong. When fourteen-year-old Riley wanted to skip school for a cricket match, his older cousin wrote a fake sick note and signed it in Riley's father's style. The trick worked for one day. Then the headmaster called home. Both boys stood before the family, and the cousin was scolded even more, because he had abetted the lie. Lawyers often say aided and abetted: aiding is helping, abetting is egging someone on. So, what verb means to help or encourage someone in wrongdoing?... Abet.
abet.example: The ship's captain was charged with abetting the smugglers by switching off the vessel's tracking signal at night.

gre.s: Although the guard never touched the jewels himself, prosecutors argued that he chose to ____ the theft by deliberately leaving the vault unlocked.
gre.clue: by deliberately leaving the vault unlocked

acolyte.hook: ACOLYTE: A COLLEAGUE who follows you everywhere like a shadow.
acolyte.story: Acolyte. A loyal follower or helper of an important person. Wherever the famous singer went at a city music festival, a small group of young musicians followed. They carried his harmonium, tuned his instruments, fetched his tea, and hung on every word he said about rhythm. Mike was one of them, proud just to be near the master. He was a devoted acolyte. The word began in the church, where an acolyte assists the priest, and it comes from a Greek word for follower. So, what word names a devoted follower of an important person?... Acolyte.
acolyte.example: The celebrity chef arrived at the food festival trailed by a dozen acolytes carrying his knives and notebooks.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the young scholar as little more than the famous theorist's ____, since she repeated his ideas without ever questioning them.
gre.clue: repeated his ideas without ever questioning them

berate.hook: BE-RATE: give someone a terrible RATING, loudly.
berate.story: Berate. To shout at or criticize someone angrily, and at length. After the school football team lost five nil, the coach marched into the dressing room. For fifteen minutes, he berated the players: lazy passing, no running, no heart. The boys stared at their muddy boots. Then the captain, Finn, quietly promised they would train twice a day, and the coach stopped mid-sentence. The trick: berate sounds like be-rate, as if someone rates your mistakes, loudly, one by one. So, what verb means to scold someone angrily and at length?... Berate.
berate.example: The passenger berated the airline clerk for twenty minutes, as if she personally had caused the fog at Shahjalal Airport.

gre.s: The coach was known to ____ his players loudly in front of the crowd, so the team was astonished when he met their worst defeat with quiet encouragement.
gre.clue: astonished when he met their worst defeat with quiet encouragement

bucolic.hook: BUCOLIC: 'boo-cow-lic', cows mooing in green fields.
bucolic.story: Bucolic. Charming in a simple, peaceful, countryside way. After years of city traffic, Sam took his children to his grandmother's village. They woke to roosters, washed in the pond, and watched cows grazing beside fields of yellow mustard. In the evening, smoke rose from clay stoves and someone played a flute far away. Sam felt his shoulders finally relax. It was a bucolic life, slow and green. Bucolic comes from the Greek for cowherd, so picture a boy leading cows across green fields. So, what word describes the simple, peaceful charm of the countryside?... Bucolic.
bucolic.example: The bucolic photographs of rice fields and grazing goats on the tourism website hid the region's serious flood problems.

gre.s: The painter's early landscapes are ____ idylls of shepherds and grazing cattle, a sharp contrast to her later images of crowded industrial cities.
gre.clue: shepherds and grazing cattle

calamitous.story: Calamitous. Causing great disaster or misfortune. In November two thousand seven, a great cyclone struck the southern coast of the delta. Winds tore roofs from homes, the sea rushed over the fields, and thousands of lives were lost. Rhea's grandmother still remembers the morning after, when the whole village stood silent among the fallen trees. It was a calamitous night. Since then, cyclone shelters and early warnings have saved countless lives. Calamitous is simply the adjective of calamity, a great disaster. So, what word describes an event that brings terrible disaster?... Calamitous.
calamitous.example: The decision to sell the team's best bowler just before the tournament proved calamitous for the club.

gre.s: What began as a minor accounting error proved ____ for the firm: within a year it had lost its largest clients, its reputation, and finally its license to operate.
gre.clue: within a year it had lost its largest clients, its reputation, and finally its license to operate

convivial.hook: CON-VIVIAL: 'vivi' means life. Full of lively company.
convivial.story: Convivial. Friendly, lively and enjoyable; fond of good company. Every Friday evening, Adam's old university friends meet at a small tea stall near the city lake. They order milk tea and samosas, argue about cricket, and tease each other until even the stall owner joins in. Strangers on the next bench often end up chatting with them. It is the most convivial hour of Adam's week. Convivial comes from the Latin for a feast, literally living together: con means with, and vivere means to live. So, what word describes a gathering that is warm, lively and friendly?... Convivial.
convivial.example: The convivial atmosphere at the tea stall near the campus gate made it everyone's favourite place to argue about politics.

gre.s: Although the conference sessions were tense, the evening banquets were ____ affairs, full of laughter and lively conversation.
gre.clue: full of laughter and lively conversation

deride.hook: DE-RIDE: laughing (ride, from Latin 'ridere') DOWN at someone.
deride.story: Deride. To mock someone or something with contempt. When Shane arrived at his city college from a village on the coast, some classmates derided his accent, copying the way he spoke and laughing behind his back. Shane's ears burned, but he kept practising with the debate team. In the final, he won the gold medal, and the same boys stood and clapped. De means down, and ride comes from the Latin for laugh, as in ridiculous: to deride is to laugh down at someone. So, what verb means to mock someone with contempt?... Deride.
deride.example: Early investors derided the idea of a motorbike ride-sharing app, but it now carries thousands of Dhaka commuters every day.

gre.s: Many critics who used to ____ the painter's style as childish now praise it as revolutionary.
gre.clue: now praise it as revolutionary

dowdy.story: Dowdy. Dull and unfashionable in appearance. Every winter, Lily wears the same faded brown cardigan, with stretched sleeves and two mismatched buttons. Her university friends tease her that it looks dowdy, like something from a grandmother's cupboard. Lily only smiles. It was her mother's, and it is the warmest thing she owns. Dowdy rhymes with cloudy: a dowdy outfit has no colour and no sparkle, just a dull grey sky. So, what word describes clothes that look dull and unfashionable?... Dowdy.
dowdy.example: Over the summer, the dowdy staff canteen with its peeling green paint was turned into a bright, modern café.

gre.s: Once dismissed as ____, with its faded wallpaper and outdated furniture, the old hotel was transformed by its new owners into the most stylish address in the city.
gre.clue: with its faded wallpaper and outdated furniture

duplicitous.story: Duplicitous. Deliberately deceptive; two-faced. In her first job, Isabel trusted a friendly colleague who praised her ideas over lunch every day. Then she learned the truth: in meetings with the boss, the same colleague called those ideas weak and quietly presented them as her own. Isabel felt sick. Her friend had been duplicitous from the start. Duplicitous shares its root with duplicate and double: a duplicitous person shows you one face and the world another. So, what word describes someone who is deliberately two-faced?... Duplicitous.
duplicitous.example: The duplicitous agent sold the same flat in Banani to three different buyers before disappearing with the money.

gre.s: The spy was so ____ that for years he convinced both governments of his loyalty while secretly betraying each to the other.
gre.clue: while secretly betraying each to the other

endow.hook: ENDOW: give a DOWRY of talent or money.
endow.story: Endow. To give someone a quality or ability; also, to provide a lasting fund of money. Lauren grew up in a small village, endowed with a sharp mind and a stubborn heart. After building a successful company, she returned to her old school and endowed a fund that will pay the fees of ten girls every year. The trick: endow sounds like dowry, the gift given at a marriage, and both words come from an old Latin root for giving. So, what verb means to give a gift, a talent, or a lasting fund?... Endow.
endow.example: Years of hiking in the hills endowed my grandmother with a stamina that still astonishes her doctors.

gre.s: Critics complained that the novelist tended to ____ his villains with such charm and wit that readers found them far more appealing than his heroes.
gre.clue: readers found them far more appealing than his heroes

ennui.hook: ENNUI (on-WEE): French for boredom. 'Oh, wee, another day.'
ennui.story: Ennui. A dull, restless boredom, when nothing holds your interest. On the fifth day of a long holiday in her quiet hometown, Sadie lay on her bed staring at the ceiling fan. She had scrolled through every app, eaten every cookie, and walked the same lane twice. She picked up a book, read one page, and put it down again. It was pure ennui. Ennui is a French word that English borrowed whole, and it shares an old root with annoy. So, what word names a restless boredom when nothing holds your interest?... Ennui.
ennui.example: By the third week of lockdown, a deep ennui had settled over the hostel, and even card games felt like chores.

gre.s: Wealthy beyond need and freed from any obligation to work, the aristocrats of the novel suffer from a pervasive ____, drifting from party to party without interest or purpose.
gre.clue: drifting from party to party without interest or purpose

equanimity.story: Equanimity. Mental calmness and composure, especially in difficulty. At the big bus terminal, Tyler's family missed the last bus home. Children were crying, bags were heavy, and ticket sellers were shouting all around. Tyler's grandfather simply sat down on a bench, opened his flask of tea, and said, "There is always a morning bus." His equanimity calmed everyone. Equa means equal, and animus means mind: equanimity is an evenly balanced mind, even in a storm. So, what word names calm composure in a difficult moment?... Equanimity.
equanimity.example: The chess player met her opponent's stunning sacrifice with equanimity, calmly sipping water before making her reply.

gre.s: Though her colleagues panicked when the funding was suddenly withdrawn, the director responded with remarkable ____, calmly drafting a new budget that same afternoon.
gre.clue: calmly drafting a new budget that same afternoon

exorcise.story: Exorcise. To drive out an evil spirit; also, to get rid of a troubling memory or feeling. For years, Max froze whenever he had to speak in public. A school play in class five had gone badly, and the memory of the laughter never left him. In university, he joined the debate club and spoke every single week. By his final year, he had exorcised that old fear completely. Exorcise begins with ex, meaning out: to exorcise is to drive something out. So, what verb means to drive out a spirit, or a troubling memory?... Exorcise.
exorcise.example: Writing a novel about the war helped the veteran exorcise the nightmares that had haunted him for decades.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the memory of her humiliating defeat, the champion trained harder than ever and returned to win the title the following year.
gre.clue: humiliating defeat

florid.hook: FLORID: covered in FLOWERS, too decorated.
florid.story: Florid. Excessively elaborate or ornate; also, red-faced. Jason's uncle insisted on writing the wedding invitation himself. It began: "With hearts overflowing like the mighty river in the golden season of love, we humbly beseech your most esteemed presence." Jason read it aloud, and his sister nearly fell off her chair. The language was hopelessly florid. Florid comes from the Latin for flowery: florid writing is so covered in flowers that you cannot see the meaning. So, what word describes writing that is far too ornate?... Florid.
florid.example: The headmaster's florid speech at prize day, packed with Latin quotations and endless metaphors, lasted almost an hour.

gre.s: Readers accustomed to the novelist's spare, unadorned prose were startled by the ____ style of her latest book, crowded with elaborate metaphors and lush adjectives.
gre.clue: crowded with elaborate metaphors and lush adjectives

foment.hook: FOMENT: FERMENT trouble, let it bubble.
foment.story: Foment. To deliberately stir up trouble, anger or revolt. Before a football final between two neighbouring villages, someone began posting false stories online: that one team had bribed the referee, that the other planned to attack fans. Tempers rose by the hour, until the elders sat both captains down together. Later they learned that one bitter man had fomented the whole quarrel. Foment comes from a Latin word for a warm compress: to foment trouble is to keep heating it until it boils. So, what verb means to stir up trouble on purpose?... Foment.
foment.example: Fake videos shared on social media were used to foment violence between rival supporters before the match.

gre.s: Officials accused the pamphleteers of trying to ____ unrest among the factory workers, though the workers insisted their anger needed no outside encouragement.
gre.clue: their anger needed no outside encouragement

hackneyed.hook: HACKNEYED: like an old HACK horse, used until worn out.
hackneyed.story: Hackneyed. Overused, and therefore unoriginal and lacking force. Rose began her GRE essay with "Since the dawn of civilization, mankind has always." Her tutor drew a red line through it. "Every third essay starts like that. It is hackneyed." He told her to begin with a real story instead. In old England, a hackney was a horse for hire, ridden by everyone until it was worn out, and a hackneyed phrase is just as tired. So, what word describes a phrase used so often that it has lost its force?... Hackneyed.
hackneyed.example: The speechwriter struck out every hackneyed phrase, from thinking outside the box to giving one hundred and ten percent.

gre.s: Students were warned that the examiners would penalize ____ openings such as "since the dawn of time," which appear in thousands of essays every year.
gre.clue: which appear in thousands of essays every year

humdrum.hook: HUM-DRUM: the same humming drumbeat, over and over.
humdrum.story: Humdrum. Dull and boring because of being routine. Every weekday, Kenny wakes at seven, takes the same bus to the same office downtown, fills in the same forms, eats the same rice and dal, and takes the same bus home. His life had become humdrum. Then one Friday, he dusted off his old guitar and began teaching the neighbourhood children. Suddenly, his humdrum week had something to look forward to. Humdrum sounds like a dull hum and a steady drum, the same flat beat repeating. So, what word describes a life of dull routine?... Humdrum.
humdrum.example: After the excitement of the wedding, the couple happily settled into a humdrum life of work, groceries and evening tea.

gre.s: Although the novelist's plots involve ordinary people with ____ jobs, her vivid prose makes even their daily routines seem thrilling.
gre.clue: even their daily routines

ideologue.story: Ideologue. A rigid, uncompromising supporter of a set of ideas. In Tanya's economics seminar, one student had a single answer for everything: the free market. Rising prices? The free market. Floods? The free market. When the teacher showed him data that did not fit, he ignored it and repeated his theory louder. Tanya realised that arguing was pointless. He was an ideologue. An ideology is a fixed system of ideas, and an ideologue is wedded to one, unable to see past it. So, what word names someone rigidly devoted to a set of ideas?... Ideologue.
ideologue.example: The think tank hired economists rather than ideologues, hoping its reports would persuade voters from every party.

gre.s: Unlike her predecessor, a pragmatist willing to bargain with any faction, the new minister was a doctrinaire ____ who regarded every compromise as a betrayal of principle.
gre.clue: who regarded every compromise as a betrayal of principle

inborn.story: Inborn. Existing from birth; natural. At just two years old, Toby could not yet speak in full sentences, but whenever he heard a drum at a wedding, he clapped exactly on the beat. Nobody had taught him. Years later, he became a celebrated drummer, and his teacher said, "His sense of rhythm is inborn. I only polished it." The word explains itself: inborn means born in you, there from the very start. A close synonym is innate. So, what word describes a talent you are born with?... Inborn.
inborn.example: Some researchers think a fear of snakes is inborn in primates, since even monkeys raised in laboratories flinch at them.

gre.s: Linguists debate whether the capacity for grammar is ____ or acquired entirely through exposure to language in early childhood.
gre.clue: or acquired entirely through exposure

morose.hook: MOROSE: MORE OF A ROSE losing its petals, wilting sadly.
morose.story: Morose. Sullen and gloomy. After Reggie's grandfather retired from the railway, he became morose. He sat on the veranda all day, said little at meals, and answered every question with a grunt. Then Reggie brought home a few rose saplings and asked for his help planting them. Within a month, the old man was up at dawn, watering and proudly showing every new bud to the neighbours. Here is a picture to remember: a morose face is like a rose that has lost its petals, drooping and gloomy. So, what word describes someone sullen and gloomy?... Morose.
morose.example: The morose shopkeeper barely looked up from his newspaper whenever a customer walked in.

gre.s: Although he had once been the life of every party, years of illness left him ____ and withdrawn, rarely speaking even to his oldest friends.
gre.clue: rarely speaking even to his oldest friends

recant.story: Recant. To publicly take back a statement or belief. In sixteen thirty-three, Galileo was forced by church authorities to recant his claim that the Earth moves around the Sun. Legend says he whispered afterwards, "And yet it moves." Centuries later, in a city classroom, Sophia's science teacher told the story, and the whole class fell silent. To recant is to sing your words backwards: re means back, and cant comes from the Latin for sing, as in chant. So, what verb means to publicly withdraw something you once declared?... Recant.
recant.example: Under pressure from the publisher, the witness recanted her claim that the novelist had copied her manuscript.

gre.s: Despite intense pressure from church authorities, the scientist refused to ____ his theory, insisting that the evidence for it was overwhelming.
gre.clue: insisting that the evidence for it was overwhelming

sacrosanct.story: Sacrosanct. So respected that no one may change or question it. In Anne's family, Friday lunch is sacrosanct. However busy everyone is, the whole family sits together at one o'clock for rice, dal and her mother's beef curry. Once, her brother tried to skip it for a friend's party, and the look on their father's face made him cancel on the spot. Sacrosanct joins two Latin words for sacred and holy: something doubly sacred that no one may touch. So, what word describes a tradition too respected to be broken?... Sacrosanct.
sacrosanct.example: In our newsroom, the rule that every quotation must be checked with its source is sacrosanct.

gre.s: For decades the rule was considered ____, but the new director treated it as merely one tradition among many, open to revision like any other.
gre.clue: open to revision like any other

salutary.hook: SALUTARY: SALUTE to something good for you.
salutary.story: Salutary. Producing good effects; beneficial, even if unpleasant. Three weeks before her GRE, Nadine felt confident, until a full mock test came back with a terrible score. She cried that evening. But the shock was salutary. It showed her exactly where she was weak, and she spent the next weeks fixing it. On test day, she scored her best ever. Salutary comes from the Latin salus, meaning health, the same root as salute: a salutary lesson is good for you, like bitter medicine. So, what word describes an unpleasant experience that does you good?... Salutary.
salutary.example: Losing a whole day's work to a crashed laptop was a salutary lesson for Nabila about saving backups.

gre.s: Though painful at the time, the defeat proved ____ for the team, forcing the players to confront weaknesses they had long ignored.
gre.clue: forcing the players to confront weaknesses they had long ignored

synoptic.hook: SYN-OPTIC: seeing (optic) everything together (syn). A SYNOPSIS.
synoptic.story: Synoptic. Giving a brief general summary or overview. The night before his history final, Ralph was buried under five thick textbooks. Then his senior handed him one sheet of paper: a synoptic chart of the whole syllabus, every ruler and treaty on a single page, joined by arrows. Ralph felt the panic leave his chest. For the first time, he could see the whole picture at a glance. Syn means together and optic means seeing: a synoptic view lets you see everything together, like a synopsis. So, what word describes a brief overview of a whole subject?... Synoptic.
synoptic.example: The museum's first gallery gives a synoptic account of Bengal's history, from ancient Pundranagar to independence.

gre.s: The chapter offers a ____ view of the war, condensing four years of campaigns into a few concise pages.
gre.clue: condensing four years of campaigns into a few concise pages

temerity.story: Temerity. Excessive boldness; audacity. On his very first day as an intern at a city bank, Reid walked into the board meeting uninvited, sat down in the chairman's empty chair, and began explaining how the bank should be run. Twelve senior officers stared at him in silence. Nobody could believe his temerity. Temerity comes from the Latin temere, meaning rashly or blindly. Do not mix it up with timidity, which sounds similar but means the very opposite. So, what word means reckless boldness, like taking the chairman's chair on your first day?... Temerity.
temerity.example: The rookie had the temerity to ask the club's legendary captain to move so that he could sit by the window.

gre.s: Few were surprised when the new intern was dismissed; he had shown the ____ to correct the chairman's grammar in front of the entire board.
gre.clue: correct the chairman's grammar in front of the entire board

tenable.hook: TENABLE: can be held (tenere, to hold). An argument that holds up.
tenable.story: Tenable. Able to be defended or maintained against criticism. In a debate competition, Mark argued that the city's traffic was caused entirely by rickshaws. His opponent, Lisa, calmly showed figures on private cars, broken signals and missing footpaths. By the end, Mark's position was no longer tenable, and he admitted it with a good-natured smile. Tenable comes from the Latin tenere, to hold, as in tenant: a tenable argument is one that can hold its ground. So, what word describes a position that can be defended?... Tenable.
tenable.example: Few archaeologists find it tenable that slaves built the pyramids, since excavations have uncovered villages where paid workers lived.

gre.s: Once the new fossil evidence emerged, the theory that birds evolved separately from dinosaurs was no longer ____.
gre.clue: Once the new fossil evidence emerged

unadorned.story: Unadorned. Plain; without decoration. Rachel's grandmother's room in their old house has white walls, a wooden bed, one shelf of books and a clay water pot. No paintings, no curtains, no clutter. Visitors from the city first find it bare. Then they sit for a while in the cool, quiet light, and somehow they do not want to leave. Its unadorned beauty stays with them. Break it apart: un means not, and adorn means decorate, so unadorned means not decorated at all. So, what word describes something plain, with no decoration?... Unadorned.
unadorned.example: The memorial is an unadorned granite block whose only feature is the list of fishermen lost in the storm.

gre.s: In contrast to the ornate, metaphor-laden style of his contemporaries, Hemingway wrote ____ prose, relying on short declarative sentences and everyday words.
gre.clue: In contrast to the ornate, metaphor-laden style of his contemporaries

verbose.hook: VERBOSE: too many VERBS, too many words.
verbose.story: Verbose. Using more words than needed; wordy. Fiona asked her classmate Tim for a short update on their group project. His reply was eight paragraphs long. It began with the weather, wandered through his cousin's wedding, and only in the last line said, "The slides are done." Fiona had to cover her mouth in the library. Tim was hopelessly verbose. Verbose shares its root with verb and verbal, from the Latin verbum, meaning word: a verbose person spills too many words. So, what word describes speech or writing that is far too wordy?... Verbose.
verbose.example: The judge's verbose ruling ran to four hundred pages, though its key finding could have fit on one.

gre.s: The editor trimmed the manuscript by half, arguing that the author's ____ style buried his best insights under paragraphs of needless elaboration.
gre.clue: paragraphs of needless elaboration

vilify.story: Vilify. To attack someone's character harshly in speech or writing. After a close call in a city league cricket match, angry fans turned on the umpire. Within hours, posts across social media called him corrupt, blind and worse, and his family was afraid to go outside. Two days later, replays showed his decision had been exactly right. But by then he had been vilified by thousands of strangers. Vilify shares its root with vile: to vilify someone is to paint them as vile and worthless. So, what verb means to harshly attack someone's character?... Vilify.
vilify.example: During the war, enemy propaganda vilified the resistance fighters as bandits and common criminals.

gre.s: Rival newspapers chose to ____ the reformer, branding her a traitor and inventing scandals, even though her proposals were modest and widely popular.
gre.clue: branding her a traitor and inventing scandals

vociferous.story: Vociferous. Expressing opinions loudly and forcefully. At a parents' meeting about a sudden rise in school fees, Shelby's mother stood up first. She spoke loudly, raised her hand high, and demanded answers. Soon dozens of parents joined in, clapping and calling out. Their vociferous protest went on until the principal agreed to review the fees. Vociferous comes from the Latin vox, meaning voice, as in vocal, plus a root meaning to carry: a vociferous person carries their voice to every corner. So, what word describes someone who voices opinions loudly and forcefully?... Vociferous.
vociferous.example: Parents were vociferous in their complaints about the new school timetable, flooding the principal's office with letters.

gre.s: The proposal met with ____ opposition from residents, who packed the town hall and shouted down every speaker in favor.
gre.clue: shouted down every speaker in favor

abeyance.hook: ABEYANCE: 'A BAY' where ships wait, temporarily paused.
abeyance.story: Abeyance. A state of temporary suspension or inactivity. For two years, the people of a remote river island watched half-built pillars standing in the water. Work on their new bridge had been held in abeyance while officials argued over funds, and children still crossed by wooden boat. Then one winter morning the cranes returned, and the whole village ran to the bank to watch. The bridge was out of abeyance at last. Abeyance sounds like a bay, where ships wait at anchor, not gone, only paused. So, what word means a state of temporary suspension?... Abeyance.
abeyance.example: The tennis federation held the player's ban in abeyance until an appeals panel had reviewed the doping test.

gre.s: Plans for the new stadium were held in ____ while the city awaited the outcome of the environmental review, though officials insisted the project had not been abandoned.
gre.clue: while the city awaited the outcome of the environmental review

alacrity.hook: ALACRITY: 'ALL A CRITTER' jumps up at once when food appears.
alacrity.story: Alacrity. Eager, happy readiness to act straight away. When the teacher asked who would help decorate the school for Victory Day, a dozen hands shot up before she finished her sentence. Simon was already at the door, holding a roll of red and green paper. The children worked with such alacrity that the hall was ready in an hour. The teacher said she had never seen them move so fast for homework. Alacrity comes from the Latin alacer, meaning lively and brisk. So, what word means cheerful eagerness to act at once?... Alacrity.
alacrity.example: When the cook offered free biryani to anyone who helped clear the tables, the boys moved with remarkable alacrity.

gre.s: Expecting resistance, the manager was startled by the ____ with which the team accepted the extra assignment, volunteering before she had finished explaining it.
gre.clue: volunteering before she had finished explaining it

aplomb.hook: APLOMB: straight as a PLUMB line, perfectly steady.
aplomb.story: Aplomb. Self-confidence and calm, especially in a difficult situation. Halfway through Tamara's convocation speech, the power failed across the hall. The microphone died, and two thousand people sat in the dark. Tamara simply raised her voice, kept speaking steadily, and finished by the light of phones held up in the crowd. Everyone praised the aplomb with which she handled it. Aplomb comes from the French for upright, like a plumb line, a weight on a string that always hangs straight. A person with aplomb stays upright in a storm. So, what word means calm self-assurance under pressure?... Aplomb.
aplomb.example: When a stray goat wandered onto the pitch, the umpire handled the interruption with aplomb, leading it gently to the boundary.

gre.s: Although she had never addressed so large an audience, the young diplomat delivered her remarks with remarkable ____, never once betraying the nervousness she later admitted to feeling.
gre.clue: never once betraying the nervousness

attenuate.story: Attenuate. To reduce the force, effect or value of something; to make thin. The great mangrove forest stands between the Bay of Bengal and the villages behind it. When a cyclone roars in, the dense mangrove forest attenuates its winds and its storm surge, so the water reaches the villages weaker than it began. Zoe learned this in geography class and felt a new love for the forest. Attenuate comes from the Latin tenuis, meaning thin, as in tenuous: to attenuate is to thin something out. So, what verb means to weaken or reduce the force of something?... Attenuate.
