One is calm and tractable: it stops at a word and turns at a gentle tug of the rein. The other kicks, bolts and refuses to cross water. Mack jokes that the second horse is his real teacher of patience. Tractable shares its Latin root with tractor, from a word meaning to pull or handle: a tractable animal, or person, is easy to handle. So, what word describes someone or something easy to manage?... Tractable.
tractable.example: Breaking the huge coding project into small tasks made it far more tractable for the new team of interns.

gre.s: Once considered ____, the problem has resisted every attempt at a solution for over forty years, baffling the best mathematicians.
gre.clue: has resisted every attempt at a solution for over forty years

venerate.hook: VENERATE: like VENUS, treated as a goddess.
venerate.story: Venerate. To honour someone or something with great respect. On the great poet Tagore's birthday, Nina's music school gathers in a hall decorated with marigolds. Students sing his songs, teachers read his poems, and a garland is placed gently before his portrait. Even the youngest children fall silent. The poet is venerated by millions, more than a century after he won the Nobel Prize. Venerate shares a root with venerable, a title for the old and wise: we venerate those we deeply honour. So, what verb means to honour with deep respect?... Venerate.
venerate.example: Musicians across Bengal still venerate Lalon Shah, singing his songs at the yearly gathering in Kushtia.

gre.s: Many cultures ____ their elders, consulting them on important decisions and honoring them in elaborate ceremonies.
gre.clue: honoring them in elaborate ceremonies

abstruse.story: Abstruse. So complex or deep that few people can grasp it. In her first week at a philosophy reading circle, Leah opened a translated page of Kant. She read one sentence five times and still could not say what it meant. The room was silent except for the ceiling fan. Even the circle's leader admitted the text was abstruse. Abstruse comes from a Latin word meaning thrust away and hidden, as if the meaning had been pushed out of reach. So, what word describes writing so deep that few people can follow it?... Abstruse.
abstruse.example: Rahim gave up on the abstruse tax manual and simply asked an accountant in Motijheel to fill in his return.

gre.s: Although the philosopher's early essays were lucid and accessible, his later work grew so ____ that even specialists confessed they could not follow its arguments.
gre.clue: even specialists confessed they could not follow its arguments

acquisitive.story: Acquisitive. Too eager to gain money or possessions. Every Friday, Neil's uncle drives out to a new housing project on the edge of the city. He already owns three flats and a shop, yet he keeps a folder of land deals beside his bed and talks about plots at every family dinner. When Neil asked what he would do with one more flat, his uncle had no answer. Acquisitive shares its root with acquire: an acquisitive person can never stop acquiring. So, what word describes someone hungry to keep gaining more and more possessions?... Acquisitive.
acquisitive.example: In an acquisitive age, the monk's tiny room with one blanket and a few books struck visitors as a quiet rebuke.

gre.s: Far from being content with his considerable wealth, the tycoon remained relentlessly ____, buying up rival companies merely to add them to his holdings.
gre.clue: buying up rival companies merely to add them to his holdings

cajole.hook: CAJOLE: CAGE them with sweet words, JOLLY them along.
cajole.story: Cajole. To persuade someone with flattery or gentle, patient coaxing. Molly wanted to join her class trip to the beach, but her father said no. So every evening she made his favourite ginger tea, praised his old cricket stories, and asked again, softly. On the fifth night he put down his cup, and said, "All right, go." Molly threw her arms around him. She had cajoled him into it. Hear the word jolly hiding inside cajole: you jolly someone along until they give in. So, what verb means to coax someone with sweet words until they agree?... Cajole.
cajole.example: Sadia cajoled her little brother into finishing his homework by promising him an extra hour of football.

gre.s: Unable to force the stubborn witness to testify, the detective tried instead to ____ him, offering compliments and small favors until he agreed to talk.
gre.clue: offering compliments and small favors

churlish.hook: CHURLISH: a grumpy CHURL who growls at everyone.
churlish.story: Churlish. Rude and bad-tempered in a mean-spirited way. On a cold January morning, Jody carried a plate of warm steamed rice cakes up to the new neighbour. He opened the door, frowned at the plate, and said, "I did not ask for this." Then he shut the door. Jody stood on the stairs, her cheeks burning. It was a churlish answer to a kind gift. A churl was a rough peasant in old English, and churlish first meant behaving like one, without any courtesy. So, what word describes a rude, ungracious response to kindness?... Churlish.
churlish.example: The guest's churlish refusal to thank his hosts for the elaborate wedding feast embarrassed his entire family.

gre.s: It would be ____ to criticize the volunteers' modest fundraiser, given how generously they had donated their own time.
gre.clue: given how generously they had donated their own time

crestfallen.hook: CREST-FALLEN: a rooster whose proud crest has drooped.
crestfallen.story: Crestfallen. Sad and disappointed after a hope collapses. Shane's school team needed one run off the last ball of the district final. He swung hard, missed, and heard the stumps rattle behind him. He walked off with his head down and his bat dragging in the dust, too crestfallen to look at his friends. His coach walked over and put an arm around the crestfallen boy. Picture a proud rooster whose red crest has drooped and fallen: that is what crestfallen looks like. So, what word describes someone deflated by a sudden disappointment?... Crestfallen.
crestfallen.example: Imran looked crestfallen when the publisher returned his first manuscript with a polite but firm rejection letter.

gre.s: The usually confident candidate looked ____ as the results came in, his campaign having fallen far short of expectations.
gre.clue: having fallen far short of expectations

ebullient.hook: EBULLIENT: BUBBLING over like boiling water.
ebullient.story: Ebullient. Cheerful and bubbling with energy. When Ivy's younger brother got into the engineering university, he burst through the front door shouting the news. He hugged their mother, danced with their grandmother, called every cousin, and ran down to the corner shop to buy sweets for the whole lane. Even at midnight he was still ebullient, talking too fast to finish a sentence. Ebullient comes from the Latin for boiling over, and an ebullient person bubbles over with joy, like milk rising in a pot. So, what word describes someone overflowing with cheerful energy?... Ebullient.
ebullient.example: The ebullient fans poured into the streets of Chattogram, dancing and waving flags after the late winning goal.

gre.s: Normally reserved and soft-spoken, the professor was uncharacteristically ____ at the reception, laughing loudly and greeting every guest with a warm embrace.
gre.clue: laughing loudly and greeting every guest with a warm embrace

estimable.story: Estimable. Worthy of great respect. For thirty-five years, Headmaster Albert Kerr cycled to a village school, through mud in the monsoon and fog in winter. He taught poor students for free in the evenings and never missed a day. When he retired, former students came from the city and even from abroad to touch his feet. He was an estimable man, and his estimable life filled the school field with gratitude. Estimable comes from the same root as esteem: an estimable person is held in high esteem. So, what word describes someone deeply worthy of respect?... Estimable.
estimable.example: The retiring headmistress was an estimable woman who had taught three generations of the same village families.

gre.s: Despite their political differences, even the senator's rivals regarded him as thoroughly ____, a public servant whose integrity had never once been questioned.
gre.clue: whose integrity had never once been questioned

evanescent.story: Evanescent. Quickly fading or disappearing. Every autumn morning, Amber's grandmother gathered night jasmine flowers from the wet grass under the tree, white petals with bright orange stems, fallen in the night. By the time the sun was high, they had wilted, and their sweet smell was gone. "Pick them early," she would say. "Their beauty is evanescent." Evanescent shares its root with vanish: something evanescent vanishes almost as soon as it appears. So, what word describes beauty that fades away almost at once?... Evanescent.
evanescent.example: Social media fame is often evanescent, and last month's viral singer may already be forgotten by her followers.

gre.s: The perfume's scent proved ____, fading within minutes of being applied despite the manufacturer's promise that it would last all day.
gre.clue: fading within minutes

exigent.story: Exigent. Pressing; needing attention right away. The night before the board exams, the river swept away the road from Kyle's river island village. Three hundred students had to reach the exam centre by nine in the morning. The headmaster rang the boat owners one by one, and by dawn a line of engine boats waited at the bank. It was an exigent situation, and exigent needs leave no room for delay. Exigent shares its root with exact, from a Latin verb meaning to demand. So, what word describes a situation that demands action right now?... Exigent.
exigent.example: Facing exigent demands from creditors, the small garment factory sold two of its machines to cover the wages.

gre.s: Because the circumstances were so ____, with the floodwaters rising by the hour, officials bypassed the usual approval process and evacuated the town at once.
gre.clue: with the floodwaters rising by the hour

fungible.hook: FUNGIBLE: FUN to swap, since one is as good as another.
fungible.story: Fungible. Interchangeable; one unit can be replaced by another identical one. When Ron borrowed a kilo of sugar from his neighbour, he returned a different kilo the next day, and nobody minded. Sugar is fungible. But when he borrowed her fountain pen, a gift from her grandfather, and lost it, no new pen could take its place. Ron felt sick with shame. Fungible comes from a Latin verb meaning to perform: one fungible item can perform the job of another. So, what word describes things that can be swapped one for another, like dollar bills?... Fungible.
fungible.example: Banknotes are fungible, so it makes no difference which particular thousand-taka note the cashier hands you.

gre.s: Unlike works of art, which are unique, commodities such as wheat are ____: one bushel can be substituted for another without any loss of value.
gre.clue: one bushel can be substituted for another without any loss of value

inimical.story: Inimical. Harmful or hostile; working against something. On the low southern coast, farmers like Roy's father once grew rice on every field. Then salt water from the sea crept further inland each year, and the soil turned white and crusty at the edges. Salt is inimical to rice; the young plants turn yellow and die. Now many families farm shrimp instead. Inimical comes from the Latin inimicus, an enemy, the opposite of amicus, a friend: an inimical force acts like an enemy. So, what word describes conditions that are harmful or hostile to something?... Inimical.
inimical.example: Soaring rents in the city center have proved inimical to the small bookshops that once lined the old streets.

gre.s: Constant noise and interruptions are ____ to the deep concentration that serious writing demands.
gre.clue: the deep concentration that serious writing demands

mendacity.story: Mendacity. Untruthfulness; the habit of lying. A land broker sold Tyler's father a plot he swore was free of any dispute. Later they learned that three other families had bought the very same plot. When Tyler confronted him, the broker invented a new story every week: a lost file, a sick clerk, a mistake at the land office. His mendacity seemed to have no end. Mendacity comes from the Latin mendax, meaning lying; do not confuse it with mendicant, which means a beggar. So, what noun means a habit of telling lies?... Mendacity.
mendacity.example: Once the auditors revealed the chairman's mendacity, shareholders demanded to know how many earlier reports had been invented.

gre.s: The memoir was celebrated as a model of candor until journalists exposed its author's ____: many of its most moving episodes had simply been invented.
gre.clue: many of its most moving episodes had simply been invented

miscreant.hook: MIS-CREANT: a MIS-CREATED person who does wrong.
miscreant.story: Miscreant. Someone who behaves badly or breaks the law. Every Friday, worshippers at a city mosque came out after prayers to find that someone had stolen their best sandals. One week, a young volunteer named Zack watched the shoe racks. He caught the miscreant, a grown man with a plastic bag full of sandals. The imam shook his head as the police led the miscreant away. The old French word meant unbelieving, so a miscreant was first a heretic, then any wrongdoer. So, what noun means a person who does wrong or breaks the law?... Miscreant.
miscreant.example: Security cameras finally caught the miscreants who had been slashing bicycle tires outside the university hostel.

gre.s: The townspeople regarded the young man as a hopeless ____ until he returned the stolen money and spent years volunteering to repay his debt to the community.
gre.clue: returned the stolen money

modish.story: Modish. Fashionable and stylish, in tune with the latest trend. Natalie walked into the holiday gathering in a handwoven sari with silver sneakers, a look she had first seen online only a week before. Her cousins crowded around to take pictures. Everyone agreed it was the most modish outfit in the room. By next year, of course, the same look would feel old. Think of the word mode, which in French means fashion: whatever is modish is in the current mode. So, what word describes something fashionable right now?... Modish.
modish.example: In the 1960s, modish young women in Dhaka wore bouffant hairstyles copied from the posters of popular film stars.

gre.s: The restaurant's décor, so ____ when it opened a decade ago, now looks hopelessly dated, a relic of a style no one wants anymore.
gre.clue: now looks hopelessly dated

obsequious.story: Obsequious. Too eager to please or obey; flattering in an embarrassing way. At Mitch's office downtown, one clerk jumped up every time the director walked in. He praised the director's ties, laughed loudest at his jokes, and once ran down three floors to fetch an umbrella nobody had asked for. His coworkers traded tired looks at each obsequious display. Obsequious holds the Latin root sequi, to follow, as in sequence: an obsequious person follows the boss everywhere, bowing. So, what word describes someone who flatters and obeys far too eagerly?... Obsequious.
obsequious.example: The new manager grew tired of the obsequious clerk who agreed with every remark and laughed at every joke.

gre.s: The courtiers' ____ praise of the king, which never wavered even when his decrees were absurd, revealed more fear than admiration.
gre.clue: never wavered even when his decrees were absurd

paradigmatic.hook: PARADIGM = a model. PARADIGMATIC = the model example.
paradigmatic.story: Paradigmatic. Serving as a typical or perfect example of something. When Professor Nash teaches essay writing, she always hands out one old answer by a former student named Rosa. It opens with a clear claim, gives three strong examples, and ends with a quiet, confident conclusion. Year after year, students study it line by line. It has become the paradigmatic essay, the model for all the rest. A paradigm is a model or pattern, so something paradigmatic is the model example of its kind. So, what word describes a perfect, textbook example of something?... Paradigmatic.
paradigmatic.example: For many economists, the rise of the garment industry is the paradigmatic case of export-led growth in a poor country.

gre.s: The trial has become ____, cited in nearly every textbook as the classic example of judicial overreach.
gre.clue: the classic example

parsimonious.hook: PARSIMONIOUS: PARSING every penny, unwilling to spend.
parsimonious.story: Parsimonious. Extremely unwilling to spend money. Ian's landlord owns two city buildings, yet he refuses to fix the broken staircase light. Tenants climb the dark stairs by the glow of their phones. When the water pump failed in June, he waited a whole week, hoping it would mend itself, rather than pay a mechanic. Even his own children call him parsimonious. Parsimonious comes from the Latin for sparing: a parsimonious person spares every coin, even when spending is badly needed. So, what word describes someone painfully tight with money?... Parsimonious.
parsimonious.example: The parsimonious landlord refused to replace a single broken bulb in the stairwell, so tenants climbed in darkness.

gre.s: The billionaire was so ____ that he installed pay phones in his mansion so that guests would have to pay for their own calls.
gre.clue: installed pay phones in his mansion

platitude.hook: PLATITUDE: a FLAT attitude remark; flat, dull, overused.
platitude.story: Platitude. A remark used so often that it has lost its meaning. When Frank missed the medical admission cut-off by a few marks, relatives called one after another. "Everything happens for a reason." "Failure is the pillar of success." Each platitude landed like a pat on the head, kind but empty. Only his sister said something real: "Let us go through your weak chapters together tomorrow." Platitude comes from the French plat, meaning flat: a platitude is a flat, worn-out saying. So, what noun means a tired, overused remark?... Platitude.
platitude.example: When the coach offered only the platitude that winning is not everything, the defeated players rolled their eyes.

gre.s: The commencement speaker disappointed the graduates by offering nothing but ____, urging them to follow their dreams and never give up.
gre.clue: urging them to follow their dreams and never give up

pliant.story: Pliant. Easily bent; also, easily influenced by others. In a craft village, Tara watched a weaver soak cane strips in water until they turned soft. Then the strips curved in his hands without a single crack, becoming the round wall of a basket. "Dry cane snaps," he said. "Wet cane is pliant." People can be pliant too, bending to whoever speaks loudest. Pliant shares its root with pliable, from a French verb meaning to bend or fold. So, what word describes something that bends easily, or a person easily swayed?... Pliant.
pliant.example: Weavers soak the cane strips overnight until they become pliant enough to be bent into baskets without cracking.

gre.s: The dictator surrounded himself with ____ advisers who never challenged his decisions, however reckless.
gre.clue: who never challenged his decisions

polymath.hook: POLY = many, MATH = learning. Learned in many things.
polymath.story: Polymath. A person with expert knowledge in many different subjects. In a school library, Piper found an old book about a great scientist from Bengal. He studied radio waves, built delicate instruments to measure how plants respond to the world, and even wrote one of the earliest science fiction stories in his mother tongue. Piper read until the librarian rang the closing bell. She had found a true polymath. Poly means many, and math comes from a Greek word for learning, so a polymath has learned many things. So, what do you call a person brilliant in many fields?... Polymath.
polymath.example: Rabindranath Tagore was a polymath who wrote novels, composed thousands of songs, painted, and founded a university.

gre.s: A true ____, she published influential papers in physics, composed music, and wrote two acclaimed novels.
gre.clue: published influential papers in physics, composed music, and wrote two acclaimed novels

portend.hook: PORTEND: POR-TEND, a portent, an omen of what's coming.
portend.story: Portend. To be a sign that something, usually bad, is coming. In late June, Rita's family watched the great river climb a little higher every evening. The water swallowed the first step of the landing, then the second. Heavy rain had been falling upstream for a week. To the old farmers, these signs portended a flood, and they began moving rice and goats to higher ground. Portend comes from the Latin for stretching forward, like a sign that points ahead to what is coming. So, what verb means to be a warning sign of future trouble?... Portend.
portend.example: Several resignations from the board in one week portended trouble for the struggling airline.

gre.s: Economists worry that the sudden drop in consumer spending may ____ a deeper recession in the coming year.
gre.clue: a deeper recession in the coming year

presage.hook: PRE-SAGE: a SAGE who tells the future BEFORE it happens.
presage.story: Presage. To be a sign of something coming, often something bad; as a noun, the sign itself. On Monday, the teacher at Zane's coaching centre handed out an easy quant sheet with an unusual smile. "Enjoy this one," he said. The students groaned, because they knew that smile. It always presaged a brutal mock test on Friday. Zane shook his head; that smile had never been a false presage. Pre means before, so picture a wise sage who sees trouble before it arrives. So, what word means to hint that something, often bad, is on its way?... Presage.
presage.example: The first cuckoo calls in the mango groves presage the arrival of spring in rural Bengal.

gre.s: Some economists warned that the sudden drop in consumer spending could ____ a deeper recession, while others insisted it was merely a seasonal fluctuation.
gre.clue: while others insisted it was merely a seasonal fluctuation

prurient.hook: PRURIENT: like an ITCH (prurire = to itch) for scandal.
prurient.story: Prurient. Showing an unhealthy interest in sex or scandal. When a young couple in Rita's apartment building quietly divorced, some neighbours could talk of nothing else. They gathered on the stairs, guessing at bedroom secrets, and one aunt even tried to read the couple's mail. Rita felt uneasy and walked away. Their prurient curiosity had nothing to do with care. Prurient comes from a Latin verb meaning to itch: a prurient mind itches for private details that are none of its business. So, what word describes an unhealthy curiosity about other people's intimate lives and scandals?... Prurient.
prurient.example: The tabloid's prurient coverage of the actress's divorce sold many copies but told readers nothing worth knowing.

gre.s: Critics charged that the documentary, despite its claims to serious journalism, merely catered to viewers' ____ curiosity, lingering on lurid details of the celebrity's private affairs.
gre.clue: lingering on lurid details of the celebrity's private affairs

pugnacious.hook: PUGNACIOUS: ready to throw a PUNCH, like a pug that barks at everyone.
pugnacious.story: Pugnacious. Eager to argue or fight. Every morning on the bus into town, Sally saw the same passenger pick a quarrel. One day it was the conductor's change, the next a stranger's elbow, then the driver's music. His voice rose, his finger jabbed the air, and the whole bus went tense whenever he climbed aboard. He was the most pugnacious man on the route. Pugnacious comes from the Latin for fighting with the fist, like pugilist, an old word for a boxer. So, what word describes someone always spoiling for a fight?... Pugnacious.
pugnacious.example: The pugnacious little terrier barked at every delivery van on the street, no matter how large.

gre.s: The usually ____ senator surprised observers by conceding the point calmly instead of launching into one of his customary attacks.
gre.clue: instead of launching into one of his customary attacks

redoubtable.hook: RE-DOUBT-ABLE: you DOUBT you can beat them.
redoubtable.story: Redoubtable. Formidable, especially as an opponent; worthy of fearful respect. In Sean's lane in the old city, nobody wanted to face his grandmother at the carrom board. At seventy, she flicked the striker with one finger and sank the queen as if it were nothing. Young men who boasted at the start went home silent. She was a redoubtable opponent. Redoubtable comes from an old French verb meaning to dread: a redoubtable rival is someone you dread to face. So, what word describes an opponent so formidable that others fear to challenge her?... Redoubtable.
redoubtable.example: The visiting team knew they faced a redoubtable bowling attack on the spin-friendly pitch at Mirpur.

gre.s: Even seasoned lawyers dreaded facing her in court, for she was a ____ advocate whose cross-examinations had demolished countless witnesses.
gre.clue: whose cross-examinations had demolished countless witnesses

ruminate.hook: RUMINATE: like a cow chewing cud, chewing a thought over and over.
ruminate.story: Ruminate. To think about something deeply, for a long time. In a quiet village, Nora watched the family cow lying under the jackfruit tree, slowly chewing the same mouthful of grass. Nora was doing much the same with a letter from a university in Japan. All afternoon she ruminated: leave her ageing parents, or stay? Ruminate comes from the Latin for chewing the cud, so to ruminate is to chew on an idea. So, what verb means to turn a thought over and over in your mind?... Ruminate.
ruminate.example: Sitting on the rooftop after midnight, Arif ruminated on whether to accept the scholarship that would take him abroad.

gre.s: Instead of acting decisively, the general would ____ for days over every decision, by which time the opportunity had usually passed.
gre.clue: Instead of acting decisively

sophistry.hook: SOPHISTRY: from the SOPHISTS, Greek teachers who could argue anything.
sophistry.story: Sophistry. A clever argument that is deliberately misleading. Andy's younger brother wanted to skip his maths homework. "If the teacher never checks homework, then homework does not really exist," he announced at dinner, "and nobody can do what does not exist." For a moment the table went quiet. Then their father said, "Very clever. Now go and do it." It was pure sophistry. The word comes from the Sophists, ancient Greek teachers famous for arguing any side for a fee. So, what noun means a clever argument designed to mislead?... Sophistry.
sophistry.example: The debate judges saw through the team's sophistry, noting that its clever statistics proved nothing about the actual motion.

gre.s: The lawyer's defense, though dazzlingly clever, was mere ____: each step seemed logical, yet the argument as a whole was designed to mislead the jury.
gre.clue: designed to mislead the jury

turbid.hook: TURBID: TURBulent water, all stirred up.
turbid.story: Turbid. Cloudy and muddy, as a liquid is when stirred up; also, confused. In August, Shelby took the ferry across the great river. The river that had looked green in winter was now thick and brown, swirling with silt, sticks and clumps of water hyacinth. When he dipped his hand in, he could not see his own fingers. The water was turbid from bank to bank. Turbid shares its root with disturb and turbulent: turbid water has been disturbed until it clouds. So, what word describes water so muddy and stirred up that you cannot see through it?... Turbid.
turbid.example: After the monsoon rains, the Padma runs turbid and brown, carrying tons of sediment toward the Bay of Bengal.

gre.s: Once so clear that visitors could see pebbles three meters down, the lake has become ____ since mining began upstream, its waters now thick with silt.
gre.clue: its waters now thick with silt

valedictory.story: Valedictory. Serving as a farewell. After thirty years delivering letters in a quiet village, the postman Harold gave a short valedictory speech under the banyan tree. He remembered the wedding cards he had carried and the letters from sons working abroad that he had placed in their mothers' hands. Old women wiped their eyes with the ends of their saris. It was the warmest valedictory moment the village had seen. Vale is Latin for farewell, and dicere means to say: valedictory words say goodbye. So, what word describes a speech given as a farewell?... Valedictory.
valedictory.example: In his valedictory column after forty years at the newspaper, the editor thanked the readers who had argued with him most.

gre.s: The retiring minister's ____ speech, delivered on her final day in parliament, graciously thanked even her fiercest opponents for decades of spirited debate.
gre.clue: delivered on her final day in parliament

verisimilitude.story: Verisimilitude. The quality of seeming true or real. Before writing her novel about tea garden workers in the hills, Sharon spent two months living near the estate. She learned how the pluckers pick two leaves and a bud, the songs they hum on the slopes, and the smell of the factory at dawn. When readers finished the book, many asked whether it was a true story. That was its verisimilitude. Veri means true, as in verify, and simil means like, as in similar: verisimilitude is being like the truth. So, what noun means the appearance of being real?... Verisimilitude.
verisimilitude.example: To add verisimilitude to the war film, the director cast actual veterans and filmed in the villages where battles had occurred.

gre.s: The novel's historical details lend it a striking ____, though every one of its characters is invented.
gre.clue: though every one of its characters is invented

abrogate.hook: AB-ROGATE: ROGUE action — wiping AWAY a law.
abrogate.story: Abrogate. To officially cancel a law, a rule or an agreement. For decades, a small-town cricket club had a written rule that only men could vote in its elections. Women had played for the club for years, yet never voted. At last Monica, its best bowler, raised it at the annual meeting. By a show of hands, the members voted to abrogate the rule. Ab means away, and rogare was the Roman word for proposing a law: to abrogate is to vote a law away. So, what verb means to officially cancel a law or agreement?... Abrogate.
abrogate.example: After seizing power, the military council abrogated the constitution and governed by decree for the next six years.

gre.s: The new regime moved swiftly to ____ the treaty its predecessor had signed, declaring that it would no longer be bound by any of its provisions.
gre.clue: would no longer be bound by any of its provisions

abscond.hook: ABS-COND: ABSent with the CONDominium money.
abscond.story: Abscond. To leave suddenly and secretly, often with money that is not yours. A smart office opened above a small-town pharmacy, promising jobs in Malaysia. Dozens of young men, Rick among them, paid in cash. One Monday they arrived to find the shutter locked, the signboard gone, and every phone switched off. The agents had absconded with everything. Rick's mother sat on the steps and said nothing. Abscond comes from a Latin verb meaning to hide away, and people who abscond vanish into hiding. So, what verb means to run off secretly, often with stolen money?... Abscond.
abscond.example: The tour operator absconded with the deposits of forty pilgrims, leaving them stranded at the airport with worthless tickets.

gre.s: Days before the auditors arrived, the firm's accountant chose to ____ with millions in client funds, slipping out of the country under a false name.
gre.clue: slipping out of the country under a false name

apposite.hook: APPOSITE: APPROPRIATE and POSITioned just right.
apposite.story: Apposite. Perfectly suited to the situation; apt. At a school debate, the topic was whether hard work matters more than talent. Nell's opponent spoke for five minutes about famous geniuses. Then Nell stood up and simply told the story of a rickshaw puller's son from her own town who had topped the district in his exams. The judges nodded slowly. Her example was perfectly apposite. Do not confuse apposite with opposite: an apposite remark sits right beside the point, not against it. So, what word describes an example perfectly fitted to the moment?... Apposite.
apposite.example: Nadia closed her history essay with an apposite line from Nazrul that captured the spirit of the independence movement.

gre.s: The speaker's anecdote, though amusing, was hardly ____: it had nothing to do with the budget crisis the committee had gathered to discuss.
gre.clue: it had nothing to do with the budget crisis

assail.story: Assail. To attack violently, with blows or with harsh words. When Sean's short film about air pollution in the city went online, he expected a few kind comments. Instead, hundreds of strangers assailed him, calling the film fake, calling him a traitor, mocking his voice. Each new notification felt like a slap. His friend Megan sat with him that night and switched off his phone. Assail comes from a Latin verb meaning to leap upon, so to assail someone is to jump on them with force. So, what verb means to attack fiercely, with fists or with words?... Assail.
assail.example: Opposition leaders assailed the transport minister after yet another launch capsized on an overcrowded river route.

gre.s: Critics were quick to ____ the report, questioning its methods, dismissing its data, and even impugning the integrity of its authors.
gre.clue: even impugning the integrity of its authors

avaricious.hook: AVARICIOUS: 'I've got to have my RICHES!'
avaricious.story: Avaricious. Extremely greedy for money. During the tourist season in the hills, one hotel owner tripled his room prices overnight. He charged guests extra for hot water, extra for blankets, even extra for the generator during power cuts. His own staff whispered that he was the most avaricious man in town. Avaricious comes from avarice, a Latin word for greed, and shares an old root with avid, both about a hungry craving. So, what word describes someone with a greedy hunger for wealth?... Avaricious.
avaricious.example: Avaricious middlemen bought the farmers' rice cheaply at harvest and sold it back to them at double the price months later.

gre.s: Far from being generous, the merchant was so ____ that he charged his own relatives interest on every loan.
gre.clue: Far from being generous

beguile.story: Beguile. To charm someone, often in order to deceive them. On the evening ferry down the river, a man in a white suit stood up with a bag of herbal oil. He told funny stories and praised every passenger's kind face, until even Frank's sceptical aunt was smiling. She bought three bottles. At home, the oil turned out to be plain mustard oil with perfume. He had beguiled the whole deck. Inside beguile hides guile, meaning cunning: to beguile is to charm with cunning. So, what verb means to charm someone in a way that tricks them?... Beguile.
beguile.example: The travel advertisement beguiled thousands of young men with promises of high wages abroad that never materialized.

gre.s: So seductive was the con artist's wit that he could ____ even skeptical investors, who handed over their savings without ever questioning his fraudulent figures.
gre.clue: So seductive was the con artist's wit

burnish.hook: BURNISH: rub until it BURNS bright.
burnish.story: Burnish. To polish something until it shines; also, to improve a reputation. Before the autumn festival every year, Dana's grandmother sits on the veranda with brass plates, a lemon and a handful of ash. She rubs and rubs until the dull metal glows gold. Dana's father, a school principal, says he is burnishing the school's name the same way, slowly, with years of good results. Hear burn in burnish: rub something until it glows as if on fire. So, what verb means to polish until shining, or to polish a reputation?... Burnish.
burnish.example: The coach hoped that a strong tournament in Sylhet would burnish his record before the board reviewed his contract.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ her reputation after the scandal, the executive donated generously to local charities and gave interviews emphasizing her humble origins.
gre.clue: donated generously to local charities

comity.hook: COMITY looks like COMMUNITY: people living in harmony.
comity.story: Comity. Courteous, considerate behaviour; mutual respect between groups or nations. In a lane in the old city, Ryan's family and their neighbours of a different faith have lived wall to wall for sixty years. During one family's holiday, plates of sweet noodles travel up Ryan's stairs; during the other's festival, plates of coconut sweets travel back down. When one family holds a wedding, the other lends chairs, cooks and patience. That quiet comity has outlasted every quarrel. Comity comes from the Latin comis, meaning courteous; do not confuse it with comedy. So, what noun means friendly respect between communities or nations?... Comity.
comity.example: Faculty members of rival departments maintained a polite comity, even sharing laboratory equipment during the funding crisis.

gre.s: Despite fierce competition in the market, the two firms maintained a surprising ____, regularly sharing research and referring clients to each other.
gre.clue: regularly sharing research and referring clients to each other

deportment.story: Deportment. The way a person behaves and carries herself; manners and bearing. At Molly's first job at a big city hotel, the trainer spent a whole week on nothing but deportment. Stand tall. Walk without hurrying. Greet every guest with a calm smile, even at three in the morning. By the end of the month, her mother said Molly even walked into the kitchen like a duchess. The word holds port, Latin for carry, as in porter: deportment is how you carry yourself. So, what noun means a person's bearing and manners?... Deportment.
deportment.example: The old dance teacher judged her students as much on their deportment off the stage as on their footwork.

gre.s: Though the young diplomat's knowledge of policy was impressive, it was his impeccable ____ that won him admirers: he remained courteous and composed even under hostile questioning.
gre.clue: remained courteous and composed even under hostile questioning

desultory.hook: DESULTORY: like a DESERT wanderer with no map, aimlessly drifting.
desultory.story: Desultory. Without plan or purpose; jumping from one thing to another. On a rainy Friday, Hunter opened his GRE book at ten. He read two words, checked his phone, ate some puffed rice, watched half a cricket highlight, flipped to geometry, then wandered back to vocabulary. By evening he had touched six topics and learned nothing. It had been a desultory day. In ancient Rome, a desultor was a circus rider who leapt from one horse to another, and a desultory mind leaps the same way. So, what word describes effort that drifts aimlessly from one thing to another?... Desultory.
desultory.example: After the power failed, the office staff made desultory attempts at work before giving up and gathering around the tea urn.

gre.s: His research, once focused and rigorous, became ____ in his later years, as he drifted from topic to topic without completing any project.
gre.clue: drifted from topic to topic without completing any project

diffident.hook: DIFFIDENT is the opposite of CONFIDENT.
diffident.story: Diffident. Shy and unsure of oneself. Becky always knew the answers in her English class, but when the teacher called on her, her voice shrank to a whisper and her eyes dropped to her desk. At the district quiz contest, she stood at the microphone with trembling hands. Then she answered every question correctly and won. Her teacher hugged her and said, "No more diffident whispering, all right?" Diffident and confident share a Latin root for trust: the confident trust themselves, the diffident do not. So, what word describes someone held back by a lack of self-confidence?... Diffident.
diffident.example: The diffident young poet read her work so quietly at the Ekushey book fair that the back rows strained to hear.

gre.s: Though brilliant, the young researcher was so ____ that she rarely presented her findings, fearing that colleagues would find fault with them.
gre.clue: fearing that colleagues would find fault with them

flummoxed.hook: FLUMMOXED: sounds like your brain just got FLUMMOXED, flopped and mixed.
flummoxed.story: Flummoxed. Completely confused; at a loss. When Tina's father tried to pay his electricity bill on a new mobile app, a stream of messages appeared: verify, verify again, enter the code, the code has expired. He pressed one button, then another, and somehow landed on a page about life insurance. He sat back, utterly flummoxed, and called Tina. She fixed it in two taps, and he laughed at himself. Hear how flummoxed sounds, like a brain that has flopped over in a muddle. So, what word describes someone so confused that they cannot work out what to do?... Flummoxed.
flummoxed.example: Grandfather was flummoxed by the new smartphone and kept answering video calls with the camera pointed at the ceiling.

gre.s: The detectives were ____ by the case, as every clue seemed to point in a different direction.
gre.clue: every clue seemed to point in a different direction

garrulous.hook: GARRULOUS: sounds like GARGLE-ous, words gargling out nonstop.
garrulous.story: Garrulous. Excessively talkative, especially about small things. Every month, Ian gets his hair cut at a tiny city salon, and every month the barber talks from the first snip to the last. He talks about his nephew's wedding, the price of onions, and a dream he once had about a goat. Ian rarely gets a word in. Still, he keeps returning to the garrulous old man. Garrulous comes from a Latin verb meaning to chatter, so a garrulous person chatters on and on. So, what word describes someone who talks too much about trivial things?... Garrulous.
garrulous.example: The garrulous rickshaw puller told me his whole family history during the twenty-minute ride to Old Dhaka.

gre.s: The usually ____ professor, whose lectures often drifted into long anecdotes, was uncharacteristically brief at the ceremony.
gre.clue: whose lectures often drifted into long anecdotes

harangue.hook: HARANGUE: HARASS with a long rant.
harangue.story: Harangue. A long, loud, angry speech; as a verb, to lecture someone that way. At holiday lunch, Ronnie's uncle noticed him checking his phone. He put down his plate and began: young people today, no respect, no patience, in my day we walked six miles to school. Twenty minutes later he was still going, louder each minute, while the biryani went cold. Ronnie stared at his plate and waited for the harangue to end. Hear harass inside harangue: a harangue harasses you with words. So, what noun means a long, angry lecture?... Harangue.
harangue.example: The referee endured a long harangue from the losing captain, who blamed every decision for his team's defeat.

gre.s: What was billed as a friendly welcome speech turned into a forty-minute ____, as the chairman berated the new employees about laziness and disrespect.
gre.clue: berated the new employees about laziness and disrespect

impugn.story: Impugn. To question or attack someone's honesty or motives. When Sadie's water filter project won first prize at the national science fair, a rival teacher stood up and claimed her father, an engineer, had built it for her. Sadie's face burned. Calmly, she took the filter apart in front of the judges and explained every layer of sand, charcoal and gravel. After that, nobody dared to impugn her honesty. Impugn shares its fighting root with pugnacious: to impugn is to fight against someone's good name. So, what verb means to call someone's integrity into question?... Impugn.
impugn.example: The rival scientist impugned her honesty, claiming without evidence that she had altered the data to fit her theory.

gre.s: Rather than addressing the substance of the study, critics tried to ____ the researchers' motives, suggesting they had been paid by industry.
gre.clue: suggesting they had been paid by industry

inchoate.hook: INCHOATE: like a chick just INCHing out of its egg, not yet formed.
inchoate.story: Inchoate. Just begun and not yet fully formed; still vague. Late one night in her dorm, Lena hummed a tune that had circled her head all week. She had a few notes, half a line about rain on a tin roof, and a feeling she could not yet name. When her roommate asked what the song was about, Lena shrugged. "It is still inchoate." Inchoate comes from a Latin verb meaning to begin: inchoate ideas have only just begun. So, what word describes an idea still in its early, unformed stage?... Inchoate.
inchoate.example: At sixteen, Rafiq had only an inchoate sense that he wanted to build things, long before he chose to study engineering.

gre.s: The committee's proposals remained ____, little more than a list of vague goals that had yet to be developed into any concrete plan.
gre.clue: had yet to be developed into any concrete plan

inundate.hook: INUNDATE: IN + UNDA (wave). Waves pour in.
inundate.story: Inundate. To flood; also, to overwhelm with too much of something. Every monsoon, the wetland near Felix's village is inundated, the fields vanishing under one shining sheet of water. Last year, Felix posted a photo of it online, a lone boat on the silver water at sunset. By morning he had been inundated with thousands of messages from strangers asking where it was. His phone would not stop buzzing. Inundate comes from the Latin unda, a wave: to inundate is to send waves pouring in. So, what verb means to flood or overwhelm?... Inundate.
inundate.example: After the singer posted her email address online, she was inundated with thousands of messages within a single night.

gre.s: The monsoon rains that year were heavy enough to ____ the low-lying villages, forcing thousands of families to flee to higher ground with whatever they could carry.
gre.clue: forcing thousands of families to flee to higher ground

invidious.story: Invidious. Likely to cause resentment, often because it is unfair. At every family gathering, Nadia's aunt compared her two sons out loud. "Shawn got a scholarship. And Robbie? Still failing English." Robbie would stare at his plate while his cousins went quiet. Even Shawn hated it. The comparison was invidious: it planted envy between two brothers who had once been best friends. Invidious comes from the Latin invidia, meaning envy, so an invidious remark breeds envy and resentment. So, what word describes an unfair comparison that stirs up resentment?... Invidious.
invidious.example: The manager found himself in the invidious position of choosing which of two loyal workers would lose their jobs.

gre.s: Teachers are warned against making ____ comparisons between siblings, which can breed lasting resentment within a family.
gre.clue: which can breed lasting resentment

loquacious.hook: LOQUACIOUS: 'loqu' means speak, as in eloquent. A loquacious person never stops speaking.
loquacious.story: Loquacious. Very talkative; fond of talking. On a boat trip into the mangrove forest, Paula's group had a guide named Mitch who never stopped speaking. He talked about the tides, the crabs scuttling on the mud, the honey collectors, the tiger prints he had seen last winter, and his own childhood on the coast. Some tourists wanted silence, but Paula loved every word. A loquacious guide, she decided, was a gift. Loquacious comes from the Latin loqui, to speak, as in eloquent: a loquacious person loves to speak. So, what word describes someone who talks a great deal?... Loquacious.
loquacious.example: Our loquacious tour guide in Sonargaon filled every quiet moment with stories about the old merchant houses.

gre.s: The usually ____ host surprised his guests by sitting in silence for most of the dinner, barely contributing a sentence.
gre.clue: surprised his guests by sitting in silence

martinet.hook: MARTINET: named after Colonel MARTINET, a famously strict French drill master.
martinet.story: Martinet. A very strict person who demands complete obedience to rules. Every morning at a cadet college, the house master inspects the boys' shoes, beds and fingernails. A crooked collar means extra laps; one minute late means a week without television. The cadets call him a martinet behind his back. Yet years later, Kevin admits that he still folds his shirts the way that martinet taught him, corners perfectly straight. The word comes from Jean Martinet, a famously strict drill master in the French army of King Louis the Fourteenth. So, what noun means a strict disciplinarian?... Martinet.
martinet.example: Our hostel warden in Rajshahi ran the place like a martinet, locking the gates at nine sharp and fining latecomers.

gre.s: Former employees describe the chef as a ____ who would dismiss a cook for a single misplaced garnish, yet his kitchen produced some of the finest food in the city.
gre.clue: would dismiss a cook for a single misplaced garnish

nonplussed.hook: NON-PLUS: 'no more' to say; you're speechless.
nonplussed.story: Nonplussed. So surprised and confused that you do not know how to react. At her cousin's wedding party, Jill was asked to say a few words. As she stood up, the groom's grandmother asked loudly, "And when is your own wedding, dear?" The whole courtyard turned to look. Jill opened her mouth, closed it, and stood there nonplussed. Her cousin rescued her with a hug. Non plus is Latin for no more: when you are nonplussed, you can say no more. So, what word describes someone too startled to know how to respond?... Nonplussed.
nonplussed.example: The quizmaster was nonplussed when two contestants gave the same wrong answer at exactly the same moment.

gre.s: The professor, who seemed to have an answer for everything, was utterly ____ by the child's simple question and stood in silence for a full minute.
gre.clue: stood in silence for a full minute

obeisance.story: Obeisance. Deep respect, or a gesture that shows it, such as a bow. On holiday mornings, Owen and his little cousins line up in front of their grandfather. One by one, they bend down and touch his feet, then touch their own foreheads. Grandfather blesses each child and slips a crisp new note into every hand. It is a small act of obeisance. Obeisance comes from the same old French word as obey, and to make obeisance is to bow your head in respect. So, what noun means a gesture of deep respect, like a bow?... Obeisance.
obeisance.example: Each morning the young musicians made obeisance to their guru, touching his feet before the lesson began.

gre.s: Courtiers were expected to perform elaborate ____ before the emperor, bowing until their foreheads touched the floor.
gre.clue: bowing until their foreheads touched the floor

obviate.story: Obviate. To remove a need or a difficulty; to make something unnecessary. For years, Rhoda's family in a river island village studied by kerosene lamp, coughing in the smoke and buying fuel every week. Then a small solar panel went up on their tin roof. Now a clean bulb glows every evening for free. The panel obviated the need for kerosene and smoky nights. Obviate holds the Latin via, meaning way: to obviate a problem is to clear it out of the way. So, what verb means to make a need or difficulty unnecessary?... Obviate.
obviate.example: Online land records could obviate the long queues and bribes that once accompanied every visit to the registry office.

gre.s: The new vaccine, if effective, would ____ the need for the costly and painful treatments currently used to fight the disease.
gre.clue: the need for the costly and painful treatments

officious.hook: OFFICIOUS: acts like an OFFICER nobody appointed.
officious.story: Officious. Too eager to give orders or offer help that nobody wants. In Sasha's apartment building, one retired neighbour appointed himself guard of everything. He told delivery men where to stand, scolded children for bouncing balls, and once followed Sasha's guests up the stairs to ask why they had come. Nobody had given him any such job. Everyone found him officious. Officious looks like office: picture a man acting as if he holds an office, when nobody gave him one. So, what word describes someone who interferes and gives orders without being asked?... Officious.
officious.example: An officious security guard insisted on checking our tickets three times before letting us into the half-empty theater.

gre.s: The ____ hall monitor, who had no real authority, nonetheless insisted on inspecting every student's bag and lecturing teachers about punctuality.
gre.clue: who had no real authority, nonetheless insisted on

opprobrium.story: Opprobrium. Harsh public criticism and disgrace. When a tannery near the city was caught pouring untreated waste into the river, the river turned black and dead fish floated to the surface. Photos spread across the country within hours. Newspapers, students and even the tannery's own workers condemned the owners. The opprobrium was so fierce that the company apologised and built a treatment plant. Do not confuse opprobrium with approbation, which means approval; they sound alike, but they are opposites. So, what noun means harsh public disgrace?... Opprobrium.
opprobrium.example: The company drew international opprobrium after a factory collapse revealed that it had ignored repeated safety warnings.

gre.s: The athlete, once a national hero, faced public ____ after the doping scandal, with sponsors abandoning him and fans burning his jersey.
gre.clue: sponsors abandoning him and fans burning his jersey

phlegmatic.hook: PHLEGMATIC: slow and calm, like thick PHLEGM.
phlegmatic.story: Phlegmatic. Calm and unemotional; not easily excited. When a sudden squall hit the ferry crossing the wide river, passengers screamed and grabbed the rails. The old captain, Ray, simply adjusted his cap, turned the wheel a little, and spoke quietly to his crew. His voice never rose once. When the boat reached the landing, everyone breathed again and thanked the phlegmatic old man. In old medicine, phlegm was one of four body fluids, thought to make a person calm and slow: a phlegmatic person stays cool. So, what word describes someone who stays calm when everyone else panics?... Phlegmatic.
phlegmatic.example: Even when the stock market crashed, my phlegmatic uncle simply finished his tea and went back to reading the newspaper.

gre.s: While the other passengers screamed as the plane lurched through the storm, the ____ pilot calmly announced that they would still land on schedule.
gre.clue: calmly announced

providential.hook: PROVIDENTIAL: as if PROVIDENCE (God) sent it.
providential.story: Providential. Happening at just the right moment, as if arranged by fate. On the way to his final viva, Shane realised he had left his thesis in a rickshaw. He stood on the roadside, sweating. Then he heard a bell. The same rickshaw puller was pedalling back toward him, waving the folder above his head. Shane waved back, almost in tears. It was a providential rescue. Providential comes from providence, the old idea of a divine care that provides what we need. So, what word describes help that arrives at exactly the right time?... Providential.
providential.example: A providential gust of wind blew the fire away from the crowded slum, giving firefighters time to arrive.

gre.s: The ____ arrival of a rescue ship, just hours before the leaking boat would have sunk, convinced the survivors that fate had intervened on their behalf.
gre.clue: just hours before the leaking boat would have sunk

salubrious.hook: SALUBRIOUS: SALUTE to health, as in 'salud!'
salubrious.story: Salubrious. Good for health. After a winter of coughing in the city's dust and smoke, Mason's grandmother went to stay with her sister in a hill village. There she woke to cool, clean air, and walked the slopes each morning. Within a month her cheeks had colour again. "This air is medicine," she said. The doctor agreed the climate was salubrious. Salubrious comes from the Latin salus, health, the same root behind salute, which once meant wishing someone good health. So, what word describes air or a place that is good for your health?... Salubrious.
salubrious.example: Many retired officers settle in the hills of Sreemangal, praising its salubrious climate and quiet tea gardens.

gre.s: Wealthy Victorians flocked to the seaside resort, convinced that its ____ air could cure everything from asthma to melancholy.
gre.clue: could cure everything from asthma to melancholy

soporific.hook: SOPORIFIC: SO POOR, a lecture so poor it makes you sleepy.
soporific.story: Soporific. Making people sleepy; also, dull. Right after lunch, in a warm classroom, the statistics teacher read his notes in a slow, flat voice. The ceiling fan turned in lazy circles, a crow called outside, and the smell of rice and dal still hung in the air. One by one, heads dropped. Even the teacher stifled a yawn. The lecture was soporific. Soporific comes from the Latin sopor, meaning deep sleep: a soporific thing pulls you toward sleep. So, what word describes something that makes you drowsy?... Soporific.
soporific.example: A heavy lunch of biryani had a soporific effect on the committee, and the afternoon session dragged on in near silence.

gre.s: Even the most enthusiastic students found the lecturer's monotone delivery ____, and many dozed off before the first hour had ended.
gre.clue: many dozed off

turpitude.story: Turpitude. Wickedness; shameful, depraved behaviour. Inspectors raided a warehouse outside the port city and found thousands of fake medicine boxes, chalk pressed into tablets and stamped with famous brand names. The owner had been selling them to pharmacies for years, knowing sick people would swallow them. The magistrate called it an act of moral turpitude, and the courtroom fell silent. Turpitude comes from the Latin turpis, meaning shameful or foul, and moral turpitude means conduct that shocks a community's sense of decency. So, what noun means deep wickedness?... Turpitude.
turpitude.example: Under the club's rules, any member convicted of moral turpitude, such as fraud, loses membership immediately.

gre.s: Voters could forgive the mayor's clumsiness and even occasional dishonesty, but his profiting from child labor exposed a degree of ____ they found unforgivable.
gre.clue: his profiting from child labor

allusive.hook: ALLUSIVE: full of ALLUSIONS (hints), not to be confused with elusive (hard to catch).
allusive.story: Allusive. Full of quiet hints that point to other things. At a poetry evening in the city, an old poet read a verse about a red sun rising over a green field, and the boys who never came home. He never named the year. Yet the whole hall went still, because everyone knew he meant the flag and the war of independence. The poem was allusive. An allusive work is full of allusions; do not confuse it with elusive, which means hard to catch. So, what word describes writing that hints at things without naming them?... Allusive.
allusive.example: The cartoonist's allusive drawings rewarded readers who knew the week's headlines, since every figure hinted at a real minister.

gre.s: Her poems are deeply ____, packed with veiled references to Persian mystics and Bengali folk songs that most readers miss on a first reading.
gre.clue: packed with veiled references

artless.hook: ART-LESS: no art of trickery. Natural and honest.
artless.story: Artless. Natural and honest, without tricks or pretence. At a grand city wedding, guests were praising the decorations in polite, careful voices. Then Rick's five-year-old niece looked up at the bride and said, "Your lipstick is on your teeth." The bride burst out laughing and fixed it. Nobody could be offended by such an artless remark. Here art means craft or cunning, as in the phrase the art of deception, so artless means free of cunning. So, what word describes words or behaviour that are innocent and natural?... Artless.
artless.example: Moni's artless letter to the company, written in plain words without any flattery, persuaded the director to fund her school.

gre.s: The child's ____ remarks, free of any calculation or flattery, charmed the guests far more than the polished speeches of the adults.
gre.clue: free of any calculation or flattery

cacophonous.hook: CACO = bad, PHONE = sound. Bad sound.
cacophonous.story: Cacophonous. Harsh, loud and unpleasant to hear. At six in the evening, Tom stands at the busiest crossing in town waiting for a bus. Horns blare from every direction, a loudspeaker shouts discounts, a drill pounds the flyover, and conductors scream route names over all of it. He presses his hands to his ears. The noise is cacophonous. Think of a symphony, sounds in harmony; cacophonous is the opposite, from Greek words meaning bad sound. So, what word describes a harsh, jarring mix of noises?... Cacophonous.
cacophonous.example: Rush hour at Farmgate is cacophonous, a blare of bus horns, shouting conductors and revving motorbike engines.

gre.s: The composer deliberately made the opening ____, layering clashing rhythms and harsh brass so that the gentle melody that follows seems all the sweeter.
gre.clue: layering clashing rhythms and harsh brass

calumny.hook: CALUMNY sounds like 'CALL YOU MONEY-thief', a lie that ruins your name.
calumny.story: Calumny. A false statement made on purpose to damage someone's good name. When Rachel became the first woman to chair the school committee in her district, anonymous posts appeared claiming she had stolen from the school fund. None of it was true; the accounts showed every cent. Yet neighbours whispered as she passed. The calumny hurt her more than any honest criticism could. Calumny comes from a Latin word for a false accusation. So, what noun means a deliberate lie that ruins a person's good name?... Calumny.
calumny.example: Anonymous accounts spread calumny about the young journalist, claiming she had been paid by foreign spies.

gre.s: The memoir was less a balanced history than an act of ____, attributing invented crimes to the author's former rivals.
gre.clue: attributing invented crimes

conjectural.story: Conjectural. Based on guesswork rather than solid proof. At an ancient ruined city in the north, a guide told Andy's group that a certain grassy mound was once a royal palace. When Andy asked how he knew, the guide admitted that nobody had ever dug there. The palace was purely conjectural. Andy liked the story anyway. A conjecture is a guess, from a Latin verb meaning to throw together, so a conjectural claim throws a few facts together into a guess. So, what word describes a claim built on guesses, not proof?... Conjectural.
conjectural.example: Since the ancient city left no written records, our picture of its government is mostly conjectural.

gre.s: Because no fossils from the period have been found, any account of the species' behavior must remain largely ____.
gre.clue: no fossils from the period have been found

dawdle.hook: DAWDLE: like a DOODLE, wasting time drawing nothing.
dawdle.story: Dawdle. To move slowly and waste time. Every morning, Mandy's little brother takes forty minutes to walk to a school five minutes away. He stops to watch a goat, kicks a stone along the lane, counts the rickshaws, and buys a single tamarind sweet. Their mother stands at the gate calling, "Stop dawdling!" He waves and dawdles on. Hear doodle in dawdle: doodling and dawdling both waste time on nothing in particular. So, what verb means to linger and waste time?... Dawdle.
dawdle.example: The children dawdled on the way home from school, stopping at every stall that sold pickles and ice lollies.

gre.s: With the deadline only hours away, the team could not afford to ____; every minute spent idling would make the final report weaker.
gre.clue: every minute spent idling

doctrinaire.hook: DOCTRINAIRE: follows the DOCTRINE no matter what.
doctrinaire.story: Doctrinaire. Rigidly sticking to a theory, whatever the real situation. A new officer sent a rule to the wetland village schools: every class must start at exactly nine. But in the monsoon, half the children came by boat across a flooded wetland, and nine o'clock meant crossing in the morning storms. Teachers begged; the officer refused. "Rules are rules." His doctrinaire attitude helped nobody. Doctrinaire comes from doctrine, a fixed set of teachings: a doctrinaire person follows the doctrine even when it fails. So, what word describes someone who applies a theory rigidly, ignoring real life?... Doctrinaire.
doctrinaire.example: The doctrinaire economist insisted that markets would fix everything, even as prices of rice and lentils doubled.

gre.s: Unlike her ____ predecessor, who insisted on following party ideology even when it produced obvious failures, the new minister was willing to adapt policies to local conditions.
gre.clue: insisted on following party ideology even when it produced obvious failures

edify.hook: EDIFY: builds you up like an EDIFICE (building).
edify.story: Edify. To teach someone in a way that improves their mind or character. Every Friday afternoon, Abby's grandfather gathered the children of the lane on his veranda. He told stories of honest farmers and brave boatmen, each ending with a question to think about. Years later, Abby realised those evenings had edified her more than any textbook. Edify shares its root with edifice, a building: to edify someone is to build up their mind and character. So, what verb means to instruct in a way that improves a person morally or intellectually?... Edify.
edify.example: Her grandfather's long evening stories were meant to edify as much as amuse, each one ending with a lesson about honesty.

gre.s: The museum's new exhibits are designed to ____ as well as entertain, teaching visitors about climate science through interactive games.
gre.clue: teaching visitors about climate science

effrontery.hook: EFFRONTERY: right in your FRONT, shamelessly.
effrontery.story: Effrontery. Shameless, insolent boldness. At the passport office, Lucy had waited in line for three hours under a hot tin roof. Then a man in sunglasses walked straight to the front, pushed his form through the window, and complained loudly that the clerk was too slow. The whole line went silent at his effrontery. The clerk calmly handed the form back. Effrontery grows from the Latin frons, meaning forehead, as in front: effrontery is barefaced cheek, shown right to your face. So, what noun means shameless, insolent nerve?... Effrontery.
effrontery.example: The contractor who built the crumbling bridge had the effrontery to bid for the job of repairing it.

gre.s: Caught plagiarizing an entire chapter, the author had the ____ to accuse his critics of jealousy, as though they rather than he were at fault.
gre.clue: as though they rather than he were at fault

explicable.story: Explicable. Able to be explained; having a clear reason. Every night at exactly midnight, Nina's dorm room filled with a strange tapping sound. Her roommates were sure it was a ghost. Nina climbed onto a chair with a torch and found the cause: a loose pipe that knocked whenever the water tank on the roof refilled. The mystery was perfectly explicable after all. Most people know inexplicable, meaning impossible to explain; take away the in, and explicable means it can be explained. So, what word describes something that has a clear, logical explanation?... Explicable.
explicable.example: The strange lights over the village became explicable once someone found the drone hobbyist living by the river.

gre.s: What at first seemed a baffling drop in sales became perfectly ____ once analysts noticed that a rival had launched a cheaper product that month.
gre.clue: once analysts noticed

fecund.hook: FECUND: FERTILE and fruitful; produces a FECUND harvest.
fecund.story: Fecund. Very fertile; producing richly; also, full of new ideas. Each year, floods leave a fresh layer of silt on the fields along the great river. When the water goes down, Sam's father scatters seed, and within weeks the land bursts green with rice, mustard and lentils. "This soil is fecund," he says proudly. Sam sees the same thing in his young cousin, a writer with a fecund imagination who fills a notebook every week. Fecund comes from the Latin fecundus, meaning fruitful. So, what word describes soil, or a mind, that produces abundantly?... Fecund.
fecund.example: The delta's fecund silt allows farmers in Bangladesh to grow three crops of rice on the same field each year.

gre.s: The novelist's ____ imagination produced more than forty books in two decades, each populated by dozens of memorable characters.
gre.clue: produced more than forty books in two decades

forbear.hook: FOR-BEAR: BEAR (endure) it FOR now, and hold yourself back.
forbear.story: Forbear. To hold yourself back from doing something. At a family dinner, Tara's uncle mocked her choice to study history. "What job will that get you?" Tara felt a hot reply rise to her tongue. She looked at her grandmother at the head of the table, took a slow breath, and forbore. Later, alone with her uncle, she explained her plans calmly. Do not confuse forbear with forebear, an ancestor; to forbear is to bear your feelings and hold back. So, what verb means to refrain from doing something you want to do?... Forbear.
forbear.example: Doctors urged my diabetic grandfather to forbear eating sweets, yet every Eid he quietly helped himself to a bowl of shemai.

gre.s: Though provoked repeatedly by the hecklers, the speaker managed to ____ from responding and simply continued his talk.
gre.clue: simply continued his talk

imbroglio.hook: IMBROGLIO: an EMBROIDERY of tangled threads.
imbroglio.story: Imbroglio. A confused, tangled situation that is hard to get out of. It started when Isabel's aunt booked a community hall for her daughter's wedding, on the very date another family had booked it for their son's. Both families had receipts. The manager blamed the owner, the owner blamed a clerk, and soon three cousins, two lawyers and a local councillor were shouting in the hall. It was a full imbroglio. Imbroglio comes from an Italian word meaning to tangle, the same idea as being embroiled. So, what noun means a confusing, tangled mess?... Imbroglio.
imbroglio.example: A double-booked wedding hall in Uttara led to an imbroglio involving two families, three caterers and the local police.

gre.s: What began as a minor accounting error grew into a diplomatic ____ involving three governments, two banks, and a tangle of contradictory lawsuits.
gre.clue: a tangle of contradictory lawsuits

inviolate.story: Inviolate. Untouched, unharmed, never broken or violated. Near a village in the hills, a small patch of forest stands around an old shrine. For generations, nobody has cut a single tree there, not even in hard winters when firewood was scarce. Monkeys swing through the branches, and the air smells of wet leaves. To the villagers the forest is inviolate, and they mean to keep it inviolate for their grandchildren. In means not, so inviolate simply means not violated. So, what word describes something kept pure and untouched?... Inviolate.
inviolate.example: The scholar kept her promise of confidentiality inviolate, refusing to name her sources even when a court demanded it.

gre.s: For centuries the sacred grove remained ____: villagers believed that anyone who cut even a single branch would bring disaster on the whole community.
gre.clue: anyone who cut even a single branch would bring disaster

limpid.hook: LIMPID: clear as a LIMPID pool where you can see the bottom.
limpid.story: Limpid. Perfectly clear and transparent; also, easy to understand. In the northeastern hills, Aaron waded into a stream flowing down from the hills, so clear that he could count the pebbles around his feet and watch tiny fish dart between them. He had never seen water like it. Later, reading a favourite essay on the bus home, he noticed the prose had the same limpid quality. Limpid is the opposite of turbid: turbid water is muddy, limpid water lets you see to the bottom. So, what word describes water, or writing, that is perfectly clear?... Limpid.
limpid.example: Divers in the limpid waters around Saint Martin's Island can watch coral and fish several meters below the surface.

gre.s: Unlike his convoluted early essays, the philosopher's later works are written in ____ prose that even beginners can follow.
gre.clue: that even beginners can follow

lugubrious.story: Lugubrious. Looking or sounding sad and gloomy, often more than the moment needs. Whenever the national team loses a cricket match, Frank's uncle plays mournful old songs on the radio, sits on the veranda with a long face, and sighs at every passing bird. His voice drops to a whisper, as if the world has ended. His wife just brings him tea and waits. Within a day, his lugubrious mood passes. Lugubrious comes from a Latin verb meaning to mourn: a lugubrious face looks as if it is in mourning. So, what word describes a gloomy, mournful manner?... Lugubrious.
lugubrious.example: The lugubrious face of the bloodhound made the children feel sorry for it, though it was perfectly content.

gre.s: The director's films are relentlessly ____: long, slow scenes of grieving widows set to funeral music leave audiences longing for even a moment of levity.
gre.clue: long, slow scenes of grieving widows set to funeral music

mawkish.hook: MAWKISH: makes you want to say 'mock-ish', sickly sweet.
mawkish.story: Mawkish. Sentimental in an exaggerated, sickly sweet way. The holiday television drama ended with a scene that lasted ten minutes. Rain poured, violins swelled, the hero knelt in the mud, and his mother's tears fell in slow motion while a sad song played twice. Sadie's grandmother wept, but Sadie groaned and reached for the remote. It was far too mawkish for her. Mawkish once meant sickly or nauseated: mawkish sentiment is so sugary it makes you a little sick. So, what word describes feeling laid on so thick that it seems false?... Mawkish.
mawkish.example: The wedding video was spoiled by mawkish background music that swelled whenever anyone so much as smiled.

gre.s: The critic praised the film for treating its tragic subject with restraint, avoiding the ____ excesses of earlier versions that had wallowed in tearful melodrama.
gre.clue: wallowed in tearful melodrama

mollify.hook: MOLLIFY: make MOLLY soft and calm again.
mollify.story: Mollify. To calm someone's anger or worry; to soften them. Rosie forgot her best friend Tina's birthday, and Tina stopped answering her calls. So Rosie cooked Tina's favourite chicken roast, wrote a long handwritten note, and turned up at her door on Friday afternoon. Tina tried to stay cold, but the smell won. By evening she was fully mollified. Mollify comes from the Latin mollis, meaning soft: to mollify someone is to soften their anger. So, what verb means to calm someone who is angry or upset?... Mollify.
mollify.example: The landlord mollified the angry tenants by lowering the rent for the months their water supply had failed.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the furious passengers, the airline manager promised full refunds and apologized personally to each traveller.
gre.clue: promised full refunds and apologized personally

numinous.hook: NUMINOUS: sounds like LUMINOUS, glowing with something divine.
numinous.story: Numinous. Having a strong spiritual or mysterious quality; filled with a sense of the sacred. Before dawn at a Buddhist monastery in the hills, Isaac sat at the back of the prayer hall. Candles flickered before a golden statue, and monks chanted in low voices. He was not a Buddhist, yet he felt a deep stillness, as if something vast were present. The moment was numinous. Numinous comes from the Latin numen, a divine presence; do not confuse it with luminous, which only means glowing. So, what word describes an experience full of the sacred and mysterious?... Numinous.
numinous.example: Standing alone in the vast cathedral at dawn, the tourist felt a numinous hush that she could not explain.

gre.s: Visitors describe the ancient forest as almost ____, a place whose silence and towering trees seem to suggest a divine presence.
gre.clue: seem to suggest a divine presence

obdurate.story: Obdurate. Stubbornly refusing to change your mind. Year after year, the parents in Jenna's village asked the owner of the school building to fix its cracked roof before the rains. He listened, nodded, and did nothing. Even when water dripped onto the children's exam papers, he refused to spend a single cent. The headmistress, the union chairman and finally a journalist all pleaded. He stayed obdurate. Obdurate shares its root with durable, from the Latin for hard: an obdurate person has hardened like stone. So, what word describes someone who stubbornly refuses to change?... Obdurate.
obdurate.example: My obdurate aunt would not leave her flooded house in Sirajganj until the water reached her kitchen shelves.

gre.s: Despite mounting evidence that his policy was failing, the minister remained ____, refusing even to consider the modest changes his own advisors proposed.
gre.clue: refusing even to consider the modest changes

perfidy.story: Perfidy. Deceitful betrayal of trust. In seventeen fifty-seven, at the Battle of Plassey, the young ruler of Bengal trusted his commander. But the commander had secretly made a deal with the British, and he held his troops back while the battle was lost. To this day, his name is a byword for perfidy across the region. Perfidy comes from the Latin for breaking faith, and it is related to fidelity: perfidy destroys fidelity. So, what noun means treacherous betrayal of trust?... Perfidy.
perfidy.example: Bengali schoolbooks still recall the perfidy of Mir Jafar, whose betrayal at Plassey helped the British win the battle.

gre.s: The spy's ____ came to light only after his death, when documents revealed that he had sold his country's secrets for decades.
gre.clue: sold his country's secrets for decades

pomposity.hook: POMPOSITY: POMP and show of importance.
pomposity.story: Pomposity. Self-important, overly grand behaviour or speech. At the opening of a small town library, a visiting official took the microphone for what was meant to be five minutes. He spoke for an hour, listing his own achievements in words so long that the children in the front row began to giggle. The library itself, he forgot to mention. The audience wilted under all that pomposity. Pomposity comes from pomp, a grand show of splendour: a pompous speaker puts on a show of his own importance. So, what noun means a puffed-up air of self-importance?... Pomposity.
pomposity.example: The new principal's pomposity amused the students, who mimicked his habit of quoting Latin at morning assembly.

gre.s: The ambassador's ____ was legendary: he insisted on being addressed by all three of his honorary titles and once refused to enter a hall through a side door.
gre.clue: insisted on being addressed by all three of his honorary titles

ramification.hook: RAMIFICATION: branches (rami) spreading out from a decision.
ramification.story: Ramification. One of the many results, often unexpected, that follow a decision. When a big garment factory moved its night shift two hours later, it seemed a small change.
