Then the tea stalls outside lost their evening customers, the local buses changed their timetable, and mothers working there needed someone new to collect their children from school. Every decision has ramifications. Ramification comes from the Latin ramus, a branch: a single choice branches out in many directions. So, what noun means one of the many branching consequences of a decision?... Ramification.
ramification.example: Few voters grasped the ramifications of the trade deal until local jute mills began closing one after another.

gre.s: The committee hastily approved the plan without weighing a single ____ of its decision; within a year, unforeseen effects had rippled through every department.
gre.clue: unforeseen effects had rippled through every department

stolid.hook: STOLID: SOLID as a stone, no emotion shows.
stolid.story: Stolid. Calm and showing little emotion, sometimes to the point of dullness. At his son's graduation, every parent was clapping and waving phones. Earl sat with his hands on his knees, his face as still as a wall. His son worried he was disappointed. But that night, Earl quietly framed the certificate and hung it in his shop for every customer to see. His stolid face had hidden a full heart. Hear solid inside stolid: a stolid face is as solid and unmoving as stone. So, what word describes someone who shows little emotion?... Stolid.
stolid.example: The stolid ferry captain steered through the storm without a word while passengers clung to the railings in panic.

gre.s: Even when the verdict was announced and his family erupted in tears, the defendant remained ____, his face betraying no hint of relief or anguish.
gre.clue: his face betraying no hint of relief or anguish

subsume.hook: SUB-SUME: SUM it UNDER a larger heading.
subsume.story: Subsume. To include something within a larger group or category. When Nadia started a small online bakery from her kitchen, she made separate pages for cakes, cookies, brownies and pastries. Customers got lost clicking between them. Her brother suggested one simple heading: sweet treats. Now every item is subsumed under that single category, and her orders have doubled. Sub means under, and sumere means to take: to subsume is to take something under a bigger heading. So, what verb means to fold something into a larger category?... Subsume.
subsume.example: After the merger, the small regional bank was subsumed under its partner's brand, and its old logo disappeared from every branch.

gre.s: Some linguists think it misleading to ____ Chittagonian into the broader category of Bengali dialects, since speakers of the two can barely understand each other.
gre.clue: since speakers of the two can barely understand each other

tendentious.hook: TENDENTIOUS: has a TENDENCY to favor one side.
tendentious.story: Tendentious. Pushing one particular point of view, especially a disputed one; biased. A video about a proposed bridge went viral in a small town. It showed only smiling supporters, played triumphant music over every scene, and cut away whenever a farmer began to explain how his land would be lost. Abigail's journalism teacher played it in class and asked what was missing. "The other side," said Abigail. It was a tendentious film. Tendentious comes from tendency: a tendentious report tends toward one side. So, what word describes reporting that is slanted to favour one view?... Tendentious.
tendentious.example: The textbook's tendentious account of the war praised one general endlessly and ignored the civilians who suffered.

gre.s: The reviewer dismissed the study as ____, noting that its authors had selected only the evidence that supported their political agenda.
gre.clue: selected only the evidence that supported their political agenda

truculent.hook: TRUCULENT: like a TRUCK driver ready to fight anyone in traffic.
truculent.story: Truculent. Aggressive and defiant, eager to fight. When a traffic sergeant at the busy crossing stopped a speeding minibus, the driver leapt out shouting. He jabbed his finger at the sergeant's chest, refused to show his licence, and dared the officer to fine him. Passengers shrank back in their seats. The sergeant stayed calm, and the driver's truculent behaviour cost him his licence. Truculent comes from the Latin trux, meaning fierce or savage: a truculent person is fierce and ready for a fight. So, what word describes someone aggressively defiant and quick to fight?... Truculent.
truculent.example: Grounded for a week, the truculent teenager slammed doors and refused to speak to anyone at dinner.

gre.s: The ____ witness refused to answer even routine questions, glaring at the prosecutor and threatening to walk out of the courtroom.
gre.clue: glaring at the prosecutor and threatening to walk out

unalloyed.hook: UN-ALLOYED: pure gold, not mixed into an ALLOY.
unalloyed.story: Unalloyed. Complete and pure, with nothing mixed in. When the national under-nineteen team won the cricket World Cup, Jim was watching on a tiny phone at a village tea stall. The moment the winning run was hit, the whole crowd leapt up, strangers hugging strangers, cups of tea flying. There was no worry, no doubt, nothing but joy. It was unalloyed happiness. An alloy is a mix of metals, like brass, so unalloyed joy is pure, like gold with nothing mixed in. So, what word describes a feeling that is pure and complete?... Unalloyed.
unalloyed.example: For the village, the news that its girls' team had reached the national final brought unalloyed delight.

gre.s: Her joy at the verdict was hardly ____, for though her brother had been freed, the real culprit had escaped justice entirely.
gre.clue: though her brother had been freed, the real culprit had escaped justice

vexation.story: Vexation. Irritation or worry caused by something troubling. Tamara spent three hours filling in an online university application, scanning every certificate and typing every address. On the final page she pressed submit, and the screen went white. Session expired. Everything was gone. She stared at the screen, then shut the laptop and walked out to the balcony to calm her vexation. Vexation comes from vex, from a Latin verb meaning to shake or harass, and a vexing problem does shake your nerves. So, what noun means a feeling of annoyance or frustration?... Vexation.
vexation.example: To the vexation of the commuters, the metro rail stopped between stations for forty minutes without any announcement.

gre.s: Much to the ____ of the organizers, heavy rain forced them to cancel the outdoor concert just an hour before it was due to begin.
gre.clue: forced them to cancel the outdoor concert

voluble.story: Voluble. Speaking easily, quickly and at length. Neal's grandmother is the heart of every family wedding. She greets each guest by name, tells the story of how she met her husband, explains three recipes, gives advice on marriage, and never seems to pause for breath. Children gather around her, laughing at her jokes. Everyone agrees she is wonderfully voluble. Voluble comes from a Latin verb meaning to roll: from a voluble speaker, words simply roll out. So, what word describes someone who talks fluently and without stopping?... Voluble.
voluble.example: The voluble street vendor kept up a steady stream of jokes and sales talk, never pausing to catch his breath.

gre.s: Usually ____ at dinner parties, chatting easily with strangers for hours, the novelist became oddly taciturn whenever anyone asked about her new book.
gre.clue: chatting easily with strangers for hours

abjure.hook: AB-JURE: 'ab' is away, 'jure' is swear (jury). To swear it away.
abjure.story: Abjure. To formally and solemnly give up a belief, a claim or a habit. Max's grandfather had smoked cheap cigarettes since he was a boy. At his first grandson's naming ceremony, in front of the whole family, he held up his last packet. "From today, I abjure these forever," he said, and dropped it into the cooking fire. The family fell silent, then clapped. He never touched one again. Ab means away and jurare means to swear, as in jury: to abjure is to swear something away. So, what verb means to solemnly renounce a belief or habit?... Abjure.
abjure.example: To join the monastery, the young banker had to abjure his car, his savings and every other worldly possession.

gre.s: Forced to ____ his heretical views before the tribunal, the astronomer publicly renounced theories he privately continued to hold.
gre.clue: publicly renounced

apprise.hook: APPRISE: give someone the PRIZE of information.
apprise.story: Apprise. To inform someone; to tell them what is happening. When her flight to Toronto was delayed by six hours, Fiona worried about her uncle waiting at the airport in the snow. So from the transit lounge, she messaged him every hour, keeping him apprised of each new departure time. When she landed, he was waiting with a warm coat. Apprise comes from a French word meaning taught or learned; do not confuse it with appraise, which means to judge the value of something. So, what verb means to keep someone informed?... Apprise.
apprise.example: Hospital staff apprised Mitu's parents of her condition every hour while she remained in the intensive care unit.

gre.s: Because the patient had a legal right to make her own decisions, the doctors were obliged to ____ her of every risk the surgery entailed.
gre.clue: had a legal right to make her own decisions

canonize.hook: CANONIZE: fired from a CANON of saints, officially added to the holy list.
canonize.story: Canonize. To officially declare someone a saint; also, to treat someone as sacred and beyond criticism. In Fletcher's literature department, one old professor's poems had been praised for so long that nobody dared question them. When Fletcher politely pointed out a weak stanza, the seminar room went cold. The professor had been canonized while still alive. A canon is an official list, such as the list of saints or of great books; to canonize is to add a name to that list. So, what verb means to treat someone as sacred, beyond any criticism?... Canonize.
canonize.example: Film students tend to canonize a handful of directors, treating every scene they shot as beyond criticism.

gre.s: Within a decade of his death, critics who had dismissed the poet began to ____ him, ranking his verse among the greatest of the century.
gre.clue: ranking his verse among the greatest of the century

castigate.hook: CASTIGATE: sounds like 'cast out at the gate', thrown out with harsh words.
castigate.story: Castigate. To scold or criticise someone very severely. After his under-sixteen team dropped five easy catches and lost to the weakest side in the league, Coach Miller gathered the boys in the dressing room. He did not shout. He listed every mistake, one by one, in a cold, hard voice, until no boy could lift his eyes from the floor. Never had he castigated them so harshly. Castigate comes from a Latin verb meaning to punish or correct, so to castigate is to punish with words. So, what verb means to scold someone fiercely?... Castigate.
castigate.example: The auditor's report castigated the city corporation for spending the drainage budget on decorative lights.

gre.s: The editorial went on to ____ the agency for its sluggish response to the flood, calling the delays inexcusable.
gre.clue: calling the delays inexcusable

clamorous.hook: CLAMOROUS: CLAMOR, the loud cry of a crowd.
clamorous.story: Clamorous. Loud and noisy, often with insistent demands. At dawn in the river town fish market, sellers hold up silver fish and shout their prices, buyers shout back lower ones, porters yell for space, and crows scream overhead. Everyone wants to be heard first. Mona covered her ears and grinned at her father. It was the most clamorous place she had ever seen. Clamorous comes from clamour, from the Latin clamare, to shout, as in exclaim. So, what word describes a crowd that is noisy and demanding?... Clamorous.
clamorous.example: Clamorous parents filled the school office on admission day, each one insisting that their child deserved a seat.

gre.s: The quiet library reading room offered a welcome refuge from the ____ market square outside, where vendors shouted their prices all day.
gre.clue: where vendors shouted their prices all day

deify.hook: DEI-fy: 'dei' means god, as in deity. To make into a god.
deify.story: Deify. To treat someone as if they were a god. After a young fast bowler took five wickets in his first World Cup match, his photo went up on every tea stall in his hometown. Fans garlanded his posters and refused to hear a single critical word. When he bowled badly in the next match, the same fans turned furious. They had deified a nineteen-year-old boy. Deify comes from the Latin deus, meaning god, as in deity: to deify is to make into a god. So, what verb means to worship a person like a god?... Deify.
deify.example: Cricket fans in South Asia often deify their star batsmen, building shrines and holding prayers before big matches.

gre.s: Biographers who used to ____ the inventor now acknowledge his flaws, presenting him as a brilliant but very human figure.
gre.clue: now acknowledge his flaws

demur.hook: DEMUR: 'Hmm, de-MURmur', a hesitant, quiet objection.
demur.story: Demur. To raise a polite objection or show reluctance. At the Thursday staff meeting, Sharon's manager announced that the whole team would work through the weekend. Most heads nodded. Sharon cleared her throat. "I am happy to help, sir, but my sister's wedding is on Friday." The manager paused, then agreed she could finish her part on Thursday night. She had demurred without offending anyone. Do not confuse demur with demure, which means shy and modest; to demur is to hesitate and quietly object. So, what verb means to politely object or hesitate?... Demur.
demur.example: When the manager suggested working through the holiday weekend, several engineers demurred, citing family plans made months earlier.

gre.s: When asked to chair the committee, the professor chose to ____, explaining politely that her research left her no time for administration.
gre.clue: explaining politely that her research left her no time

deprecate.hook: DEPRECATE: like DEPRECIATE, lowering something's value.
deprecate.story: Deprecate. To criticise something or speak of it as having little value. When Riley's younger cousin showed the family his first painting, a river at sunset, their uncle glanced at it and said, "Painting will not feed you. Study something useful." The boy's shoulders dropped. Riley quietly hung the painting in his own room. He was tired of hearing his uncle deprecate everything except engineering. A common form is self-deprecating, playing down your own worth; think of depreciate, to lose value. So, what verb means to belittle or disapprove of something?... Deprecate.
deprecate.example: Some older musicians deprecate fusion bands for mixing folk melodies with electric guitars, calling it a betrayal of tradition.

gre.s: Although many modern linguists ____ strict grammar rules as elitist and arbitrary, most teachers still insist on them in student essays.
gre.clue: as elitist and arbitrary

dilatory.story: Dilatory. Slow to act, often deliberately, in order to delay. After a storm tore the roof off his shop on the coast, Steve filed an insurance claim. The company asked for one more form, then a second photo, then a new signature, then a letter from the union office. Six months passed. Each time he called, a polite voice promised it was nearly done. The company's dilatory tactics were wearing him down. Hear delay in dilatory: dilatory people delay and delay. So, what word describes someone who is slow to act, often on purpose?... Dilatory.
dilatory.example: Lawyers for the company used dilatory tactics, requesting endless postponements so that the case would drag on for years.

gre.s: Frustrated by the contractor's ____ progress, the city imposed daily fines for every week the project fell behind schedule.
gre.clue: fell behind schedule

dissemble.hook: DIS-SEMBLE: DIS-RESEMBLE, showing a face that doesn't resemble your true feelings.
dissemble.story: Dissemble. To hide your real feelings or motives behind a false face. When Trish's mother-in-law served her famous spicy fish paste, the dried fish paste was so salty that Trish's eyes watered. Everyone was watching. Trish took a second bite, smiled warmly, and said it was delicious. She dissembled well, and the old lady glowed with pride. Dissemble shares its root with dissimilar: your outward face is dissimilar to what you really feel. Do not confuse it with disassemble, to take apart. So, what verb means to hide your true feelings?... Dissemble.
dissemble.example: The spy had learned to dissemble so well that even her closest friends never guessed her true loyalties.

gre.s: Unable to ____ her disappointment, the candidate frowned openly as the results were announced.
gre.clue: frowned openly

felicitous.hook: FELICITOUS: FELICITY = happiness. A happily perfect choice.
felicitous.story: Felicitous. Well chosen and perfectly suited to the moment; pleasing. At the farewell for their literature teacher, the students asked Shelby to say a few words. She stood up, paused, and quoted a single line of a beloved poet about coming back to the banks of a river at home. The teacher, who had taught them that very poem, pressed a hand to her heart. It was a felicitous choice. Felicitous comes from felicity, happiness, from the Latin felix: a felicitous phrase brings happiness by fitting perfectly. So, what word describes words perfectly chosen for the occasion?... Felicitous.
felicitous.example: Naming the new bridge after the village poet proved a felicitous decision that pleased both residents and officials.

gre.s: The editor praised the translator's ____ choice of words, which captured the original poem's music without sacrificing its meaning.
gre.clue: captured the original poem's music without sacrificing its meaning

fervid.story: Fervid. Burning with strong feeling, sometimes overheated. At a student rally for road safety, sixteen-year-old Aaron climbed onto a bench with a megaphone. His voice cracked with passion as he spoke of the friend he had lost to a speeding bus. Sweat ran down his face; his fists shook. The crowd roared after every sentence. It was a fervid speech, more fire than logic, but no one could ignore it. Fervid comes from a Latin verb meaning to boil, like fervour and fervent. So, what word describes passion that burns intensely, even feverishly?... Fervid.
fervid.example: Her fervid speech on the rights of garment workers drew a standing ovation from the students at Dhaka University.

gre.s: The candidate's ____ supporters, who chanted for hours in the rain, contrasted with the lukewarm reception she received elsewhere.
gre.clue: who chanted for hours in the rain

gawky.hook: GAWKY: like a young GOOSE that hasn't learned to walk.
gawky.story: Gawky. Awkward and clumsy, often because someone is tall and thin. At fourteen, Alex grew taller than his father in a single year. His arms seemed too long for his sleeves, his feet tripped over doorsteps, and at his cousin's wedding he knocked over a whole tray of rice pudding while trying to dance. Everyone laughed, and so did he. Years later, the gawky boy became a graceful national swimmer. Picture a young heron on a riverbank, all legs and neck, stumbling as it learns to walk: that is gawky. So, what word describes someone tall, clumsy and awkward?... Gawky.
gawky.example: In old family photographs my father looks gawky, all elbows and knees in a school uniform two sizes too big.

gre.s: The once ____ teenager, who used to trip over his own feet, had grown into a dancer of remarkable poise and elegance.
gre.clue: who used to trip over his own feet

hidebound.hook: HIDEBOUND: bound tight in an old HIDE (skin).
hidebound.story: Hidebound. Stuck in old ways and closed to new ideas. When a young teacher at a small-town high school suggested science projects instead of memorised answers, the senior teachers shook their heads. "We have taught this way for thirty years," said one. "Why change now?" The headmaster refused to try it for even a single term. The school was hidebound. Hidebound once described thin cattle whose hide clung tightly to their bones; a hidebound mind is just as tight and cannot stretch. So, what word describes people stuck rigidly in old habits?... Hidebound.
hidebound.example: Young doctors complained that the hospital's hidebound rules required paper files even after computers had been installed.

gre.s: The institute's ____ administrators rejected every proposal for curricular reform, insisting that methods good enough for their grandparents were good enough for today's students.
gre.clue: insisting that methods good enough for their grandparents were good enough

imperturbable.story: Imperturbable. So calm that nothing can upset you. During a power cut in the middle of an evening mock test at a small-town coaching centre, the room fell dark, and students began whispering in panic. Their teacher, an elderly woman named Helen, simply lit a candle, placed it on her desk, and said, "Your paper is the same in the dark. Keep writing." Her voice never wavered. The students relaxed. She was imperturbable. To perturb is to disturb, so an imperturbable person cannot be disturbed. So, what word describes someone who stays completely calm under pressure?... Imperturbable.
imperturbable.example: The imperturbable air traffic controller guided the damaged plane down without once raising her voice.

gre.s: The chess champion remained ____ throughout the tournament; neither her opponent's taunts nor the roaring crowd produced so much as a flicker of emotion on her face.
gre.clue: neither her opponent's taunts nor the roaring crowd

impolitic.story: Impolitic. Unwise; likely to cause offence or trouble. At his first big job interview, Tucker was asked why he had left his last company. Instead of a careful answer, he said his former boss was lazy and the company badly run. The interviewers exchanged a look. Even if every word was true, it was an impolitic thing to say. To be politic is to be wise and tactful, so impolitic means unwise and tactless. So, what word describes a remark that is honest but foolish, bound to cause trouble?... Impolitic.
impolitic.example: Announcing a fare hike on the eve of Eid, when millions travel home, was an impolitic move by the railway ministry.

gre.s: Though privately he agreed with the protesters, the ambassador judged it ____ to say so publicly, since doing so would surely offend the host government.
gre.clue: since doing so would surely offend the host government

ingenuous.hook: IN-GENU-ous: genuine, innocent, without tricks. Not to be confused with ingenious (clever).
ingenuous.story: Ingenuous. Innocent, trusting and naive, with a childlike simplicity. At the central station, a stranger told Ruby, just arrived from her village, that he could get her a ticket at half price if she paid him first. She handed over the money with a grateful smile. Luckily her cousin arrived in time to stop him. Ruby was not foolish, only ingenuous; she simply assumed everyone was honest. Ingenuous looks like genuine, open and sincere; do not confuse it with ingenious, which means clever. So, what word describes someone innocently trusting?... Ingenuous.
ingenuous.example: Fresh from his village, Babul was so ingenuous that he believed every street vendor who swore his goods were imported.

gre.s: The politician's seemingly ____ manner, all wide eyes and simple questions, concealed a shrewd and calculating mind.
gre.clue: concealed a shrewd and calculating mind

munificent.story: Munificent. Giving money or gifts on a grand and generous scale. The tin-roofed primary school in Hank's coastal village had leaking walls and no library. Then a former pupil who had built a business in Italy came home for a visit. Within a year, he had paid for a new brick building, two thousand books, a computer room, and scholarships for every girl in class five. The villagers called it a munificent gift. Munificent comes from Latin words meaning gift-making: a munificent person makes gifts on a grand scale. So, what word describes extremely generous giving?... Munificent.
munificent.example: Thanks to a munificent gift from former students, the old college library in Barishal finally received a new roof.

gre.s: Far from being the miser his neighbors believed him to be, the reclusive farmer proved ____, leaving his entire fortune to the village school.
gre.clue: leaving his entire fortune to the village school

occlude.hook: OCCLUDE: CLOSE it off (claudere = to close).
occlude.story: Occlude. To block or close off. Every monsoon, the street outside Neil's city building floods within an hour of heavy rain. When city workers finally lifted the iron drain covers, Neil watched them pull out plastic bags, bottles and even a torn pillow. The rubbish had completely occluded the drains, so the rain had nowhere to go but the street. Occlude comes from the Latin for shutting up, the same root found in include and exclude. So, what verb means to block a passage completely?... Occlude.
occlude.example: Heavy dust from the brick kilns occluded the air filters, so the clinic's machines had to be cleaned every week.

gre.s: The tall new apartment towers threaten to ____ the river view from the old houses, which until now have looked directly onto the water.
gre.clue: which until now have looked directly onto the water

punctilious.hook: PUNCTILIOUS: PUNCTUAL to the point; every point exactly right.
punctilious.story: Punctilious. Extremely careful about rules, manners and small details. Bill, the head cashier at a small-town bank, arrives at exactly eight each morning. He counts every bundle of notes twice, checks every signature letter by letter, and in thirty years has never made an error. Even the young clerks straighten their collars when he walks in. He is punctilious. Punctilious shares its root with punctual, from the Latin for a point: a punctilious person gets every small point right. So, what word describes someone careful about every tiny detail?... Punctilious.
punctilious.example: My punctilious grandfather recorded every taka he spent in a notebook, down to the price of a single cup of tea.

gre.s: The diplomat was famously ____, observing every formality of protocol down to the order in which guests were greeted.
gre.clue: observing every formality of protocol

qualm.hook: QUALM: a small QUALITY check of your conscience.
qualm.story: Qualm. A sudden feeling of doubt or unease, especially about whether you are doing the right thing. At a city grocery, the shopkeeper gave Annie change for a fifty-dollar note, though she had paid with a twenty. She was halfway home, planning what to buy with it, when a qualm stopped her on the pavement. She thought of his tired face. She turned around and walked back. Qualm sounds almost like calm, but it is the opposite: a qualm unsettles a calm conscience. So, what noun means a twinge of doubt about your own conduct?... Qualm.
qualm.example: Faisal felt a sudden qualm about lending his savings to a cousin who had never repaid a loan before.

gre.s: She felt not the slightest ____ about reporting her own manager to the auditors, since she had watched him falsify the accounts with her own eyes.
gre.clue: since she had watched him falsify the accounts with her own eyes

recapitulate.story: Recapitulate. To summarise and repeat the main points. On the last day before the final exam, Professor Nash taught nothing new in her economics class. Instead, she walked through the whole term, chapter by chapter: supply and demand, inflation, trade, growth. In one hour she recapitulated four months of lectures. Students who had been lost all term suddenly saw how everything fit together. Recapitulate is the long form of recap, from the Latin for a heading: you go back over the headings. So, what verb means to summarise the main points again?... Recapitulate.
recapitulate.example: Before the vote, the chairperson recapitulated both sides of the debate so that latecomers could follow the discussion.

gre.s: Having presented her evidence over several dense chapters, the author uses the final pages to briefly ____ her central arguments, so that readers leave with the key points fresh in mind.
gre.clue: so that readers leave with the key points fresh in mind

retrench.hook: RE-TRENCH: dig back into a TRENCH, cutting back.
retrench.story: Retrench. To cut back on spending or costs. When prices rose sharply, Ruby's family sat down at the dining table with a notebook. They cancelled the cable connection, walked instead of taking rickshaws for short trips, and cooked fish twice a week instead of every day. Her father even gave up his evening cigarettes. It was hard, but the family had retrenched. Retrench comes from an old French verb meaning to cut back, related to trench, a long cut in the earth. So, what verb means to reduce spending in hard times?... Retrench.
retrench.example: When remittances from abroad fell, many families in Sylhet had to retrench, postponing weddings and selling land.

gre.s: Faced with a steep decline in enrollment, the college was forced to ____, suspending construction of its new library and freezing all hiring.
gre.clue: suspending construction of its new library and freezing all hiring

sagacious.story: Sagacious. Wise and showing sound judgment. Two brothers in a northern village had argued over a mango orchard for three years, while the fruit rotted unpicked. Finally they went to the village elder, Agnes Kent. She listened all afternoon, then said, "One brother divides the orchard; the other chooses first." The quarrel ended that evening. Everyone agreed her solution was sagacious. Sagacious comes from the Latin sagax, sharp-sighted; it also sounds like sage, and a sagacious person truly is one. So, what word describes someone wise in judgment?... Sagacious.
sagacious.example: The sagacious village elder settled the land dispute in an afternoon, offering a compromise that both families accepted.

gre.s: Investors trusted the ____ banker, whose cautious predictions had been proved correct through three market crashes.
gre.clue: whose cautious predictions had been proved correct through three market crashes

sinecure.hook: SINE-CURE: 'without care' — a job with no worries.
sinecure.story: Sinecure. A job that pays well while asking almost nothing of you. Melissa's uncle was named honorary adviser to a big company board, a post given to him by an old friend. He visits the office once a month, drinks tea, signs a few papers, and goes home. For this he receives a large salary and a car with a driver. It is a sinecure. Sine cura is Latin for without care: a sinecure brings pay without cares. So, what noun means a comfortable, well-paid post with almost no duties?... Sinecure.
sinecure.example: His uncle found him a sinecure at the state corporation, where he signed a few papers each month and collected a full salary.

gre.s: The ambassadorship was widely regarded as a ____, a reward for political loyalty that demanded almost no work yet came with a generous salary and a seaside villa.
gre.clue: demanded almost no work yet came with a generous salary

skullduggery.hook: SKULL-DUGGERY: digging up skulls at night; secret, shady business.
skullduggery.story: Skullduggery. Underhanded, dishonest trickery. The election for president of the town chess club should have been simple. Then thirty new members appeared on the list the night before the vote, people no one had ever seen at a board. Ballot papers went missing, and one candidate's posters were torn down at dawn. When an honest treasurer checked the records, the skullduggery was laid bare. Picture shady figures digging in a graveyard at night: skullduggery sounds like the secret, shady business it is. So, what noun means sneaky, dishonest scheming?... Skullduggery.
skullduggery.example: The club election collapsed amid skullduggery, with forged membership cards and votes cast by members long dead.

gre.s: The merger was finalized only after months of ____, including leaked documents, secret side deals, and bribed officials.
gre.clue: leaked documents, secret side deals, and bribed officials

stanch.story: Stanch. To stop something from flowing out, especially blood. A boy slipped from a mango tree in Rose's village and cut his leg on a broken branch. Blood ran down onto the dry soil. Rose, who had just finished a first aid course, folded her scarf into a tight pad, pressed down hard, and held it steady until she had stanched the bleeding. Stanch is the verb, to stop a flow; its close cousin staunch usually describes someone loyal and firm. So, what verb means to stop a flow, especially of blood?... Stanch.
stanch.example: Volunteers piled sandbags along the embankment to stanch the floodwater pouring into the low fields.

gre.s: The central bank raised interest rates sharply in a desperate effort to ____ the flight of capital that had already drained much of the country's reserves.
gre.clue: had already drained much of the country's reserves

timorous.story: Timorous. Nervous, fearful and lacking confidence. On her first day at a new city school, Lily stood at the classroom door clutching her bag. She said her name so softly that the teacher had to lean close to hear it. At lunch she sat alone, hardly eating. Then a girl named Rita slid her a samosa and said, "Sit with us." Day by day, the timorous newcomer found her voice. Timorous comes from the Latin timor, meaning fear, the same root as timid. So, what word describes someone shy and easily frightened?... Timorous.
timorous.example: The timorous intern rehearsed her short presentation a dozen times, terrified that the directors would laugh at her.

gre.s: Unlike his ____ predecessor, who avoided every controversy, the new chairman tackled the company's problems head-on.
gre.clue: who avoided every controversy

vacillate.hook: VACILLATE: OSCILLATE like a fan, swinging back and forth.
vacillate.story: Vacillate. To keep changing your mind; to waver between choices. Should Nate study computer science or medicine? On Monday he chose computers, and on Tuesday medicine. On Wednesday, after a long phone call with his aunt, he switched back. By Friday his mother had stopped asking. The admission deadline came closer, and still he vacillated. Vacillate comes from a Latin verb meaning to sway, and it rhymes with oscillate, which also means swinging back and forth, like a table fan turning its head. So, what verb means to keep wavering between options?... Vacillate.
vacillate.example: Shuvo vacillated for weeks between studying medicine and computer science, changing his mind almost every evening.

gre.s: Rather than committing to a clear strategy, the coach continued to ____ between attacking and defensive formations, confusing his own players.
gre.clue: Rather than committing to a clear strategy

wheedle.story: Wheedle. To coax or flatter someone into giving you what you want. Tommy wanted to borrow his elder brother's motorcycle for a trip to the hills. He did not ask directly. Instead he polished his brother's shoes, brought him tea in bed, and praised his new haircut three times in one morning. By lunchtime, the keys were in his hand. He had wheedled them out of him. Hear the whine in wheedle: a wheedling voice is sweet on top, with a little whine underneath. So, what verb means to get something through sweet coaxing?... Wheedle.
wheedle.example: My niece wheedled a new phone out of her grandmother by massaging her feet and praising her cooking all week.

gre.s: Too proud to demand a raise outright, the clerk tried to ____ one from his employer, praising her leadership at every opportunity and hinting at his financial troubles.
gre.clue: praising her leadership at every opportunity

adulterate.hook: ADULTERATE: an ADULT trick to cheat by mixing in cheap stuff.
adulterate.story: Adulterate. To make something impure by mixing in something cheaper or harmful. Shelby's mother had bought turmeric powder from the same market stall for years. One day, a mobile court tested the stall's stock and found brick dust mixed into the bright yellow powder. Shelby's mother stared at her jar. The seller had been adulterating it all along. Adulterate comes from a Latin verb meaning to corrupt: an adulterated product has been corrupted by cheap additions. So, what verb means to spoil something pure by mixing in an inferior substance?... Adulterate.
adulterate.example: Food inspectors in Dhaka fined several shops for adulterating turmeric powder with brick dust to increase its weight.

gre.s: Inspectors discovered that the supplier had found a way to ____ the saffron with dyed corn silk, passing off the cheap filler as the costly spice.
gre.clue: passing off the cheap filler as the costly spice

aggrandize.story: Aggrandize. To increase someone's power or importance, or to make something seem greater than it is. When a local businessman paid for a short new road, he had his name painted on six giant billboards along it. He told reporters the road would change the whole district. The villagers noticed it was barely half a kilometre long. He had used the road to aggrandize himself. Hear grand inside aggrandize: to aggrandize is to make someone or something look grander. So, what verb means to inflate one's own importance or power?... Aggrandize.
aggrandize.example: The dictator's statues and portraits were designed to aggrandize a man who had never actually fought in a single battle.

gre.s: Rather than ____ his own role, the modest scientist repeatedly credited his students for the discovery.
gre.clue: the modest scientist repeatedly credited his students

burgeon.hook: BURGEON: a BURGER shop that grows into a giant chain overnight.
burgeon.story: Burgeon. To grow or spread quickly. When Jasmine opened a tiny stall selling homemade rice cakes near her university gate, she had one stove and one helper. Within two years, her orders burgeoned. She now runs three shops, employs twelve women from her neighbourhood, and delivers to offices across the city. Her mother still cannot believe it began with one frying pan. A burgeon was once a bud, and like buds bursting open in spring, a burgeoning business grows fast. So, what verb means to grow and flourish rapidly?... Burgeon.
burgeon.example: Online clothing shops have burgeoned across Bangladesh, with thousands of small sellers now taking orders through social media.

gre.s: Scientists warn that, unless strict controls are introduced, the city's population will continue to ____, straining already overloaded water supplies.
gre.clue: straining already overloaded water supplies

chary.story: Chary. Cautious and wary; slow to give or to trust. Last year, Trevor lent his carefully written notes to a classmate, who copied them and passed them off as his own. Trevor's marks suffered. Now, when anyone asks for his notes, he hesitates, asks why, and shares only a page or two. He has become chary of lending anything. Chary comes from an old English word linked to care: a chary person takes great care before trusting. So, what word describes someone wary and reluctant to give or risk?... Chary.
chary.example: After being cheated once by a fake recruiting agency, Kamal was chary of any job offer that asked for money in advance.

gre.s: Having lost heavily in the last market crash, investors were understandably ____ of new technology stocks, refusing to commit money without years of proven profits.
gre.clue: refusing to commit money without years of proven profits

circumscribe.hook: CIRCUM-SCRIBE: draw (scribe) a CIRCLE around it.
circumscribe.story: Circumscribe. To restrict something within limits; literally, to draw a line around it. Karen's grandmother was the best student in her village school in the nineteen sixties. But at fifteen she was married, and her world shrank to one kitchen, one courtyard and one household. She never stopped reading the newspaper, word by word, by the window. Her life had been circumscribed by others, yet her mind had not. Circum means around, as in circle, and scribe means write: to circumscribe is to draw a boundary around. So, what verb means to confine something within narrow limits?... Circumscribe.
circumscribe.example: Her illness circumscribed her travels, but from her balcony in Old Dhaka she wrote vivid stories about the whole country.

gre.s: The new law sought to ____ the president's powers, limiting his ability to declare emergencies without parliamentary approval.
gre.clue: limiting his ability to declare emergencies

contretemps.hook: CONTRE-TEMPS: French for 'against time' — bad timing.
contretemps.story: Contretemps. An awkward, unexpected mishap or a small quarrel. At Jody's engagement, the groom's aunt arrived wearing exactly the same red silk sari as Jody's mother. The two women stopped at the gate and looked each other up and down, and the guests went silent. Then Jody's mother took the aunt's arm and insisted they pose for a photo together. The little contretemps became everyone's favourite story of the night. Contretemps is French for against the time: a moment that goes wrong at the worst possible time. So, what noun means an embarrassing little mishap or squabble?... Contretemps.
contretemps.example: A minor contretemps over who would cut the wedding cake briefly soured the mood between the two families.

gre.s: The diplomats' brief ____ over seating arrangements, though embarrassing at the time, was soon forgotten amid the far weightier negotiations that followed.
gre.clue: soon forgotten amid the far weightier negotiations

enthrall.hook: ENTHRALL: like a THRALL (slave) to the story.
enthrall.story: Enthrall. To hold someone's complete attention; to fascinate. During a long power cut in a quiet village, the children gathered around Mark's grandfather on the dark veranda. He told them about a giant fish that lived under the old bridge, his voice dropping low, a lantern flickering on his face. Nobody moved. Nobody even swatted the mosquitoes. The story enthralled them. A thrall was a slave in old English, so an enthralling story holds you as its captive. So, what verb means to capture someone's full attention?... Enthrall.
enthrall.example: The documentary on deep-sea creatures enthralled my younger brother, who watched it four times in a single weekend.

gre.s: Her storytelling could ____ even the most restless audience: children who usually fidgeted through lessons sat motionless until the final word.
gre.clue: children who usually fidgeted through lessons sat motionless until the final word

equivocate.hook: EQUI-VOCATE: EQUAL VOICES, saying both yes and no at once.
equivocate.story: Equivocate. To give vague answers on purpose, so as not to commit to anything. When Faye asked her landlord directly whether the rent would rise next year, he smiled. "Well, it depends. Prices change. We will see. Maybe yes, maybe not, it is hard to say." She asked again and got another cloud of words. He was equivocating. Equi means equal and voc means voice: someone who equivocates speaks with two equal voices, yes and no at once. So, what verb means to dodge a question with deliberately unclear answers?... Equivocate.
equivocate.example: When the journalist asked whether layoffs were planned, the company spokesman equivocated, saying only that all options were being studied.

gre.s: Pressed to say whether she supported the bill, the candidate continued to ____, offering answers so qualified that both sides claimed her as an ally.
gre.clue: offering answers so qualified that both sides claimed her

excoriate.hook: EX-CORIATE: to strip off the skin (corium), with harsh words.
excoriate.story: Excoriate. To criticise someone extremely harshly. Six months after a new bridge opened over a coastal canal, a long crack split its deck. Engineers found that the builders had used far less steel than the plan required. In parliament and in every newspaper, the contractors were excoriated. One editorial called the bridge a monument to greed. Excoriate comes from the Latin for stripping off the skin, so to excoriate someone is to flay them with words. So, what verb means to criticise with fierce severity?... Excoriate.
excoriate.example: In a fiery editorial, the newspaper excoriated the factory owners who had locked the fire exits.

gre.s: Reviewers did not merely criticize the novel; they chose to ____ it, condemning its plot, its prose, and its author's integrity in the harshest possible terms.
gre.clue: in the harshest possible terms

exculpate.story: Exculpate. To show or declare that someone is not guilty. When a gold bangle disappeared from a city house, the family blamed their young housekeeper, Shirley. She wept and swore she had not taken it. A week later, a plumber clearing the bathroom drain pulled out the missing bangle, slipped from the owner's own wrist. The discovery exculpated Shirley completely, and the family begged her forgiveness. Ex means out of, and culpa means guilt, as in culprit: to exculpate is to lift someone out of guilt. So, what verb means to clear someone of blame?... Exculpate.
exculpate.example: DNA tests finally exculpated the farmer, who had spent eleven years in prison for a murder he did not commit.

gre.s: The newly discovered letters seemed to ____ the accused general, showing that he had opposed the massacre rather than ordered it.
gre.clue: showing that he had opposed the massacre rather than ordered it

factious.story: Factious. Causing disagreement and splitting a group into rival sides. The drama club at Shannon's college had always felt like a family. Then two senior members began fighting over who would direct the spring play. Soon every rehearsal split into two camps that sat on opposite sides of the room and refused to share props. The play was cancelled. Their factious quarrel had broken the club. Factious comes from faction, a rival group within a group: a factious person creates factions. So, what word describes behaviour that splits a group into warring sides?... Factious.
factious.example: The factious student union split into three groups that could not agree even on the date of the annual festival.

gre.s: The once unified party had grown so ____ that its members spent more energy attacking rival wings than opposing the government.
gre.clue: spent more energy attacking rival wings than opposing the government

gainsay.story: Gainsay. To deny or contradict something. At the cricket club meeting, a senior member insisted that the young spinner, Ryder, was not good enough for the first team. Then the coach simply read out the season's figures: the most wickets, the best economy, and two match-winning spells in the final week. Nobody could gainsay those numbers. The senior member quietly sat down. Gain here is an old form of against, so to gainsay is to say against. So, what verb means to deny or contradict something?... Gainsay.
gainsay.example: There is no gainsaying the importance of the garment sector, which employs millions of workers across Bangladesh.

gre.s: No one could ____ the champion's skill; even her fiercest critics admitted that she was the finest player of her generation.
gre.clue: even her fiercest critics admitted

indecorous.story: Indecorous. Not in keeping with good manners or proper behaviour. During the quiet moment of a wedding ceremony, just as the officiant asked the bride for her consent, a guest's phone rang loudly with a film song. Instead of silencing it, he answered and began discussing cricket scores at full volume. Elders turned and frowned. Lina's grandmother shook her head at such indecorous behaviour. Indecorous is the opposite of decorous, from decorum, the rules of proper conduct. So, what word describes behaviour that is improper for the occasion?... Indecorous.
indecorous.example: Several members of parliament considered it indecorous for a minister to dance on stage at a campaign rally.

gre.s: Many guests found the best man's crude jokes at the memorial service ____, since such levity seemed out of place at so solemn an occasion.
gre.clue: seemed out of place at so solemn an occasion

ineluctable.hook: IN-E-LUCTABLE: you can't struggle (luctari) out of it.
ineluctable.story: Ineluctable. Impossible to avoid; certain to happen. All winter, Sam found reasons to skip his exam preparation: a wedding, a cricket series, a cold. He hoped for a strike, a flood, anything that might postpone the board exam. But the date did not move. On the morning itself, he sat in the hall with a pen in his trembling hand. The exam had been ineluctable all along. Ineluctable comes from the Latin for something you cannot struggle out of: no matter how you wriggle, it arrives. So, what word describes something you simply cannot escape?... Ineluctable.
ineluctable.example: Rising sea levels make the ineluctable retreat of some coastal villages a matter of planning rather than debate.

gre.s: Many historians once believed the empire's decline was ____, the result of forces no ruler could have resisted; newer scholarship stresses specific mistakes that might easily have been avoided.
gre.clue: forces no ruler could have resisted

inveigle.hook: INVEIGLE: like a VEIL over the truth to lure someone in.
inveigle.story: Inveigle. To persuade someone by flattery or trickery into doing something. A smooth-talking agent visited Ryan's grandfather. He praised the old man's wisdom, drank tea with him three afternoons in a row, and spoke of a scheme that would double his savings in a year. At last the grandfather handed over his pension savings. Only later did the family discover the scheme was a fraud. He had been inveigled. Inveigle comes from a French word meaning to blind: an inveigler blinds you with sweet talk. So, what verb means to lure someone into something through deception?... Inveigle.
inveigle.example: With flattering letters and fake awards, a bogus publisher inveigled dozens of first-time poets in Khulna into paying for worthless print runs.

gre.s: Through a combination of flattery and false promises, the con artist managed to ____ several elderly investors into handing over their life savings.
gre.clue: Through a combination of flattery and false promises

lambaste.hook: LAMBASTE: LAMB gets BASTED (beaten) with harsh words.
lambaste.story: Lambaste. To criticise or scold someone fiercely. Nick's team handed in a project report full of copied paragraphs and careless errors. The next morning, their professor held it up before the whole class and lambasted them for twenty minutes: lazy research, sloppy writing, no respect for the reader. Nick's ears burned. He rewrote every page that week. Lambaste joins two old English verbs, lam and baste, both meaning to beat: to lambaste is to give someone a verbal beating. So, what verb means to scold someone fiercely?... Lambaste.
lambaste.example: Food bloggers lambasted the new restaurant on Gulshan Avenue for serving cold biryani at outrageous prices.

gre.s: Rather than praising the minister's long-delayed reforms, opposition leaders chose to ____ them as too little, too late, and a betrayal of earlier promises.
gre.clue: too little, too late, and a betrayal of earlier promises

lassitude.story: Lassitude. A heavy tiredness that drains body and mind of energy. During an April heatwave in the north, the temperature stayed above forty degrees for a week. Bella could barely lift her books. The ceiling fan only pushed hot air around, the streets were empty by noon, and even the stray dogs lay flat in the shade. A deep lassitude settled over the whole city. Lassitude comes from the Latin lassus, meaning weary; do not confuse it with latitude, which is about freedom or distance. So, what noun means a heavy, draining weariness?... Lassitude.
lassitude.example: Weeks of dengue fever left Rumana in a lassitude so deep that she could barely climb the stairs to her flat.

gre.s: The sweltering afternoon induced a general ____ among the delegates; several dozed in their seats, and no one had the energy to challenge the chairman's proposals.
gre.clue: no one had the energy to challenge the chairman's proposals

lionize.hook: LIONIZE: treated like the LION, king of the jungle.
lionize.story: Lionize. To treat someone as a celebrity and make a great public fuss over them. When a fisherman's daughter from a coastal island won a gold medal at an international mathematics contest, she flew home to a crowd at the airport. Television channels interviewed her, and her school named a classroom after her. She was lionized everywhere she went, though mostly she wanted to sleep. To lionize someone is to treat them like a lion, the most admired animal of all. So, what verb means to treat someone as a celebrity?... Lionize.
lionize.example: When the young mountaineer returned from Everest, newspapers lionized her and schools invited her to speak every week.

gre.s: Although the press rushed to ____ the scientist after her discovery, she found the constant attention exhausting and retreated from public life.
gre.clue: she found the constant attention exhausting

obstreperous.hook: OBSTREPEROUS: makes an OBSTACLE with noise.
obstreperous.story: Obstreperous. Noisy and hard to control. The night train to the coast was quiet until a group of young men boarded at a junction. They played music on loudspeakers, shouted across the carriage, and argued with the ticket checker who asked them to sit down. Children woke and cried. When the guard finally moved the obstreperous group to the last coach, the passengers breathed with relief. Obstreperous comes from a Latin verb meaning to roar against: an obstreperous crowd roars against all control. So, what word describes people who are noisy and unruly?... Obstreperous.
obstreperous.example: The flight attendants had to calm an obstreperous passenger who kept shouting about the delay and pounding the seat.

gre.s: The substitute teacher could not control the ____ students, who shouted over one another, ignored her instructions, and refused to stay in their seats.
gre.clue: shouted over one another, ignored her instructions

pellucid.hook: PELLUCID: like LUCID, light shines through.
pellucid.story: Pellucid. Perfectly clear; easy to understand. In her first statistics class, Tamara was terrified of probability. Then Professor Hayes walked in with a jar of red and white marbles. He drew them out one at a time, wrote each result on the board, and built the whole idea slowly from what everyone could see. By the end of the hour, Tamara understood it completely. His explanation was pellucid. Pellucid contains lucid, from the Latin for light: a pellucid explanation lets the light shine right through. So, what word describes an explanation so clear that anyone can follow it?... Pellucid.
pellucid.example: The physicist's pellucid lecture on black holes left even the history students in the audience nodding along.

gre.s: The textbook's ____ explanations, free of jargon and full of simple examples, made a notoriously difficult subject accessible to beginners.
gre.clue: free of jargon and full of simple examples

perspicacious.story: Perspicacious. Quick to notice and understand what others miss. Everyone at a small export company admired the polite new accountant. Only Sheila, the oldest clerk, noticed that his invoices always ended in round numbers and that he never took a holiday. She checked quietly and uncovered a scheme that had been draining money for a year. Her boss called her the most perspicacious person in the building. Perspicacious comes from a Latin verb meaning to see through: a perspicacious mind sees through appearances. So, what word describes someone sharp enough to notice what everyone else misses?... Perspicacious.
perspicacious.example: A perspicacious bank teller noticed that the signature on the cheque was slightly off and quietly called the manager.

gre.s: A ____ observer of political trends, she foresaw the government's collapse months before other analysts noticed even the first signs of trouble.
gre.clue: foresaw the government's collapse months before other analysts

prefigure.hook: PRE-FIGURE: a FIGURE of what's coming BEFORE it arrives.
prefigure.story: Prefigure. To be an early sign or picture of something that comes later. At eight, Tess took apart the family radio and rebuilt it, with one screw left over. Her grandfather saw something more. Twenty years later, Tess was leading a team that builds small satellites. That afternoon with the radio had prefigured her whole career. Pre means before, and a figure is a shape: to prefigure is to show the shape of something before it arrives. So, what verb means to be an early hint of what is to come?... Prefigure.
prefigure.example: The young cricketer's fearless innings in school matches prefigured the attacking style that later made him a national star.

gre.s: The architect's student sketches, with their sweeping curves and conspicuous absence of right angles, seem to ____ the radical designs that would later make her famous.
gre.clue: that would later make her famous

prevaricate.hook: PREVARICATE: PRE-VARY the truth, twist it.
prevaricate.story: Prevaricate. To speak evasively in order to avoid telling the truth. Ryan's mother asked him directly whether he had gone to his coaching class that afternoon. "Well, I was near the coaching centre," he said, "and I saw some friends, and the traffic was terrible, and the teacher often starts late anyway." She folded her arms. He was prevaricating, and they both knew it. Prevaricate comes from a Latin verb meaning to walk crookedly: a prevaricator walks around the truth instead of straight to it. So, what verb means to dodge the truth with evasive talk?... Prevaricate.
prevaricate.example: Asked by her mother where she had spent the afternoon, Tania prevaricated, mumbling something about a group study session.

gre.s: Pressed repeatedly about the missing funds, the treasurer continued to ____, offering vague answers that neither admitted nor denied any wrongdoing.
gre.clue: offering vague answers that neither admitted nor denied any wrongdoing

prolix.story: Prolix. Using far too many words; tediously long. At a wedding reception, the bride's uncle was asked to say a few words of blessing. He spoke for forty minutes. He began with his own childhood, quoted three poets and repeated every point twice, while the biryani grew cold on the tables. Nobody remembered a word of that prolix speech. Prolix comes from a Latin word meaning stretched out: a prolix speech stretches on far past its point. So, what word describes speech or writing that is wordy and tedious?... Prolix.
prolix.example: The ministry's prolix report ran to nine hundred pages, but its real findings could have fit on a single sheet.

gre.s: The editor urged the author to cut the manuscript in half, complaining that its ____ style buried every interesting idea under pages of needless detail.
gre.clue: buried every interesting idea under pages of needless detail

propitiate.story: Propitiate. To win or regain someone's favour by doing something to please them. Shawn forgot his wife's birthday. The next morning he came home from the bazaar with a big fish, a bunch of white tuberose flowers and a box of her favourite sweets. Then he cooked the fish himself, rather badly. She tried to stay angry but finally laughed. He had propitiated her. Propitiate is related to propitious, meaning favourable: to propitiate someone is to make them favourable to you again. So, what verb means to soothe someone's anger and win back their favour?... Propitiate.
propitiate.example: To propitiate his angry wife after forgetting their anniversary, Habib cooked her favorite hilsa curry and bought jasmine garlands.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the furious shareholders, the board announced a generous special dividend and promised to replace the chief executive whose blunders had cost them so much.
gre.clue: announced a generous special dividend

querulous.story: Querulous. Complaining in a whining, irritable way. Mister Chandler on the third floor complains about everything. The lift is too slow, the guard sleeps too much, the children downstairs are too loud, the mango seller cheats him, and even the rain falls at the wrong time. Each complaint comes in the same thin, peevish voice, and the building manager hides when he sees him coming. Mister Chandler is querulous. Querulous comes from a Latin verb meaning to complain, the same root that gives us quarrel. So, what word describes someone who constantly complains in a whiny voice?... Querulous.
querulous.example: The querulous passenger in the next seat complained about the food, the temperature and the movie throughout the long flight.

gre.s: Age had made the once-genial professor ____: he now found fault with every seminar, every meal, and every student, and his letters to the dean consisted largely of complaints.
gre.clue: his letters to the dean consisted largely of complaints

recondite.hook: RECONDITE: RE-CON-DITE, hidden like a secret condo deep in the hills.
recondite.story: Recondite. Known only to a few experts; obscure and hard to understand. At a university seminar, a visiting scholar spoke for two hours on the grammar of an ancient Buddhist text, in a language few people still read. Sami understood perhaps one sentence in ten. Yet the five specialists in the front row nodded eagerly, taking notes. The subject was recondite. Recondite comes from a Latin word meaning hidden away: recondite knowledge is tucked away where few can reach it. So, what word describes knowledge known only to a small circle of experts?... Recondite.
recondite.example: The old librarian could answer recondite questions about Mughal coinage that stumped even university professors.

gre.s: Although the treatise addresses ____ questions of medieval theology, its author writes so clearly that even general readers can follow it.
gre.clue: even general readers can follow it

somnolent.hook: SOMNOLENT: like inSOMNIA's opposite; full of sleep.
somnolent.story: Somnolent. Sleepy and drowsy; also, causing sleep. After a holiday lunch of spiced rice, creamy beef curry, chicken roast and three kinds of dessert, Sid's whole family drifted to the living room. The ceiling fan hummed, the curtains glowed in the afternoon light, and his grandfather's soft snoring set a slow rhythm. One by one, every cousin fell asleep on the floor. It was a somnolent afternoon. Somnolent comes from the Latin somnus, meaning sleep, the same root as insomnia. So, what word describes a drowsy, sleepy mood?... Somnolent.
somnolent.example: On a hot afternoon the somnolent village seemed deserted, with only a few goats wandering past the closed shops.

gre.s: The ____ atmosphere of the warm lecture hall, combined with the speaker's monotone, left half the audience struggling to stay awake.
gre.clue: left half the audience struggling to stay awake

supplicate.hook: SUPPLICATE: on your knees, SUPPLYING prayers.
supplicate.story: Supplicate. To plead humbly and earnestly for something. When the great river swallowed his family's land, an old farmer named Joe travelled to the district office. He waited on a bench all day. When the officer finally called him in, Joe folded his hands and begged for a small plot on the new embankment, enough for a house and a few chickens. He supplicated without pride, for his grandchildren. Supplicate comes from a Latin verb meaning to bend down and plead: a supplicant bends low and begs. So, what verb means to beg humbly and earnestly?... Supplicate.
supplicate.example: Standing before the visa officer, the elderly man could only supplicate for permission to attend his son's graduation abroad.

gre.s: Defeated and desperate, the rebel leaders could only ____ the emperor, kneeling humbly before the very throne they had once vowed to destroy.
gre.clue: kneeling humbly before the very throne

vitiate.hook: VITIATE: makes it VICIOUS, corrupts it.
vitiate.story: Vitiate. To spoil or weaken something so that it no longer works properly. For six months, Isabel's team grew rice seedlings in a university greenhouse to test a new fertiliser. Then they discovered that a helper had been watering the untreated trays from the wrong tank, one already mixed with fertiliser. That one mistake vitiated the entire experiment, and the data could not be trusted. Vitiate comes from the Latin vitium, meaning fault or vice: a single fault can vitiate a whole result. So, what verb means to spoil something by introducing a flaw?... Vitiate.
vitiate.example: A missing signature on the final page vitiated the entire land contract, and the sale had to begin again.

gre.s: A single undisclosed conflict of interest can ____ an otherwise rigorous study, rendering its conclusions suspect.
gre.clue: rendering its conclusions suspect

antedate.story: Antedate. To come before something in time; to precede. At an ancient dig site in the delta, archaeologists have dug up coins, beads and the walls of a fortified town well over two thousand years old. Standing beside the trench with her university group, Fran touched a row of ancient bricks. These ruins antedate the Mughal capital nearby by many centuries. Ante means before, as in antenatal care, the care given before birth; do not confuse it with anti, which means against. So, what verb means to come earlier in time than something else?... Antedate.
antedate.example: The ancient ruins at Mahasthangarh antedate the Mughal mosques of Dhaka by well over a thousand years.

gre.s: Recent excavations suggest that farming in the valley may ____ the arrival of the first nomadic herders by several thousand years.
gre.clue: the arrival of the first nomadic herders by several thousand years

aspersion.hook: ASPERSION: SPRINKLING dirt on someone's name.
aspersion.story: Aspersion. A damaging remark that attacks someone's reputation. When Rhea's mother stood for a women's seat in the village council election, leaflets appeared on every tea stall in the village. They hinted that she had misused flood relief money, without a single fact. Neighbours began to look at her differently. She answered by pinning the full relief accounts beside every leaflet. Aspersion comes from a Latin verb meaning to sprinkle: to cast aspersions is to sprinkle dirt on someone's good name. So, what noun means a remark that attacks someone's reputation?... Aspersion.
aspersion.example: The coach refused to cast aspersions on the referee, saying only that his team had simply played badly.

gre.s: Unable to fault the research itself, her rivals resorted to an anonymous ____ on her character, hinting at plagiarism they could never prove.
gre.clue: hinting at plagiarism they could never prove

captious.hook: CAPTIOUS: tries to CAPTURE you in tiny errors.
captious.story: Captious. Quick to find fault over tiny, unimportant things. Miles's new flatmate complained about everything. The rice had too much water, the towel was folded the wrong way, the fan was half a speed too fast, and Miles's alarm rang one minute too early. No detail was too small. After a month, Miles started looking for a new flat. Captious comes from a Latin word for catching or seizing: a captious person tries to catch you out on every trifle. So, what word describes someone who nitpicks over trivial faults?... Captious.
captious.example: Our captious neighbor complained to the building committee that the children's chalk drawings spoiled the look of the courtyard.

gre.s: Reviewers dismissed the critic's essay as merely ____: instead of engaging with the book's central argument, he spent ten pages complaining about misplaced commas.
gre.clue: complaining about misplaced commas

clangor.story: Clangor. A loud, harsh, continuous clanging noise. Next to Toby's flat in the old city is a row of metal workshops. From early morning until late evening, hammers strike iron sheets, grinders scream, and steel pipes crash onto concrete. The clangor rattles his windows and follows him into his dreams. When he finally moved to a quiet street, he could not sleep for the silence. Clangor grows from clang: imagine the clang, clang, clang of a whole street of hammers. So, what noun means a loud, continuous clanging noise?... Clangor.
clangor.example: The clangor of pots and steel ladles from the restaurant kitchen next door woke Shimul every morning at five.

gre.s: The ____ of the shipyard, where hammers rang against steel day and night, made conversation nearly impossible for nearby residents.
gre.clue: where hammers rang against steel day and night

cogitate.hook: COGITATE: 'Cogito, ergo sum' — I think, therefore I am.
cogitate.story: Cogitate. To think deeply and carefully about something. In the final of a district chess tournament, twelve-year-old Mia stared at the board for twenty minutes without touching a piece. Her opponent fidgeted, the spectators whispered, and the clock ticked loudly. Mia kept cogitating, her chin in her hands. Then she moved a single pawn, and three moves later she won. Cogitate is the verb behind the famous Latin line of Descartes, cogito, ergo sum: I think, therefore I am. So, what verb means to think something over deeply?... Cogitate.
cogitate.example: The chess prodigy cogitated over a single move for twenty minutes while the hall waited in complete silence.

gre.s: Rather than react impulsively to the offer, the cautious investor preferred to ____ for several days, weighing every possible risk before making a decision.
gre.clue: weighing every possible risk before making a decision

desiccate.hook: DESICCATE: think DESERT — dry. Also desiccated coconut, the dried kind.
desiccate.story: Desiccate. To remove all moisture; to dry something out completely. On the southern beach, Jamie's family spreads thousands of small fish on bamboo racks under the winter sun. For days, the sea wind and sunlight draw the water out, until the fish are hard, stiff and light as paper. That is how dried fish is made: the fish are desiccated so they last for months. Desiccate comes from the Latin siccus, meaning dry, which also gives us desiccated coconut, the dried kind used in sweets. So, what verb means to dry something out completely?... Desiccate.
desiccate.example: Fishermen near Kuakata spread their catch on bamboo racks so that the sun and sea breeze can desiccate it into shutki.

gre.s: Archaeologists can study the ancient fruit only because the desert air tends to ____ organic material so thoroughly that it never decays.
gre.clue: the desert air

discomfit.story: Discomfit. To make someone feel awkward and thrown off balance. Susie had rehearsed her thesis defence for weeks. Then the external examiner leaned forward and asked, in a mild voice, why her survey of four hundred farmers included no women. Susie opened her mouth, closed it, and felt her face go hot. The question had discomfited her completely. Discomfit once meant to defeat an army; today it means to throw a person off balance, and it sounds close to discomfort, which is exactly how it feels. So, what verb means to unsettle someone and make them uneasy?... Discomfit.
discomfit.example: The examiner's long silence after her answer discomfited Priya more than any difficult question could have.

gre.s: The seasoned politician usually remained composed under fire, yet the student's pointed question about his voting record seemed to ____ him, and he stammered through his reply.
gre.clue: he stammered through his reply

distend.story: Distend. To swell outward because of pressure from inside. On the morning of a village fair, Randy blew up balloons for his little sister's stall. He kept filling one red balloon, breath after breath, until its skin stretched thin and almost see-through. It burst with a bang that scattered the chickens. A distended balloon has only so much stretch. Dis means apart, and tend means stretch, as in extend: to distend is to stretch out from within. So, what verb means to swell from internal pressure?... Distend.
distend.example: Malnourished children often have distended bellies, a symptom that doctors in rural clinics are trained to recognize quickly.

gre.s: After swallowing its prey whole, the python's body began to ____ visibly, its skin stretching to accommodate an animal nearly twice its own width.
gre.clue: its skin stretching to accommodate

enervate.hook: TRAP: ENERVATE looks like ENERGIZE but means the opposite: it takes the NERVE out.
enervate.story: Enervate. To drain someone's energy and leave them weak. During a May heatwave, the power in Ruben's neighbourhood went out at noon and did not return until midnight. No fan, no light, no cold water. Ruben lay on the floor beside an open window, too limp to read or even talk. The heat had enervated him completely. Watch out: enervate sounds like energize but means the opposite; it comes from the Latin for cutting out the sinews, the cords of strength. So, what verb means to sap someone's energy?... Enervate.
enervate.example: Months of night shifts at the call center enervated Tareq so badly that he fell asleep on the bus every afternoon.

gre.s: Far from invigorating the patients, the experimental drug seemed to ____ them, leaving most too weak to leave their beds.
gre.clue: leaving most too weak to leave their beds

expatiate.hook: EX-PATIATE: wander out (spatiari) in long speech.
expatiate.story: Expatiate. To speak or write at great length about something. Ask Uncle Kirk a simple question about mangoes, and he will expatiate for an hour. He will explain the difference between two famous mango varieties, the soil of the northern orchards, the right week to pick each variety, and how his own father once grafted a tree. His nieces now ask only when they have a free afternoon. Expatiate comes from a Latin verb meaning to wander far and wide, just as he wanders far beyond the question. So, what verb means to speak at length on a subject?... Expatiate.
expatiate.example: At every family dinner, my uncle expatiates on the glory days of Abahani football until the dessert has gone cold.

gre.s: Given just five minutes at the conference, the speaker could not ____ on her research as she had hoped, and offered only a brief summary of her findings.
gre.clue: offered only a brief summary of her findings

extemporize.hook: EX-TEMPOR-IZE: OUT of the moment (tempus = time).
extemporize.story: Extemporize. To make something up on the spot, without preparation. Halfway through Nadine's talk at a city conference, the power failed and the projector went black. Nadine took a breath, stepped away from the podium, and simply told the story of her research, drawing her main graph in the air with her hands. She had extemporized brilliantly. Ex tempore is Latin for out of the moment: to extemporize is to create in the moment. So, what verb means to improvise without rehearsal?... Extemporize.
extemporize.example: When the projector failed, the young engineer extemporized a lively talk using only a whiteboard and a marker.

gre.s: When the actor forgot his lines on opening night, he was forced to ____, inventing dialogue so convincingly that the audience never suspected anything had gone wrong.
gre.clue: inventing dialogue so convincingly

forebode.hook: FORE-BODE: BODING ill BEFORE it happens.
forebode.story: Forebode. To be a warning that something bad is coming. Early one evening on a coastal island, the sky turned a strange copper colour and the wind fell completely still. Old Mike, who had fished these waters for fifty years, pulled his boat far up the sand and moved his family to the cyclone shelter. Such stillness, he said, forebodes a storm. That night, the cyclone arrived. Fore means before, and to bode is to signal: to forebode is to signal trouble before it comes. So, what verb means to give warning of coming harm?... Forebode.
forebode.example: The empty shelves and unpaid staff seemed to forebode the closure of the old bookshop on Nilkhet Road.

gre.s: The dark clouds massing over the hills seemed to ____ disaster, and the villagers, fearing a flood, began moving their livestock to higher ground.
gre.clue: fearing a flood

immure.story: Immure. To shut someone away within walls; to confine. In the last month before her medical licensing exam, Rachel immured herself in a small room on the roof of her uncle's house. She left only for meals, kept the curtains drawn, and saw nothing but books and bare walls for thirty days. When she finally walked out into the sunlight, her cousins barely recognised her. Immure comes from the Latin murus, meaning wall, as in mural: to immure is to wall someone in. So, what verb means to confine someone within walls?... Immure.
immure.example: During the final weeks before her exams, Laila immured herself in her bedroom, emerging only for meals.

gre.s: Rather than mingling with other scholars, the reclusive historian chose to ____ himself in the archive for months at a time.
gre.clue: Rather than mingling with other scholars

infelicity.hook: IN-FELICITY: NOT FELICITOUS, not well chosen.
infelicity.story: Infelicity. An unfortunate, badly chosen word or action; also, unhappiness. At his cousin's wedding, Frank gave a toast praising the groom's loyalty, then added, "He was loyal to his last girlfriend for five whole years too." The room froze. The bride's smile stiffened. Frank meant it kindly, but it was a painful infelicity, and he apologised all evening. Infelicity is the opposite of felicity, happiness: a felicitous phrase fits perfectly, while an infelicity lands badly. So, what noun means a badly chosen remark that does not fit the moment?... Infelicity.
infelicity.example: The speechwriter caught an unfortunate infelicity in the draft, where a tribute to flood victims had been called a celebration.

gre.s: The translation is generally elegant, yet one glaring ____ mars the final chapter: a solemn funeral oration rendered in breezy, comic slang.
gre.clue: a solemn funeral oration rendered in breezy, comic slang

irresolute.story: Irresolute. Unable to decide; hesitant and indecisive. At a famous sweet shop, Bobby stood before the glass case for fifteen minutes. Syrup balls or cheese balls? Sticky sweets or milk fudge? Each time he pointed, he changed his mind, and the queue behind him grew longer. The shopkeeper finally packed a little of everything into one box. Bobby was cheerful but hopelessly irresolute. Resolute means firm and determined, from resolve, so irresolute means lacking resolve. So, what word describes someone who cannot make up their mind?... Irresolute.
irresolute.example: Standing irresolute at the crossroads, the hiker studied his map for ten minutes before choosing the mountain path.

gre.s: The ____ committee debated the proposal for months without reaching a decision, while the problem it was meant to solve grew worse.
gre.clue: debated the proposal for months without reaching a decision

jocund.story: Jocund. Cheerful and light-hearted. On the spring New Year morning, the city's streets fill with people dressed in red and white. Children wear painted tigers on their cheeks, drummers lead the procession from the Fine Arts Institute, and families eat soaked rice and fried fish under the trees of the park. Strangers smile at strangers. Even the traffic police are humming. It is the most jocund morning of the year. Jocund sounds like jocular and joke, and it shares their cheerful spirit. So, what word describes a cheerful, merry mood?... Jocund.
jocund.example: The jocund boatmen sang and joked as they rowed the wedding party across the river to the bride's village.
